**D) As long as nobody objects, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.**

As long as + present + can correctly sets a real group condition. Objects is present; can move is present capability under that proviso.

**Tip:** ** As long as supports present modal results as well as will.
**E) Unless anyone will complain, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.**

** No will after unless in standard condition clauses.

Trap: unless + will is wrong; use Unless anyone complains… Will does not belong in the unless-clause.
highlights: If it had not been for
tasks.solution_overview:
Flat tyre camping plans and a Thursday rehearsal — If it had not been for / But for, weren't for versus hadn't been for, and no will after unless.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If it had not been for + would + V1 mixes past obstacle with present/future-facing result. But for + noun is a compact equivalent. Keep If it weren't for (present) distinct from If it hadn't been for (past). As long as + present can support can; unless must not take will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept had not been for / But for when the tyre story lands on tonight. Reject was not for + would have as non-standard here. Strip will from unless anyone will complain.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have more free evenings.
I wish I had more free evenings.
If only the train hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
If the coach hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
Supposing the café closed early, where would we study?
tactical_explanations:
**A) I wish I would have more free evenings.**

** Present state wish → I wish I had…, not would have.

Trap: wish + would have is wrong for a present lack; use wish + past simple (had). Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes about states.
**B) I wish I had more free evenings.**

Wish + past simple correctly expresses an unreal present desire about free time. Had is the backshift from present have.
**C) If only the train hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.**

If only + past perfect cause with wouldn't be now is a valid mixed regret linking past delay to present queue. The delay is finished; the queue is happening.

**Tip:** ** Past perfect after if only can feed a present would/wouldn't result.
**D) If the coach hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.**

Same mixed pattern with ordinary if instead of if only. Past unreal cause → present continuous-looking result with wouldn't + be + -ing.

**Tip:** ** If / if only both allow this past→present mix when times match.
**E) Supposing the café closed early, where would we study?**

Supposing + past simple introduces a second-conditional hypothesis with would in the question. Closed + would we study is the tentative-scenario frame.

**Tip:** ** Supposing / suppose ≈ if for tentative scenarios.
tasks.solution_overview:
Free evenings, delayed coaches, and a café that might close — killing wish I would have, keeping mixed past→present, and welcoming supposing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes; use wish + past simple (had). If only / if + past perfect can feed a present would/wouldn't be … now result. Supposing + past introduces second-conditional hypotheses with would in the question.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For present state wishes, choose had over would have. Accept mixed delay→queue lines with if or if only. Treat supposing like if + past for tentative scenarios.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.
Even if the tickets were free, we will still stay home.
Whether or not it rains, the charity run will start at nine.
If so be the weather improves, we will hike.
If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.**

Even if + present + will correctly means the result holds despite the condition. Expense does not block the festival plan.

**Tip:** ** Even if ≠ if; the main clause can still use real-future will.
**B) Even if the tickets were free, we will still stay home.**

** Were in the even if-clause → would in the result.

Trap: even if + past (were) wants would stay, not will stay. Match even if tense to the result: past → would; present → will.
**C) Whether or not it rains, the charity run will start at nine.**

Whether or not + present + will correctly says the run happens regardless of rain. The start time is fixed either way.

**Tip:** ** Whether or not = no matter if.
**D) If so be the weather improves, we will hike.**

** Prefer plain if + present in modern exam English.

Trap: if so be is archaic and not exam-standard; use If the weather improves… Stick to standard if + present for real futures.
**E) If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.**

If need be is an accepted fixed phrase meaning if it is necessary, here with can. Do not "correct" it to if needs be in formal keys.

**Tip:** ** If need be is a set idiom — leave it.
highlights: Even if the tickets were, we will
tasks.solution_overview:
Festival tickets, a charity run, weather, and taxis — even if, whether or not, and fixed if need be, while rejecting tense clashes and archaic if so be.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Even if + present + will means the result holds despite the condition; even if + past wants would, not will. Whether or not + present + will says the plan happens regardless. If so be is archaic; if need be is an accepted idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match even if tense to the result mood. Accept whether or not for rain-proof plans. Prefer standard If the weather improves… over if so be, and leave if need be alone as a set phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she were to apply for the scholarship, she would need two references.
If she was to have applied last term, she would need two references now.
Were he to practise daily, his serve would improve within weeks.
If I knew then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If she were to apply for the scholarship, she would need two references.**

If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional way to mark a hypothetical future step. Were to + V1 softens the plan into something remote or tentative.
**B) If she was to have applied last term, she would need two references now.**

** Keep formal keys on clear were to / had + V3 patterns.

Trap: was to have applied mixed with would need now is over-stacked and non-standard for this item. Prefer clear mixed or third forms; avoid was to have + mismatched results.
**C) Were he to practise daily, his serve would improve within weeks.**

Were he to practise… correctly inverts were to for a hypothetical training plan. Same meaning as If he were to practise…

**Tip:** ** Were + subject + to + V1 replaces If + subject + were to.
**D) If I knew then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.**

** Then + past ignorance → had known, not knew.

Trap: knew then is underpowered for a clear past knowledge gap; the standard line uses had known then. Past counterfactual knowledge → past perfect in the if-clause.
**E) If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.**

Classic form: past perfect for past ignorance, would have chosen for the past decision. This is the polished exam hindsight pattern.

**Tip:** ** Had known then… would have + V3 is the safe form.
tasks.solution_overview:
Scholarships, serving practice, and module choices — advanced were to / Were … to inversion and the polished had known then pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional hypothetical. Were he to practise… inverts the same idea. Was to have applied stacked with a mismatched result is overcomplicated. Past counterfactual knowledge wants had known then, not underpowered knew then.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept were to / Were … to for formal unlikely steps. Prefer clear mixed or third forms over was to have stacks. Choose If I had known then… would have chosen… for hindsight module regrets.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'd rather you didn't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
I'd rather you don't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
It's time we left for the airport.
It's time we leave for the airport.
Suppose you won free concert tickets — what would you do?
tactical_explanations:
**A) I'd rather you didn't stream loud videos while I'm revising.**

Would rather + past simple correctly softens a present preference about someone else's behaviour. Didn't stream is the polite backshift, not a past-time narrative.
**B) I'd rather you don't stream loud videos while I'm revising.**

** I'd rather you didn't…, not don't.

Trap: after I'd rather you, use past simple, not present don't. Same backshift habit as wish — prefer past after I'd rather you.
**C) It's time we left for the airport.**

It's time + past simple is the standard formal pattern for present urgency. Left means we should leave now, not that we already departed.
**D) It's time we leave for the airport.**

** Prefer past after it's time in formal true/false items.

Trap: careful exam keys usually want It's time we left, not leave. It's time + past is the marked formal choice.
**E) Suppose you won free concert tickets — what would you do?**

Suppose + past + would correctly frames a second-conditional daydream. Won + would you do matches if + past + would.

**Tip:** ** Suppose / supposing pattern like if + past.
tasks.solution_overview:
Loud videos, airport departures, and free concert tickets — extending conditional logic into I'd rather you, it's time + past, and suppose.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

I'd rather you + past softens a present preference about someone else's behaviour. It's time + past marks present urgency in careful exam English. Suppose + past + would frames a second-conditional daydream. These share the same backshift instinct as wish and second conditionals.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject I'd rather you don't… and It's time we leave… in favour of past forms. Accept Suppose you won… what would you do? as if + past with would.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the inflation rate drops, household budgets will feel less pressure next quarter.
Had the storm not hit, the outdoor market would still be open this afternoon.
If only I could have attended the reunion last month.
I wish I could have attended the reunion last month.
Unless having finished the essay, she will not join us.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the inflation rate drops, household budgets will feel less pressure next quarter.**

First conditional with a real possible macro change and a future lifestyle effect. Drops is present; will feel is open future.
**B) Had the storm not hit, the outdoor market would still be open this afternoon.**

Mixed: past unreal storm (Had … not hit) with present result (would still be open). Negative inversion can feed a present would result when this afternoon is the effect time.
**C) If only I could have attended the reunion last month.**

If only + could have + V3 correctly regrets a missed past ability or opportunity. Last month locks the regret in closed past.
**D) I wish I could have attended the reunion last month.**

Wish + could have + V3 matches the same past missed opportunity. Wish and if only parallel here for past ability regrets.
**E) Unless having finished the essay, she will not join us.**

** Unless + subject + verb; no bare -ing clause.

Trap: unless needs a finite clause (Unless she has finished…), not Unless having finished… Avoid a dangling -ing after unless.
tasks.solution_overview:
Household budgets, a storm-hit market, a missed reunion, and a dangling unless -ing — advanced first, mixed inversion, and could have regrets.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A light economy first conditional stays present + will. Had … not hit can feed a present would still be… result. Wish / if only + could have + V3 regrets missed past ability. Unless needs a finite clause — not Unless having finished…

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept real-future inflation → budget relief. Accept negative Had-inversion into a present market result. Parallel if only / wish + could have for last month. Rebuild unless with subject + finite verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It's high time we booked the campsite.
If you come to the hike, bring a reusable bottle.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather holds.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather will hold.
No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm would go off.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It's high time we booked the campsite.**

It's high time + past simple correctly marks present urgency with the same backshift as wish / it's time. Booked means we should book now.
**B) If you come to the hike, bring a reusable bottle.**

Clear first-conditional imperative result: if + present, imperative bring… Instructions work fine as first-conditional results.
**C) I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather holds.**

Provided + present (holds) correctly sets a real weather condition for a future plan with will come. Holds stays present in the proviso.
**D) I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather will hold.**

** Strip will from provided clauses.

Trap: provided the weather will hold wrongly inserts will into the condition. Same rule as if / as long as: no will in the proviso clause.
**E) No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm would go off.**

** No sooner… than + past simple — leave would out.

Trap: no sooner… than needs a simple past result (went off), not conditional would go off. No sooner is past sequencing, not a conditional frame.
highlights: If you come to the hike, bring
tasks.solution_overview:
Campsite booking, hike bottles, Sunday cycling, and a fire alarm — it's high time, imperative first conditionals, provided + present, and a no sooner false friend.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

It's high time + past marks present urgency. First conditionals may use an imperative result (bring…). Provided takes present, not will. No sooner… than is past sequencing with simple past (went off), not conditional would go off.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept booked / bring / holds as clean backshift, imperative, and proviso patterns. Reject will after provided. Do not force would onto a no sooner narrative.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of overdue library books has risen since March.
A number of neighbours was unable to join the street clean-up.
Neither the coach nor the players were copied on the match email.
Each of the flatmates have filed a chore preference form.
There are several typos in the potluck recipe list.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of overdue library books has risen since March.**

The head of this sentence is "the number," which names one count of overdue books, not the books themselves. Singular subjects take singular verbs, so "has risen" is the right match. Mentally swapping in "that total has risen" makes the agreement feel natural.
**B) A number of neighbours was unable to join the street clean-up.**

"A number of neighbours" means several neighbours, so the verb must be plural — rewrite as "were unable," not "was." The article switch from the to a flips the meaning from one total to many people. Do not let the singular word "number" fool you here.
**C) Neither the coach nor the players were copied on the match email.**

With neither…nor, agreement follows the nearer subject — the one sitting just before the verb. Here that noun is plural "players," so "were copied" is correct. Ignore "coach" when you choose the verb; proximity, not the first noun, decides.
**D) Each of the flatmates have filed a chore preference form.**

**E) There are several typos in the potluck recipe list.**

The delayed subject after "there" is plural "typos," so "there are" agrees correctly. In there-constructions the real subject follows the verb — match that noun's number, not a fake dummy subject. Here several typos make the plural verb unavoidable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of unresolved tickets are alarming the helpdesk.
Neither the sponsor nor the team captains was invited to the closed meeting.
There seems to be several inconsistencies between the two diaries.
The managing editor, as well as the reporters, have approved the feature.
A number of clauses in the lease survive completion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of unresolved tickets are alarming the helpdesk.**

** The number of → singular, any tense.

Trap: "The number of unresolved tickets" needs singular "is alarming," not "are alarming." Continuous/progressive forms still follow the head subject's number. Helpdesk drama does not pluralise "number."
**B) Neither the sponsor nor the team captains was invited to the closed meeting.**

** Plural nearer noun → were/are.

Trap: nearer plural "team captains" needs "were invited," not "was invited." Long second nouns after nor are still plural when marked -s. Closed-meeting detail is irrelevant.
**C) There seems to be several inconsistencies between the two diaries.**

** There seem to be + plural noun.

Trap: prefer "there seem to be several inconsistencies" to match the plural complement. Seem/appear after there must still track the real subject's number in careful usage. Two diaries make the plural clear.
**D) The managing editor, as well as the reporters, have approved the feature.**

** As well as = insert, not and.

Trap: singular managing editor plus as well as the reporters needs "has approved," not "have approved." Reporters after as well as are not co-subjects. Feature approval is the object only.
**E) A number of clauses in the lease survive completion.**

"A number of clauses" correctly takes plural "survive." Present simple plural has no -s: survive, not survives. Completion timing does not change agreement.
tasks.solution_overview:
Helpdesk alarms, closed meetings, diary mismatches, a feature approval, and lease clauses: four failures and one clean "a number of" success. Soft connectors are designed to hide plural complements.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The number of with a wrong plural progressive, neither…nor with was, there seems to be several, as well as with a plural verb, and a correct plural survive after a number of. At this level, seems/appears after there must still track what follows.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Always check the complement after seems/appears to be. Progressive and perfect forms still follow the head subject's number. Present simple plurals after a number of take no -s on the verb (survive, not survives).

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the shop nor its branches is bound by the Sunday rule.
Every one of the contingent prizes has been disclosed in the notes.
There remain, after the rethink, three material open points.
The coach, together with the squad captains, was accountable for the overspend.
The data released this morning confirm the earlier forecast.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the shop nor its branches is bound by the Sunday rule.**

** Its branches are still plural.

Trap: nearer plural "branches" needs "are bound," not "is bound." Possessives ("its") before the nearer noun do not singularise it. Sunday-rule content is irrelevant to number.
**B) Every one of the contingent prizes has been disclosed in the notes.**

"Every one of the contingent prizes" correctly takes singular "has been disclosed." Passive perfect still keeps singular agreement with every one. Notes disclosure does not pluralise the subject.
**C) There remain, after the rethink, three material open points.**

Plural "three material open points" correctly takes "remain," even with a mid-sentence insert. Ignore the comma aside ("after the rethink") and match the postponed plural subject. Rethink wording is padding only.
**D) The coach, together with the squad captains, was accountable for the overspend.**

Singular coach correctly takes "was accountable" despite together with the squad captains. Together with never creates a plural subject. Overspend accountability stays with the coach grammatically.
**E) The data released this morning confirm the earlier forecast.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "confirm." Time adjuncts ("this morning") are irrelevant to number. Earlier forecast is the object, not the subject.
tasks.solution_overview:
Sunday trading rules, prize disclosures, rethink asides, squad accountability, and morning data raise difficulty with inserts and passives — the agreement rules themselves stay fixed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neither…nor with a false singular, every one of in the passive, there remain with a mid-sentence aside, together with, and formal plural data. Comma asides between there and the subject change nothing. Possessives before a nearer plural noun do not singularise it.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find the subject first; the verb will usually announce itself. Ignore padding between there and the postponed subject, and keep every one singular even in passive perfect.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of practice drills was revised after the club meeting.
Neither the tutor nor the students' mentors has objected to the timetable.
There is, contrary to the notice, several unpaid bills still on the fridge.
Each branch that operates abroad file a local safety certificate.
The number of noise complaints has stabilised since the quiet hours.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A number of practice drills was revised after the club meeting.**

** A number of + plural NP → plural verb.

Trap: "A number of practice drills" needs "were revised," not "was revised." Long plural noun phrases after a number of still take plural verbs. Club-meeting timing does not singularise the drills.
**B) Neither the tutor nor the students' mentors has objected to the timetable.**

** Possessive before a plural nearer noun ≠ singular.

Trap: nearer plural "mentors" needs "have objected," not "has objected." "Students'" only marks possession; mentors remain plural. Timetable objections do not change number.
**C) There is, contrary to the notice, several unpaid bills still on the fridge.**

** Delete the aside; match the plural noun.

Trap: plural "bills" needs "there are," despite the interrupting phrase. Cross out the contrary-to aside before choosing is/are. Unpaid bills on the fridge stay plural.
**D) Each branch that operates abroad file a local safety certificate.**

** Each + relative clause → still singular verb.

Trap: "Each branch" needs singular "files," not "file." Relative clauses after each ("that operates abroad") do not licence a plural verb. Local certificates are the object only.
**E) The number of noise complaints has stabilised since the quiet hours.**

"The number of noise complaints" correctly takes singular "has stabilised." Keep contrasting the number (singular) with a number (plural). Quiet hours describe the time frame, not the subject's number.
tasks.solution_overview:
Club drills, tutor mentors, fridge bills, overseas branches, and noise complaints use interruptions and relative clauses as noise. Mentally delete them, then apply the familiar tests.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A number of, neither…nor, there is with a contrary-to aside, each with a relative clause, and a clean the-number-of singular. Relative clauses after each do not licence a plural verb. Asides after there still leave the delayed subject's number in charge.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cross out interrupting phrases and relative clauses, then re-run a number / the number, proximity, there is/are, and each. Keep contrasting the number (singular) with a number (plural) on the last clean line.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the parent club nor the satellite teams was named in the report.
The box office, along with the front-of-house stewards, approve large group bookings.
There appear to be a single bottleneck in the check-in workflow.
Every set of rehearsal notes for the cast is reviewed by the director.
The data on which the ranking rests are drawn from audited scores.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the parent club nor the satellite teams was named in the report.**

** Satellite teams are still plural after nor.

Trap: nearer plural "teams" needs "were named," not "was named." Extra adjectives before the nearer noun do not change its plural number. Report content is irrelevant to agreement.
**B) The box office, along with the front-of-house stewards, approve large group bookings.**

** Institutional singular + along with → singular verb.

Trap: singular "box office" plus along with stewards needs "approves," not "approve." Box office is a singular institutional subject here. Front-of-house stewards stay in the insert.
**C) There appear to be a single bottleneck in the check-in workflow.**

** There appears to be + singular noun.

Trap: the complement "a single bottleneck" is singular, so write "there appears to be," not "there appear to be." Appear/seem after there must track a singular complement too — not only plurals. One bottleneck, singular verb.
**D) Every set of rehearsal notes for the cast is reviewed by the director.**

"Every set" is singular, so "is reviewed" is right. "Set of notes" is one unit; every keeps it singular. Director review is the passive agent, not the subject.
**E) The data on which the ranking rests are drawn from audited scores.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "are drawn," even inside a which-clause sandwich. Relative clauses around data do not convert it to singular on formal papers. Audited scores are the source, not a singulariser.
highlights: There appear to be a single
tasks.solution_overview:
Top-band reverse traps: satellite teams, a box-office institution, a single bottleneck after appear, rehearsal-note sets, and audited ranking data. Read for the actual head noun, not the surrounding formality.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neither…nor with a false singular, along with on an institutional singular, there appear with a singular complement (the reverse of the usual plural trap), every set, and formal plural data inside a which-clause sandwich. Appear/seem after there must track singular complements too — not only plurals.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the head: teams, box office, bottleneck, set, data. Institutional singulars like "box office" stay singular despite human stewards in an along-with insert. "Every set of notes" is one unit.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the organiser nor the registered helpers have accepted the revised timetable.
The general editor, together with outside advisers, has cleared the disclosure.
There remain, for the avoidance of doubt, two rules still in force.
Each of the house agreements provides for stepped fines.
The data furnished by the target school support a higher ranking.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the organiser nor the registered helpers have accepted the revised timetable.**

Nearer plural "helpers" correctly takes "have accepted." Long nearer nouns after nor still obey proximity. Revised-timetable content does not affect number.
**B) The general editor, together with outside advisers, has cleared the disclosure.**

Singular general editor governs "has cleared" despite together with outside advisers. Together with outside advisers is parenthetical only. Disclosure clearance stays with the editor grammatically.
**C) There remain, for the avoidance of doubt, two rules still in force.**

Plural "two rules" correctly takes "remain" despite the formal aside. Padding between there and the subject changes nothing. Avoidance-of-doubt wording is decorative.
**D) Each of the house agreements provides for stepped fines.**

"Each of the house agreements" takes singular "provides." Agreements in the of-phrase stay out of the verb slot. Stepped fines are the object of the preposition, not the subject.
**E) The data furnished by the target school support a higher ranking.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "support." Past participles like "furnished" do not singularise data. Higher ranking is the claim, not the subject.

**Tip:** ** Furnished data still take a plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
Five correct formal-register models: timetable acceptance, disclosure clearance, rules still in force, stepped fines, and school ranking data. Internalise how inserts still leave a single grammatical subject in charge.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neither…nor with a plural nearer noun, together with, there remain with legalistic padding, each of, and formal plural data with a past participle. Dual adviser references and "for the avoidance of doubt" asides look heavy but change nothing about number.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm proximity, strip together-with inserts, ignore padding between there and the subject, keep each singular, and keep data plural. These lines are what correct formal agreement looks like under exam conditions.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of material safety clauses was triggered overnight.
Neither the organiser nor the other stewards in the group was prepared to waive the rule.
There is, when one examines the schedules carefully, more than two conflicting dates.
The lead reviewer, as well as the marking team, were responsible for the opinion.
The data that the model relies on have been restated twice this year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A number of material safety clauses was triggered overnight.**

** A number of + plural noun → were.

Trap: "A number of material safety clauses" needs "were triggered," not "was triggered." Dense noun phrases still follow the a-number-of plural rule. Overnight timing does not singularise the clauses.
**B) Neither the organiser nor the other stewards in the group was prepared to waive the rule.**

** Modifiers after the nearer noun change nothing.

Trap: nearer plural "stewards" needs "were prepared," not "was prepared." Extra modifiers after the nearer noun ("in the group") do not make it singular. Waiving the rule is content only.
**C) There is, when one examines the schedules carefully, more than two conflicting dates.**

** More than two after there → there are.

Trap: "More than two conflicting dates" is plural, so write "there are," not "there is." Quantity phrases greater than one take plural after there. The long when-clause is only an interruption.
**D) The lead reviewer, as well as the marking team, were responsible for the opinion.**

** As well as leaves the head singular.

Trap: singular lead reviewer plus as well as the marking team needs "was responsible," not "were responsible." Marking team after as well as is not a co-subject. Opinion content does not affect number.
**E) The data that the model relies on have been restated twice this year.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "have been restated." Prefer plural agreement with data on formal exams unless the paper allows informal singular data. The model-relies-on clause does not singularise data.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four agreement failures surround one clean formal-data line: overnight safety clauses, steward waivers, conflicting dates, a reviewer's opinion, and restated model data. Strip inserts before you judge.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A number of, neither…nor with extra modifiers, there is with a long when-clause, as well as with a false plural, and plural data with a present perfect passive. Quantity phrases greater than one take plural after there. As well as still never makes a co-subject of the marking team.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat plural data as the safe exam default on the last line. For the false lines, delete modifiers and asides, then re-apply a number, proximity, there is/are, and as well as. "More than two" is a plural cue after there.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the nominee captain nor the shadow captains have disclosed their interests.
The number of days between practices has improved after the fitness drive.
There appear to be fewer exceptions in this month's checklist.
Every parcel that exceeds the weight limit requires a second label.
The head teacher, along with the independent governors, have tabled a dissenting note.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the nominee captain nor the shadow captains have disclosed their interests.**

Nearer plural "shadow captains" correctly takes "have disclosed." Doublets after nor still obey proximity. Interest disclosures do not change number.
**B) The number of days between practices has improved after the fitness drive.**

**C) There appear to be fewer exceptions in this month's checklist.**

Plural "fewer exceptions" correctly takes "there appear to be." Fewer is a plural cue; match appear accordingly. Checklist content does not affect number.
**D) Every parcel that exceeds the weight limit requires a second label.**

**E) The head teacher, along with the independent governors, have tabled a dissenting note.**

Close on a mixed set recycling neither…nor, the number, there appear, every, and along with — around captains' interests, practice gaps, checklist exceptions, heavy parcels, and a dissenting governors' note. One parenthetical plural distractor remains.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Four clean lines and one along-with failure on "head teacher … have tabled." Fewer after there is a plural cue that correctly takes appear. Every with a relative clause stays singular. The number of days stays singular.

Work through each construction in order: proximity after nor, singular the number, plural there appear + fewer, singular every + relative clause, then strip along with on the last line. Once the governors sit only in the insert, "has tabled" is obvious.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Cyclists must wear a helmet on this coastal path.
The match might be cancelled beyond any possible doubt.
You need not bring a dish to the potluck if you are short on time.
We can must reserve a table before seven.
She ought to stretch before the morning run.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Cyclists must wear a helmet on this coastal path.**

"Must" here lays down a non-negotiable coastal-path rule, and the bare infinitive "wear" is the right shape after a pure modal. The sentence is asking for a hard requirement, not a suggestion, so the strength matches the job.
**B) The match might be cancelled beyond any possible doubt.**

"might" only encodes weak possibility, so pairing it with "beyond any possible doubt" cancels the meaning. Soften the adverbials or upgrade the modal — you cannot keep both.
**C) You need not bring a dish to the potluck if you are short on time.**

"Need not" correctly lifts the duty: bringing a dish is optional if time is short. That is absence of obligation, not a ban on bringing food.
**D) We can must reserve a table before seven.**

English allows only one pure modal before the main verb, so "can must reserve" is ungrammatical. Choose ability ("can reserve") or obligation ("must reserve"), never both.
**E) She ought to stretch before the morning run.**

"Ought to stretch" is sound advice before a run: "ought" always partners with "to" plus the base verb. The strength is recommendation, which fits a warm-up tip.
tasks.solution_overview:
This warm-up walks through everyday modal jobs: hard rules, weak guesses, waived duty, and advice.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Check that each modal has exactly one job and that its strength matches the rest of the sentence. Watch for a stacked double modal and for certainty wording that fights a weak hedge like "might."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the modal first, then ask whether the claim is obligation, permission, advice, or mere possibility. If the adverbials demand absolute certainty, a soft modal cannot stay.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Visitors must to leave wet umbrellas by the door.
You must not to feed the ducks near the jetty.
The delay may stem from a signal failure on the branch line.
They must have knew about the surprise party earlier.
The results could confirm the hypothesis in every scenario without exception.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Visitors must to leave wet umbrellas by the door.**

"must" takes a bare infinitive, so write "must leave," not "must to leave." The extra "to" is borrowed from patterns like "need to" or "ought to," which do not apply here.
**B) You must not to feed the ducks near the jetty.**

After "must not," keep the bare infinitive: "must not feed," not "must not to feed." Prohibition uses the same base-verb pattern as positive "must."
**C) The delay may stem from a signal failure on the branch line.**

"May stem" hedges carefully: a signal failure is a possible cause of the delay, not a proven one. The softness of "may" matches incomplete evidence.
**D) They must have knew about the surprise party earlier.**

Modal perfect needs a past participle: "must have known," not "must have knew." "Knew" is simple past; after "have" you need the participle form.
**E) The results could confirm the hypothesis in every scenario without exception.**

"Could" encodes possibility, so it cannot underwrite an unconditional claim that the results confirm the hypothesis "in every scenario without exception." Soften the claim or harden the modal.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four of these lines bury form traps around "must," modal perfect, and over-strong "could." Only the cautious "may" sentence is clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Pure modals take a bare infinitive — no "to" after "must" or "must not." Modal perfect needs have + past participle. Soft possibility cannot promise a guaranteed outcome.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for illicit "to," wrong participles after "have," and certainty clashes. If the structure is clean, check whether the modal’s force matches the claim.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The post cannot have arrived yet — the box is still empty.
Neighbours might have overlooked the note on the gate.
We ought revise the packing list before we leave.
Guests may request an extra blanket at reception.
The ferry will likely be delayed for certain and without any doubt.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The post cannot have arrived yet — the box is still empty.**

"Cannot have arrived" is a solid negative modal-perfect deduction: empty mail boxes back the claim that the post has not come yet. The form (cannot + have + past participle) is exactly right for ruling out a past event on present evidence.
**B) Neighbours might have overlooked the note on the gate.**

"Might have overlooked" softens a past guess — possible, not proven. That is the right strength when the neighbours may simply have missed the note.
**C) We ought revise the packing list before we leave.**

"Ought" requires "to": write "ought to revise," not "ought revise." Even though "ought" feels like "should," it keeps its "to."
**D) Guests may request an extra blanket at reception.**

"May request" marks permission: guests are allowed to ask reception for an extra blanket. House-rule English often uses "may" for allowed actions.
**E) The ferry will likely be delayed for certain and without any doubt.**

"Will likely" already hedges, so adding "for certain and without any doubt" contradicts the hedge. Keep one line of force — either the soft prediction or the certainty claim, not both.
tasks.solution_overview:
Modal perfects for past deduction sit beside permission "may," one missing "to" after "ought," and a hedge that fights its own certainty tag.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Check structure first: "ought" must keep "to," and modal perfect needs have + past participle. Then test whether hedges and certainty phrases can coexist.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the job — past deduction, permission, advice, or prediction — then ask if the form and the strength both fit. Clash of hedge + "without doubt" is an automatic fail.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Swimmers must shower before entering the pool.
The forecast must show sunshine, though we have no evidence at all.
She could have posted the parcel before the cut-off.
You need not to renew the library card today.
The coach should reconsider the batting order.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Swimmers must shower before entering the pool.**

"Must shower" correctly imposes a non-negotiable pool hygiene rule with a bare infinitive. Safety and facility rules almost always take this shape.
**B) The forecast must show sunshine, though we have no evidence at all.**

Strong epistemic "must" cannot coexist with "though we have no evidence at all." Without evidence, downgrade to "may" or "might"; do not use deduction-strength "must."
**C) She could have posted the parcel before the cut-off.**

"Could have posted" correctly frames an open past possibility: maybe the parcel went before the cut-off, maybe not. The modal-perfect form is clean.
**D) You need not to renew the library card today.**

Modal "need not" takes a bare infinitive: "need not renew," not "need not to renew." Do not confuse it with main-verb "need to."
**E) The coach should reconsider the batting order.**

"Should reconsider" is measured coaching advice about the batting order. The strength is recommendation, which fits a strategic rethink.
tasks.solution_overview:
Obligation, epistemic deduction, advice, and waived duty sit side by side — including a "must" that has no evidence and a stray "to" after "need not."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Match modal strength to evidence: hard "must" needs solid grounds; "need not" takes a bare infinitive. Keep advice and past-possibility shapes ("should," "could have") clean.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask: rule, guess, advice, or no-duty? Then check form. Flag any strong deduction undercut by "no evidence," and any extra "to" after modal "need not."

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The nurse should have flagged the allergy sooner.
Campers may not light fires after dusk under site rules.
He must sign the consent form before the trial starts.
The clouds might suggest a short shower rather than a storm.
We could shorten the hike if we take the ridge path.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The nurse should have flagged the allergy sooner.**

"Should have flagged" correctly criticises a past missed duty with modal perfect: the allergy ought to have been noted sooner. That is mild past reproach, not a present rule.
**B) Campers may not light fires after dusk under site rules.**

"May not light" denies permission under campsite rules after dusk. In regulatory context, "may not" routinely means "are not allowed to."
**C) He must sign the consent form before the trial starts.**

"Must sign" correctly imposes a hard pre-trial requirement with a bare infinitive. Pure modals never take "to" before the main verb.
**D) The clouds might suggest a short shower rather than a storm.**

"Might suggest" hedges an interpretation of the clouds without overclaiming a storm. Soft epistemic modals protect you when signs admit more than one reading.
**E) We could shorten the hike if we take the ridge path.**

"Could shorten" marks a feasible shorter route via the ridge, not a guaranteed outcome. Possibility is exactly the right strength.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five sentences are deliberately sound: past missed duty, rule-based prohibition, hard obligation, hedged reading of the sky, and a feasible shortcut.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm that each modal’s strength matches the claim and that forms stay clean — bare infinitives after pure modals, modal perfect where the past is in play.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each letter, name the job (reproach, ban, rule, hedge, option). If form and force both fit, mark true — there is no planted crash in this set.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The museum might close early with absolute certainty.
Hosts ought to warn guests about the steep stairs.
They cannot have ignored the fire alarm in the hallway.
You should of updated the packing list after the forecast changed.
Volunteers need not bring their own tools to the park clean-up.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The museum might close early with absolute certainty.**

"Might" and "absolute certainty" cancel each other out. Keep the soft modal and soften the claim, or upgrade the modal if you truly mean certainty.
**B) Hosts ought to warn guests about the steep stairs.**

"Ought to warn" correctly advises a prudent courtesy before guests meet the steep stairs. "Ought to" behaves like strong "should."
**C) They cannot have ignored the fire alarm in the hallway.**

"Cannot have ignored" is a firm negative deduction about a past event: given a hallway fire alarm, ignoring it is treated as logically untenable.
**D) You should of updated the packing list after the forecast changed.**

"Should of" is a mishearing of "should have." In writing, always use "have" after a modal — never the preposition "of."
**E) Volunteers need not bring their own tools to the park clean-up.**

"Need not bring" correctly lifts the obligation to supply tools for the clean-up. Volunteers may still bring tools; they simply are not required to.
tasks.solution_overview:
Certainty clashes and the classic "should of" spelling trap dominate this set, alongside clean advice, negative past deduction, and waived obligation.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Match modal strength to adverbials, write "have" never "of" after a modal, and keep "ought to" / "need not" forms intact.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First hunt form errors ("of" for "have"). Then ask whether a weak modal can survive words like "absolute certainty." Clean advice and "cannot have" deductions pass.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Students must have finished the quiz by now — every desk is empty.
You may borrow my spare charger if yours is dead.
She might to join us after rehearsal.
Drivers should check tyre pressure before a long trip.
The cake need not be iced until tomorrow morning.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Students must have finished the quiz by now — every desk is empty.**

"Must have finished" is a strong past deduction backed by empty desks right now. Present evidence often licenses "must have" about the recent past.
**B) You may borrow my spare charger if yours is dead.**

Formal double-negative deduction and progressive "ought to have been" are legitimate advanced shapes. Reject stacked obligation ("should must") and the redundant "need not have to" pairing — one marker of waived duty is enough.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Cannot have been other than …" forces a strong positive reading in formal dress. Progressive past advisability keeps "ought to have been -ing." Never stack two obligation modals or two no-duty markers.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Fail "should must" and "need not have to" on sight. Pass formal exhaustion deduction, continuous past updating that fell short, and soft "mightn't have realised."

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbours painted the fence. → The fence was painted by the neighbours.
The cake was baked yesterday. → The chef baked the cake yesterday, and we know that for certain.
Several windows were broken by the storm.
The photograph was cropped before posting. → The photograph cropped itself before posting.
My sister watered the plants. → The plants were watered by my sister.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The neighbours painted the fence. → The fence was painted by the neighbours.**

The active sentence names the neighbours as painters and the fence as the thing painted. The passive correctly promotes the fence to subject, uses was painted, and keeps the neighbours in a by-phrase, so meaning is unchanged.
**B) The cake was baked yesterday. → The chef baked the cake yesterday, and we know that for certain.**

The passive The cake was baked yesterday never names a chef and never claims certainty about who did it. The rewrite invents both a baker and "we know that for certain," which adds knowledge the source never supplied. A fair active would stay vague about the agent.

Repair: keep an agentless active or omit invented certainty — for example, Someone baked the cake yesterday.
**C) Several windows were broken by the storm.**

This is a clear past passive: plural windows with were broken, past participle broken, and an explicit cause in by the storm. Form and meaning line up cleanly.
**D) The photograph was cropped before posting. → The photograph cropped itself before posting.**

Photographs do not crop themselves. The rewrite invents a reflexive agent and erases the implied human editor that cropped is meant to leave open. Patient nouns are not self-acting agents.

Repair: keep The photograph was cropped before posting, or name a real editor if the source supplies one.
**E) My sister watered the plants. → The plants were watered by my sister.**

My sister watered the plants flips cleanly to The plants were watered by my sister. Object becomes subject, past simple becomes was/were + past participle, and the agent stays as by my sister.
tasks.solution_overview:
This card checks whether active↔passive flips keep the same tense, the same people, and the same level of certainty.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on past simple passive form (was/were + past participle) and honest agents. If the first side hides the doer, the rewrite must not invent a chef, a reflexive photograph, or extra certainty. Clean flips keep the original object as subject and the named agent in a by-phrase.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat each arrow as a meaning check, not a creative rewrite. Ask: same participants? same tense? same certainty? Agentless passives stay agentless unless the source names the doer.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tickets were booked last Friday.
Mistakes were made during the rehearsal. → The rehearsal made mistakes deliberately.
The librarian shelved the returns. → The returns were shelved by the librarian.
The concert was cancelled yesterday. → Someone cancelled the concert yesterday, and we know exactly who.
The parcel been delivered by the courier this morning.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The tickets were booked last Friday.**

Were booked is a correct past passive focusing on the tickets. No agent is required when the booker is unimportant or unknown, and last Friday sits naturally with the past form.
**B) Mistakes were made during the rehearsal. → The rehearsal made mistakes deliberately.**

Mistakes were made during the rehearsal is a classic agentless hedge. It does not say the rehearsal caused the mistakes on purpose. The rewrite smuggles in both agency and deliberately, changing force and meaning.

Repair: leave the passive as is, or name a real person only if the source does.
**C) The librarian shelved the returns. → The returns were shelved by the librarian.**

The librarian shelved the returns becomes The returns were shelved by the librarian without losing participants. Shelved is the right participle, and the agent stays explicit.
**D) The concert was cancelled yesterday. → Someone cancelled the concert yesterday, and we know exactly who.**

The concert was cancelled yesterday hides the canceller. Claiming someone cancelled it and "we know exactly who" fabricates identity the passive never supplied.

Repair: keep the agentless passive, or use Someone cancelled the concert yesterday without fake certainty.
**E) The parcel been delivered by the courier this morning.**

The parcel been delivered drops the required auxiliary. Passive needs was delivered or has been delivered, not bare been + past participle.

Repair: The parcel was delivered by the courier this morning (or has been delivered…).
tasks.solution_overview:
Start here by checking be + past participle, then ask whether any rewrite adds people, intent, or certainty the first clause never stated.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Agentless passives are fine when the doer is unknown. Fake-agent rewrites that add deliberately or "we know exactly who" fail the meaning test. Incomplete forms like bare been delivered also fail form.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First confirm a proper be (or has/have been) before the participle. Then check that any by-phrase or active rewrite comes from words already on the page, not guesswork about motive or identity.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Volunteers designed the mural. → The mural was designed by volunteers.
The bridge was repaired in 2019.
Lost dogs are returned by the local shelter.
The groceries unpacked by my brother yesterday.
The coach cancelled practice. → Practice was cancelled by the coach.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Volunteers designed the mural. → The mural was designed by volunteers.**

Volunteers designed the mural flips to The mural was designed by volunteers. The object becomes subject, designed becomes was designed, and the agent is retained. Number agreement is right: the mural was, not were.
**B) The bridge was repaired in 2019.**

The bridge was repaired in 2019 is a grammatical agentless past passive. The time phrase fits the finished past frame without needing an agent.
**C) Lost dogs are returned by the local shelter.**

Lost dogs are returned by the local shelter uses present simple passive for a habitual process, with a clear by-agent. Form and meaning are both sound.
**D) The groceries unpacked by my brother yesterday.**

The groceries unpacked by my brother yesterday is missing its auxiliary. A lone past participle cannot make a finite passive clause; you need were unpacked (or have been unpacked).

Repair: The groceries were unpacked by my brother yesterday.
**E) The coach cancelled practice. → Practice was cancelled by the coach.**

The coach cancelled practice becomes Practice was cancelled by the coach. Tense matches, the object becomes subject, and the coach stays as by-agent.
highlights: are returned by the local shelter
tasks.solution_overview:
Most items here are clean voice flips or stand-alone passives; one line drops the auxiliary entirely.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Past and present be + past participle, with or without by. Habitual present passives (are returned) are fair. A lone past participle with a by-phrase is not a finite clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for was/were/are before the participle. If you can ask Were they unpacked? but the word were is missing from the sentence, mark false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist was shared online. → The playlist shared itself online.
No lessons can be scheduled this week. → This calendar prevents anyone from scheduling lessons deliberately.
The invitation was sent by the host. → We know the mayor personally sent the invitation.
The tent was damaged during the wind. → The wind damaged the tent.
The guests were notify of the delay on Monday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The playlist was shared online. → The playlist shared itself online.**

A playlist cannot share itself. The reflexive rewrite invents an impossible agent and treats the patient as if it performed the action on itself.

Repair: keep The playlist was shared online, or name a real sharer if known.
**B) No lessons can be scheduled this week. → This calendar prevents anyone from scheduling lessons deliberately.**

No lessons can be scheduled this week is a neutral modal passive. The rewrite invents a calendar that prevents scheduling and adds deliberately, changing both modality and force.

Repair: keep the modal passive without inventing prevention or intent.
**C) The invitation was sent by the host. → We know the mayor personally sent the invitation.**

by the host names the host, not the mayor. Upgrading the agent into a more specific celebrity invents identity the source never gave.

Repair: keep The invitation was sent by the host, or The host sent the invitation.
**D) The tent was damaged during the wind. → The wind damaged the tent.**

during the wind supplies the cause of the damage. The wind damaged the tent restates that cause in the active without inventing a human doer, so the meaning holds.
**E) The guests were notify of the delay on Monday.**

were notify uses the base verb after be. Passive needs the past participle: were notified.

Repair: The guests were notified of the delay on Monday.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four traps invent agents, intent, or wrong verb forms; only one pair keeps the same event and cause.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Reflexive nonsense (shared itself), invented prevention/intent, upgrading the host into the mayor, and base verbs after were. Event causes like the wind are allowed when the passive already situates the damage there.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When reversing passive→active, use only participants the original allows. For form errors, demand past participles after be, never the base verb.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The suitcase is being weighed by airport staff.
The teacher has marked three essays. → Three essays have been marked by the teacher.
The photos will be printed after the trip.
The dog must be walked before dinner.
The attic was cleared by an old school friend.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The suitcase is being weighed by airport staff.**

Is being weighed is present continuous passive, with airport staff retained as the agent. Being sits correctly between is and the past participle weighed.
**B) The teacher has marked three essays. → Three essays have been marked by the teacher.**

Present perfect active The teacher has marked three essays flips to Three essays have been marked by the teacher. Perfect passive stacks been after have/has.
**C) The photos will be printed after the trip.**

Will be printed is a clean future passive; the agent is optional and the time phrase after the trip fits well.
**D) The dog must be walked before dinner.**

Must be walked places obligation on the walk itself. Modal + be + past participle is the standard pattern for obligation passives.
**E) The attic was cleared by an old school friend.**

Was cleared by an old school friend is a sound past passive with an explicit agent. Cleared is the correct participle of clear.
highlights: have been marked by the teacher
was cleared by an old school friend
tasks.solution_overview:
All five lines are well-formed passives across continuous, perfect, future, modal, and past patterns.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Templates to lock in: is being + PP, have/has been + PP, will be + PP, modal + be + PP, and was + PP with by. Agents appear only when named.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm be (in the right tense or after the modal) sits before a past participle, then accept by only when the agent is known. Every line here passes that check.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The recipes are still being debated. → We know precisely which cousin is debating them.
Dad sent us the bus timetable. → We were sent the bus timetable by Dad.
The lamp crashed overnight. → The lamp was crashed overnight by itself intentionally.
New park rules have been posted by the city council.
The birthday banner design by Maya last week.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The recipes are still being debated. → We know precisely which cousin is debating them.**

are still being debated hides who is debating. Claiming we know precisely which cousin invents both identity and certainty the progressive agentless passive never supplied.

Repair: leave the agentless continuous passive as written.
**B) Dad sent us the bus timetable. → We were sent the bus timetable by Dad.**

Dad sent us the bus timetable allows the indirect-object subject We were sent the bus timetable by Dad. Double-object verbs often permit this flip without changing meaning.
**C) The lamp crashed overnight. → The lamp was crashed overnight by itself intentionally.**

Crash is intransitive here; was crashed… by itself intentionally is ungrammatical and adds nonsense intent. The lamp crashed overnight already states an event, not deliberate agency.

Repair: keep The lamp crashed overnight, or use was damaged if you mean an external cause.
**D) New park rules have been posted by the city council.**

New park rules have been posted by the city council is present perfect passive with a clear agent and plural agreement (have been, not has been).
**E) The birthday banner design by Maya last week.**

The birthday banner design by Maya last week lacks be + past participle. A bare noun phrase plus by does not make a passive clause.

Repair: The birthday banner was designed by Maya last week.
highlights: have been posted by the city council
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch three failure modes: inventing a discussant, forcing an intransitive into a reflexive intentional passive, and dropping be before the participle.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Progressive agentless passives invite fake-agent traps. Double-object send allows recipient passives. Intransitive crash resists agentive by itself intentionally. by alone never creates a passive without be + PP.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept only agents already named in the source. Reject invented cousins, self-crashing lamps, and bare design by… strings that lack an auxiliary.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The club is considering the proposal. → The proposal is being considered by the club.
All hikers must carry a map. → A map must be carried by all hikers.
The delay was occurred during the morning rush.
Mum postponed the picnic. → The picnic was postponed by Mum.
The pool filters are cleaned every Friday by the caretaker.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The club is considering the proposal. → The proposal is being considered by the club.**

The club is considering the proposal becomes The proposal is being considered by the club. Continuous active flips to is/are being + past participle with the agent retained.
**B) All hikers must carry a map. → A map must be carried by all hikers.**

All hikers must carry a map flips to A map must be carried by all hikers. The obligation modal stays as must; force is unchanged.
**C) The delay was occurred during the morning rush.**

Occur is intransitive, so was occurred is ungrammatical. Delays occur; they are not "occurred by" someone in this pattern.

Repair: The delay occurred during the morning rush, or The delay was caused during the morning rush.
**D) Mum postponed the picnic. → The picnic was postponed by Mum.**

Mum postponed the picnic becomes The picnic was postponed by Mum. Regular participle postponed matches the active verb, and meaning is preserved.
**E) The pool filters are cleaned every Friday by the caretaker.**

The pool filters are cleaned every Friday by the caretaker is present habitual passive with an explicit agent. Form and routine meaning both work.
highlights: is being considered by the club
must be carried by all hikers
tasks.solution_overview:
Four transformations or stand-alone passives are sound; one forces an intransitive into was + past participle.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Continuous and modal passives that keep agent and force. Habitual present passives. The classic trap was occurred — occur does not passivise that way.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the verb can take an object in the active. If it cannot (occur, arrive, happen), reject was + PP. Otherwise check that continuous and modal flips keep be in the right shape.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deposit will be paid on 15 March.
IT locked the old tablets. → The old tablets were locked by IT.
The complaint has been escalate to the landlord.
The toast was delivered by a tired waiter.
The school awarded the prize to a Year 9 pupil. → The prize was awarded to a Year 9 pupil by the school.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The deposit will be paid on 15 March.**

Will be paid is a correct future passive; the date adverbial on 15 March sits fine after it.
**B) IT locked the old tablets. → The old tablets were locked by IT.**

IT locked the old tablets becomes The old tablets were locked by IT. Plural tablets take were, and the agent stays named.
**C) The complaint has been escalate to the landlord.**

has been escalate uses a base verb where the past participle belongs. Perfect passive needs has been escalated.

Repair: The complaint has been escalated to the landlord.
**D) The toast was delivered by a tired waiter.**

The toast was delivered by a tired waiter is a clean past passive with the agent retained. Delivered is the right participle.
**E) The school awarded the prize to a Year 9 pupil. → The prize was awarded to a Year 9 pupil by the school.**

The school awarded the prize to a Year 9 pupil becomes The prize was awarded to a Year 9 pupil by the school. The prize is subject, the to-phrase stays, and by the school names the agent.
highlights: was delivered by a tired waiter
was awarded to a Year 9 pupil by the school
tasks.solution_overview:
Scan for the broken perfect passive that uses a base verb after been; everything else is a clean passive or voice flip.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Future and past passives with agents, complex award patterns that keep to-phrases, and the form error been escalate.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Perfect passive demands has/have been + past participle. If you see been + bare verb, mark false. Otherwise check that who did what to whom stays the same across the arrow.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rumour was confirmed this morning. → The class president confirmed the rumour this morning, so we know the speaker.
Staff uniforms are going to be washed next week.
The suitcase arrived damaged. → The suitcase was arrived damaged by the airline deliberately.
Nothing further can be done until the rain stops. → The groundskeeper is refusing to do anything further on purpose.
The posters were update last night by the art club.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The rumour was confirmed this morning. → The class president confirmed the rumour this morning, so we know the speaker.**

Repair: keep The rumour was confirmed this morning without inventing an agent.

Trap: was confirmed this morning does not name the class president. The rewrite fabricates both the speaker and the claim that we therefore know who spoke.
**B) Staff uniforms are going to be washed next week.**

Staff uniforms are going to be washed next week is a well-formed going-to future passive. Be sits before the participle washed.
**C) The suitcase arrived damaged. → The suitcase was arrived damaged by the airline deliberately.**

Repair: The suitcase arrived damaged, or The suitcase was damaged in transit.

Trap: Arrive is intransitive, so was arrived is wrong, and deliberately invents intent the arrival event never stated.
**D) Nothing further can be done until the rain stops. → The groundskeeper is refusing to do anything further on purpose.**

Repair: keep the modal passive; do not turn can be done into is refusing… on purpose.

Trap: Nothing further can be done until the rain stops is a neutral modal passive about possibility. Rewriting it as a groundskeeper refusing on purpose invents both an agent and motive.
**E) The posters were update last night by the art club.**

Repair: The posters were updated last night by the art club.

Trap: were update uses a base verb after be. Passive needs were updated.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only one sentence is a clean future passive; the others invent speakers and motives or break form with intransitives and base verbs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Fake speakers after agentless was confirmed, going-to passives, illegal was arrived, modal passives twisted into deliberate refusal, and were update.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject any rewrite that names a person or purpose the source never gave. For form, demand be + past participle and respect intransitive verbs.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The organisers had already finalised the seating. → The seating had already been finalised by the organisers.
Access to the gym is restricted to members.
The samples are currently taste by the judges.
Our cousins invited us to the barbecue. → We were invited to the barbecue by our cousins.
The mouldy bread was thrown away immediately.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The organisers had already finalised the seating. → The seating had already been finalised by the organisers.**

Had already finalised flips to had already been finalised by the organisers. Past perfect passive stacks been after had and keeps the agent.
**B) Access to the gym is restricted to members.**

Access to the gym is restricted to members is a present passive stating a standing rule. The to-phrase keeps the limitation clear; no agent is required.
**C) The samples are currently taste by the judges.**

Repair: The samples are currently being tasted by the judges.

Trap: are currently taste uses a base verb. Progressive sense wants are currently being tasted (or are currently tasted in a habitual reading), never taste after are.
**D) Our cousins invited us to the barbecue. → We were invited to the barbecue by our cousins.**

Our cousins invited us to the barbecue becomes We were invited to the barbecue by our cousins. The recipient can be the passive subject, and the to-phrase stays.
**E) The mouldy bread was thrown away immediately.**

The mouldy bread was thrown away immediately is a clean agentless past passive focusing on the bread. Thrown is the irregular participle of throw.
tasks.solution_overview:
Check the perfect and invitation passives against the originals, then catch the tasting line that uses a base verb where a participle belongs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Past perfect passive (had been), standing-rule present passives, continuous sense that needs being + PP, invite as recipient passive, and irregular thrown.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Stack been after had/has/have for perfect passives. For currently + verb, prefer being + past participle when the action is in progress. Keep to-phrases when the active has them.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The scores were announced by the process itself intentionally.
The guide will present the route on Tuesday. → The route will be presented by the guide on Tuesday.
Bikes should not be left in the hallway.
The vacancy was filled last month. → We know exactly which neighbour filled the vacancy.
The translation is being check by a native speaker.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The scores were announced by the process itself intentionally.**

Repair: The scores were announced (by the organisers / by officials), without reflexive intent.

Trap: A process cannot intentionally announce scores. Both the agent and the intent word are wrong; by… itself intentionally is almost always a fail.
**B) The guide will present the route on Tuesday. → The route will be presented by the guide on Tuesday.**

The guide will present the route on Tuesday becomes The route will be presented by the guide on Tuesday. Object becomes subject, will be stays, and the time phrase is kept.
**C) Bikes should not be left in the hallway.**

Bikes should not be left in the hallway is a modal passive prohibition. Negation sits with the modal: should not be + past participle.
**D) The vacancy was filled last month. → We know exactly which neighbour filled the vacancy.**

Repair: keep The vacancy was filled last month without naming a neighbour.

Trap: was filled last month names no agent. We know exactly which neighbour filled the vacancy invents both a person and certainty.
**E) The translation is being check by a native speaker.**

Repair: The translation is being checked by a native speaker.

Trap: is being check uses a base verb after being. Continuous passive needs is being checked.
highlights: will be presented by the guide
tasks.solution_overview:
Reject intentional process-agents and invented neighbours; accept future and modal passives that keep force; fix continuous passives that use a base verb after being.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Nonsense by the process itself intentionally, clean will be presented, modal prohibitions, fake exactly which neighbour claims, and being check.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

After being, always demand a past participle. Agentless passives forbid precise neighbour-identification. Modal should not be left is a fair prohibition when form is intact.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The passport application is being processed this week.
Security locked the gates at midnight. → The gates were locked at midnight by security.
Further tips can be found in the guidebook.
The internship offers have been accepted by both students.
The agenda was circulated to all attendees before noon.
tactical_explanations:

The passport application is being processed this week is present continuous passive without an agent, focusing on the ongoing process.
**B) Security locked the gates at midnight. → The gates were locked at midnight by security.**

Security locked the gates at midnight becomes The gates were locked at midnight by security. Meaning is preserved; the time adverbial can sit before the by-phrase.
**C) Further tips can be found in the guidebook.**

Further tips can be found in the guidebook is a modal passive typical of how-to notes. No need to invent who finds the tips.

The internship offers have been accepted by both students is present perfect passive with plural agreement and a clear by-agent.
**E) The agenda was circulated to all attendees before noon.**

can be found in the guidebook
have been accepted by both students
tasks.solution_overview:
A clean set of model passives: continuous, past with agent, modal, perfect, and recipient phrases.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

is being processed, were locked… by security, can be found, have been accepted, was circulated to…. Use these as reference shapes when harder traps appear later.

Confirm be + past participle in each pattern, keep time and to-phrases, and do not invent finders for tips that stay agentless. All five pass here.
