tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It is said that the ferry service stopped overnight.
They gave the runners revised numbers. → Revised numbers were given to the runners.
The fridge crashed. → The fridge was crashed by the update script on purpose.
A decision has yet to be reached on the picnic date.
The costumes will have been fitted before the play opens.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It is said that the ferry service stopped overnight.**

It is said that the ferry service stopped overnight is a standard impersonal reporting passive. No speaker needs to be named; the hedge is intentional.

**Tip:** ** It is said/believed/expected that… hedges without naming a speaker.
**B) They gave the runners revised numbers. → Revised numbers were given to the runners.**

They gave the runners revised numbers allows Revised numbers were given to the runners. Dropping vague they is fine; inventing a named VIP would not be.
**C) The fridge crashed. → The fridge was crashed by the update script on purpose.**

Repair: keep The fridge crashed, or say The fridge was damaged by… only if the source supplies a non-intentional cause.

Trap: The fridge crashed states an event. Adding by the update script on purpose invents both an agent and deliberate intent the original never stated.
**D) A decision has yet to be reached on the picnic date.**

A decision has yet to be reached on the picnic date embeds a perfect passive inside yet to be reached — formal and correct for unfinished decisions.
**E) The costumes will have been fitted before the play opens.**

The costumes will have been fitted before the play opens is future perfect passive: will have been + past participle, with a clear deadline clause.
tasks.solution_overview:
Impersonal reporting and future perfect passives are fair game; the crash rewrite fails by inventing culprit and intent.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

It is said that…, double-object passives that drop vague they, intransitive crash twisted into on purpose, has yet to be reached, and will have been fitted.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept impersonal and nested perfect passives that do not name fake agents. Reject any rewrite that turns an event into deliberate sabotage without evidence in the source.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The scores were being finalised when the lights froze. → We know the junior scorer was finalising them alone.
Nobody can be blamed for the weather delay. → The bus driver is to blame for the weather delay.
The manuscript got published without peer review. → The manuscript published without peer review by itself.
Concerns have been raised about crowded platforms.
The tokens are expired by the security protocol every night intentionally by the tokens themselves.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The scores were being finalised when the lights froze. → We know the junior scorer was finalising them alone.**

Repair: leave the continuous passive without naming a scorer.

Trap: were being finalised when the lights froze still hides the agent. Claiming we know a junior scorer was finalising them alone invents identity and solitude the continuous passive never gave.
**B) Nobody can be blamed for the weather delay. → The bus driver is to blame for the weather delay.**

Repair: keep Nobody can be blamed for the weather delay.

Trap: Nobody can be blamed for the weather delay directly contradicts naming the bus driver as blameworthy. Negation forbids that rewrite.
**C) The manuscript got published without peer review. → The manuscript published without peer review by itself.**

Repair: The manuscript got published without peer review (or was published…), without by itself.

Trap: Even if get-passive is colloquially fine, by itself erases any external publisher and invents self-publication. Get-passive still implies an external process.
**D) Concerns have been raised about crowded platforms.**

Concerns have been raised about crowded platforms is a standard present perfect passive, often kept agentless in everyday English. Form and tone are both sound.
**E) The tokens are expired by the security protocol every night intentionally by the tokens themselves.**

Repair: The tokens are expired by the security protocol every night — one clear by-agent, no reflexive intentionality.

Trap: The tokens are expired by the security protocol every night intentionally by the tokens themselves stacks contradictory agents and intent. Form and meaning both collapse.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four lines smuggle in named people, blame, or reflexive agents; only the concerns sentence keeps a sober agentless perfect passive.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Continuous passives that still hide agents, nobody versus a named blame target, get-passive twisted into by itself, have been raised, and stacked intentional reflexive nonsense.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Respect negation and agentlessness. One clear by-agent is enough; reflexive intentional stacks and blame flips almost always fail.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The roadblocks were lifted last week. → Last week saw the roadblocks lift themselves.
Fans expect a decision by Friday. → A decision is expected by Friday.
The wiring diagram should have been attached to the handbook.
The council owns the riverside path. → The riverside path is owned by the council.
The samples were being store in the cold room overnight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The roadblocks were lifted last week. → Last week saw the roadblocks lift themselves.**

Repair: keep The roadblocks were lifted last week, or name a real authority if known.

Trap: Roadblocks do not lift themselves. The reflexive rewrite is absurd; were lifted already states the correct passive.
**B) Fans expect a decision by Friday. → A decision is expected by Friday.**

Fans expect a decision by Friday becomes A decision is expected by Friday. Here by Friday is a deadline, not a fake human agent, and the meaning still fits.
**C) The wiring diagram should have been attached to the handbook.**

The wiring diagram should have been attached to the handbook is modal perfect passive for past criticism or missed duty: should have been + past participle.
**D) The council owns the riverside path. → The riverside path is owned by the council.**

The council owns the riverside path flips cleanly to The riverside path is owned by the council. Ownership passives are common when naming who holds something.
**E) The samples were being store in the cold room overnight.**

Repair: The samples were being stored in the cold room overnight.

Trap: were being store uses a base verb after being. Continuous passive needs were being stored.
tasks.solution_overview:
Separate by-time from by-agent, accept modal perfect and ownership passives, and reject reflexive nonsense plus base verbs after being.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Reflexive lift themselves, is expected by Friday (deadline, not agent), should have been attached, is owned by the council, and were being store.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When by introduces a time, it is not an agent phrase. Modal perfect passives and ownership passives are fair when form is intact. After being, demand a past participle.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The shortlist will be announced tomorrow. → Tomorrow the panel chair will announce the shortlist, and that is certain.
Two seats have been reserved for the grandparents.
The bakery produces these loaves in Poland. → These loaves are produced in Poland.
The breach was reported anonymously. → A named neighbour reported the breach to take revenge.
The forms need signing before the trip. → The forms need to be signed before the trip.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The shortlist will be announced tomorrow. → Tomorrow the panel chair will announce the shortlist, and that is certain.**

Repair: keep The shortlist will be announced tomorrow without naming a chair.

Trap: will be announced tomorrow does not identify the panel chair or make that identity certain. Certainty claims about a hidden agent fail the meaning test.
**B) Two seats have been reserved for the grandparents.**

Two seats have been reserved for the grandparents is present perfect passive with a clear beneficiary for-phrase and plural agreement (have been).
**C) The bakery produces these loaves in Poland. → These loaves are produced in Poland.**

The bakery produces these loaves in Poland can become These loaves are produced in Poland. Dropping the generic producer is allowed when place remains; inventing a celebrity baker would not be.
**D) The breach was reported anonymously. → A named neighbour reported the breach to take revenge.**

Repair: keep The breach was reported anonymously.

Trap: anonymously blocks naming a neighbour and inventing revenge. An anonymous passive forbids a named-agent active with motive.
**E) The forms need signing before the trip. → The forms need to be signed before the trip.**

Need signing and need to be signed are both acceptable obligation passives here; the paraphrase keeps the same duty before the trip.

**Tip:** ** need signing ≈ need to be signed in formal British usage.
tasks.solution_overview:
Dropping a generic producer is fine; naming a chair, neighbour, or revenge motive is not. Also accept need to be signed as a paraphrase of need signing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Certainty about a hidden announcer, beneficiary for-phrases, place passives that omit a generic bakery, anonymous passives forbidding named revenge, and need signing ≈ need to be signed.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the rewrite adds a specific person or purpose. If yes and the source hid the agent (or said anonymously), mark false. Generic omission and obligation paraphrases can still be true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had the warning been heeded, the flood might have been avoided.
They are repairing the path now. → The path is repaired now by them as we speak.
The visitor was shown the garden before lunch.
It was agreed that bedtime would remain unchanged for six months.
The photos cannot be shared externally without permission.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Had the warning been heeded, the flood might have been avoided.**

Had the warning been heeded and might have been avoided are both passive perfect shapes inside a conditional. Each layer still needs been + past participle.

**Tip:** ** Stacked passives in conditionals still need been + PP each time.
**B) They are repairing the path now. → The path is repaired now by them as we speak.**

Repair: The path is being repaired now by them as we speak.

Trap: They are repairing the path now describes an action in progress. Is repaired now is simple passive and does not match as we speak; you need is being repaired.
**C) The visitor was shown the garden before lunch.**

The visitor was shown the garden before lunch is a double-object passive with the recipient as subject. Show/give/offer commonly allow this pattern.
**D) It was agreed that bedtime would remain unchanged for six months.**

It was agreed that bedtime would remain unchanged for six months reports a decision without naming voters. Do not invent which relative agreed.
**E) The photos cannot be shared externally without permission.**

The photos cannot be shared externally without permission is a modal passive prohibition. The without-phrase is part of the meaning and should stay.
tasks.solution_overview:
Advanced shapes: conditional perfect passives, impersonal it-passives, and recipient subjects. The weak line mismatches progressive meaning with a simple passive.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Had been heeded / might have been avoided, is being repaired versus is repaired for as we speak, was shown, It was agreed that…, and cannot be shared… without permission.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Stacked passives in conditionals still need been + PP each time. Progressive active needs continuous passive. Do not invent who agreed in impersonal reporting passives.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The motion was passed unanimously. → Every club member who opposed it still somehow passed it deliberately.
Little progress has been made on the kitchen renovation. → The landlord personally stalled the kitchen renovation on purpose.
The cookies were allowed to cool before icing. → The cookies allowed themselves to cool before icing.
The community centre based in Leeds oversees local youth clubs. → Local youth clubs are overseen by the community centre based in Leeds.
The password must changed every ninety days.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The motion was passed unanimously. → Every club member who opposed it still somehow passed it deliberately.**

Repair: keep The motion was passed unanimously.

Trap: Unanimously already states the outcome. Inventing opposing members who somehow passed it deliberately contradicts the source and makes a paradoxical agent story.
**B) Little progress has been made on the kitchen renovation. → The landlord personally stalled the kitchen renovation on purpose.**

Repair: leave the progress passive without fake blame.

Trap: Little progress has been made on the kitchen renovation is agentless. Naming a landlord who personally stalled it on purpose invents both agent and motive.
**C) The cookies were allowed to cool before icing. → The cookies allowed themselves to cool before icing.**

Repair: keep The cookies were allowed to cool before icing.

Trap: were allowed to cool implies an external controller. Allowed themselves invents reflexive agency the allow-passive does not support.
**D) The community centre based in Leeds oversees local youth clubs. → Local youth clubs are overseen by the community centre based in Leeds.**

The community centre based in Leeds oversees local youth clubs becomes Local youth clubs are overseen by the community centre based in Leeds. The same centre remains the agent, Leeds detail included.

**Tip:** ** Carry modifiers of the agent into the by-phrase when they identify which centre.
**E) The password must changed every ninety days.**

Repair: The password must be changed every ninety days.

Trap: must changed is missing be. Modal passives need must be changed.
highlights: are overseen by the community centre
tasks.solution_overview:
Only the community-centre oversight pair keeps the same agent under a clean voice flip. The rest invent blame, reflexive cool-downs, or drop be after a modal.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Paradoxical vote rewrites, fake landlord stalling, allowed themselves versus were allowed, overseen by with modifiers kept, and must changed.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject blame and reflexive agency the source never stated. Modal passives always need be before the participle. Carry identifying modifiers of the agent into the by-phrase when they matter.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been briefed by the nurse, the parents approved the treatment. → The parents were briefed by the nurse and then approved the treatment.
The library books are to be returned within fourteen days.
What remains to be decided is the venue. → Someone has already decided the venue, and we know who.
The rare manuscript was being carefully restored when funding paused.
Under no circumstances should guest passwords be shared without encryption.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having been briefed by the nurse, the parents approved the treatment. → The parents were briefed by the nurse and then approved the treatment.**

Having been briefed by the nurse unpacks fairly into The parents were briefed by the nurse and then approved the treatment. The same nurse remains the agent; nothing new is invented.

**Tip:** ** Participial passives still obey the no-fake-agent rule.
**B) The library books are to be returned within fourteen days.**

The library books are to be returned within fourteen days uses be to + passive for scheduled obligation: are to be + past participle.

**Tip:** ** are to be + PP is formal diary-style passive.
**C) What remains to be decided is the venue. → Someone has already decided the venue, and we know who.**

Repair: keep What remains to be decided is the venue.

Trap: What remains to be decided is the venue means the venue is still open. Claiming someone has already decided it — and that we know who — reverses the meaning.
**D) The rare manuscript was being carefully restored when funding paused.**

The rare manuscript was being carefully restored when funding paused is past continuous passive. The adverb carefully can sit between being and the participle.
**E) Under no circumstances should guest passwords be shared without encryption.**

Under no circumstances should guest passwords be shared without encryption keeps the modal passive after inversion: should… be shared. Inversion does not remove be.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four advanced passives hold: participial, be-to, continuous, and inverted modal. The venue line fails because it turns an undecided state into a fabricated completed act.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Having been briefed… unpacking fairly, are to be returned, remains to be decided versus already decided, was being carefully restored, and inverted should… be shared.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Participial and inverted passives still obey the no-fake-agent rule. to be decided signals incompleteness — never rewrite it as a known finished decision. Inversion does not remove be.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No conclusions can be drawn from this data. → This data prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately.
The school newsletter is expected to be published before the open day.
They had the boilers replaced overnight. → The boilers were replaced overnight.
It is believed the mix-up was caused by a booking error. → We know which clerk caused the mix-up and that the clerk acted deliberately.
Were the rules not to be enforced, the queue would lengthen. → If the rules were not enforced, the queue would lengthen.
tactical_explanations:
**A) No conclusions can be drawn from this data. → This data prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately.**

Repair: keep No conclusions can be drawn from this data.

Trap: No conclusions can be drawn from this data is a neutral modal passive. Saying the data prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately invents both agency and intent.
**B) The school newsletter is expected to be published before the open day.**

The school newsletter is expected to be published before the open day nests two passives: is expected + to be published. Both layers are well formed for a formal forecast.

**Tip:** ** Expect + to-infinitive passive is common in formal forecasts.
**C) They had the boilers replaced overnight. → The boilers were replaced overnight.**

They had the boilers replaced overnight pairs with The boilers were replaced overnight. Causative have + object + PP often aligns with a simple passive of the object without inventing who did the work.
**D) It is believed the mix-up was caused by a booking error. → We know which clerk caused the mix-up and that the clerk acted deliberately.**

Repair: keep the belief passive without certainty-plus-motive claims.

Trap: It is believed the mix-up was caused by a booking error is a hedge. Naming a clerk and alleging deliberate action fabricates both agent and intent.
**E) Were the rules not to be enforced, the queue would lengthen. → If the rules were not enforced, the queue would lengthen.**

Were the rules not to be enforced paraphrases cleanly as If the rules were not enforced…. Formal inversion still encodes the same passive enforcement meaning.
highlights: prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately
Were the rules not to be enforced
tasks.solution_overview:
At the top band, watch nested passives and inverted conditionals that still keep meaning, and reject any rewrite that adds deliberate clerks, motives, or prevention the source never stated.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neutral can be drawn twisted into deliberate prevention, is expected to be published, causative had… replaced aligning with were replaced, belief passives forbidding clerk-plus-motive, and Were… not to be enforced ≈ If… were not enforced.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Belief and modal hedges forbid certainty-plus-motive rewrites. Nested expectation passives and inverted formal conditionals stay true when they preserve force and participants.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.
The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.
The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.
The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.
The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.**

"Who" correctly refers to a person in a restrictive clause that identifies which neighbour we mean. The clause is essential, so there are no commas, and nothing else tries to occupy the subject slot.
**B) The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.**

leftover "it" doubles the object after the relative has already taken that job. Repair: drop "it" — "The recipe which my aunt shared needs less salt." One object slot, one filler.
**C) The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.**

a library is a thing, so "who" is the wrong pronoun. Repair: "The library which/that opens on Sundays stays busy all day." Reserve "who" for people.
**D) The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines which bus; no commas are needed because the clause is essential to identify it. The relative is the subject of "stops," and the sentence reads cleanly.
**E) The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.**

after commas (non-restrictive), exam English wants "which," not "that." Repair: "The park, which was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow." Commas signal extra information — and "that" is not welcome there.
tasks.solution_overview:
These five sentences all turn on relative clauses that pick out a neighbour, a recipe, a library, a bus, or a park.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Ask whether the head noun is a person or a thing, and whether commas mark the clause as extra information. Also check that the relative pronoun itself fills the subject or object slot — no leftover object pronoun such as "it."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

In defining (no-comma) clauses, "who/that" fit people and "which/that" fit things. After commas, use "which" for things, never "that," and never leave a second object after the relative. Mark each sentence true only when those three checks all clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.
The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.
The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.
The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.
The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.**

"Whose" correctly shows possession: the soup belongs to the chef. You could rephrase as "the chef's soup," which is exactly what "whose" encodes in a relative clause.
**B) The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.**

"who's" expands to "who is," so "who's helmet" would mean "who is helmet" — nonsense. Repair: "The cyclist whose helmet cracked bought a new one." You need possession, not a contraction.
**C) The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.**

Non-restrictive "which" with commas correctly adds non-essential detail about a known concert. The commas tell you the clause is extra information, so "which" is the right pronoun for a thing.
**D) The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.**

Restrictive "that" for people is acceptable in defining clauses that identify which students. The clause is essential, so there are no commas, and the grammar stands as written.
**E) The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.**

a garage is not a person, so "who" is wrong. Repair: "The garage, which stores our bikes, needs a new lock." Places and buildings take "which," not "who."
tasks.solution_overview:
Here the focus shifts to possession, contractions, and the familiar who/which split across a chef, a cyclist, a concert, students, and a garage.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate "who's" (who is / who has) from "whose" (belonging). Keep "who" for people and "which" for places, buildings, and events — especially once commas mark a non-restrictive clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you can rephrase as "X's Y," you almost always want "whose." Expand every "who's" before you tick true. For things with commas, expect "which"; for people in defining clauses, "who" or "that" are both acceptable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.
The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.
The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.
The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.
The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.**

a comma-bound clause must use "which," not "that." Repair: "The festival, which locals love, fills the square each July." The commas already signal that the clause is extra information.
**B) The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.**

Formal "whom" correctly marks the object of "hired": we hired the tutor, so the relative stands for him/her. The structure is careful exam English and fully grammatical as written.
**C) The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.**

Restrictive "which" correctly defines which kettle; no commas are required because the clause is essential. British formal writing often prefers "which" even in defining clauses about things.
**D) The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.**

Informal object "who" is widely accepted here: we invited the friend, and bare "who" as object is grammatical in modern usage. Exams may prefer "whom" after a preposition, but bare object "who" is usually fine.
**E) The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.**

residual "them" doubles the object after "that" already stands for the photos. Repair: "The photos that Maya printed are still on the table." The relative already equals the object.
tasks.solution_overview:
This set mixes comma rules, object relatives (who/whom), and another leftover pronoun around a festival, a tutor, a kettle, a friend, and some photos.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Spot commas first — they ban "that" in careful exam English. Then ask whether the relative is the object of the verb inside the clause, and whether any residual "them/it" still sits where the relative already sits.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Non-restrictive → "which" for things. Object of "hired" can be formal "whom"; bare object "who" is usually accepted without a preposition. If the clause already does the object's job, delete any leftover pronoun before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The runner who finished first still looked fresh.
The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.
The café whose windows face the river stays open late.
The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.
The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The runner who finished first still looked fresh.**

Restrictive "who" correctly identifies the runner; the clause is needed to pick out which person, so there are no commas. The relative is the subject of "finished," and the sentence is a textbook defining clause.
**B) The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.**

Defining "that" correctly restricts which map we borrowed. The relative is the object of "borrowed," which is a standard, fully grammatical pattern for things.
**C) The café whose windows face the river stays open late.**

"Whose" can mark possession for things as well as people: "the café whose windows…" means "the café's windows." The possessive relative is the right tool here.
**D) The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.**

"Who's" correctly expands to "who is" before "opening." Try the expansion in place — "the singer who is opening the show" — and the sentence still works, so the contraction is justified.
**E) The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.**

Restrictive "which" correctly defines the film the class watched. Either "which" or "that" works in defining clauses about things, and no commas are needed.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five sentences are clean models — use them as a reference sheet for people, things, possession, and a genuine contraction.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm defining "who/that/which," possessive "whose" for a café's windows, and "who's" that really expands to "who is." Nothing here is trying to trick you with commas or leftover pronouns.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask person vs thing, then ask whether you need belonging or a contraction. If every piece fits — relative, head noun, and role inside the clause — mark true and move on.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.
The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.
Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.
The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.
The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.**

Preposition + "whom" is the formal, correct pattern when the cousin is the object of "with": we share a flat with the cousin. The structure is polished exam English.
**B) The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.**

non-restrictive needs "which," not "that." Repair: "The playlist, which includes every song from the trip, is private." Commas + "that" is a classic exam fail.
**C) Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.**

possession requires "whose," not the contraction "who's." Repair: "Anyone whose keys are missing should check lost property." "Who is keys" is nonsense, so you wanted belonging.
**D) The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.**

Defining "which" correctly identifies the museum we visited. Object relatives can keep "which/that," and the clause is essential, so no commas are required.
**E) The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.**

Restrictive "that" for a person is acceptable in a defining clause that identifies which coach. "Who" is often preferred for people, but "that" is not an error here.
tasks.solution_overview:
Preposition + whom, commas that ban "that," and another who's/whose swap sit across a cousin, a playlist, keys, a museum, and a coach.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

After a preposition referring to a person, prefer "whom." Commas still forbid "that" for things. Expand every "who's" before you mark possession true — "who is keys" never works.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for a preposition immediately before the relative, then for commas, then for contractions. Defining "which/that" for places and people can stand when the rest of the grammar is clean.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.
The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.
The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.
Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.
The friends who cake the party brought later left early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.**

"From which" correctly links a thing after a preposition: we order bread from the bakery. Keeping the preposition with "which" is the formal pattern exams reward.
**B) The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.**

"Whom" correctly marks the volunteer as the object of "praised": neighbours praised the volunteer. If you can replace the relative with "him/her," "whom" is justified.
**C) The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.**

residual "it" doubles the object after "that" already stands for the novel. Repair: "The novel that Sam finished last night still sits on the shelf." One clause, one object slot.
**D) Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Brighton. Place names with commas almost always take "which," not "that," because the clause is extra information about an already-named city.
**E) The friends who cake the party brought later left early.**

word order inside the relative collapses — "who cake the party brought" is not English. Repair: "The friends who brought the party cake later left early." Keep the clause's internal order like a normal statement after the relative.
tasks.solution_overview:
Preposition + which, object whom, a residual "it," a city name with commas, and a collapsed word-order clause share the spotlight.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep the preposition with "which/whom" in formal answers. Delete leftover object pronouns. Rebuild any relative clause whose internal order has collapsed into nonsense.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the relative clause as a mini-statement after the pronoun. If an "it" remains where that mini-statement already has its object, cut it. If word order inside the clause fails, rewrite it as a normal statement and only then judge the whole sentence.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.
The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.
Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.
The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.
The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.**

"To whom" is the formal object pattern after a preposition: the parcel was delivered to the neighbour. Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people in exam English.
**B) The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.**

a suitcase's zip needs "whose," not "who's." Repair: "The suitcase whose zip is broken stays in the loft." "Who's" never marks possession — expand it and the error is obvious.
**C) Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.**

"Whose" correctly marks possession for people in a defining clause: drivers' licences have expired. The pattern works with plural noun heads just as with singular.
**D) The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines which beach we walked along. Object "that/which" can often be omitted in informal style ("The beach we walked along…"), but keeping "that" is fully correct.
**E) The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.**

non-restrictive about a person needs "who," not "that." Repair: "The headteacher, who announced the trip, answered questions calmly." Commas + person → who; commas + thing → which; never that.
tasks.solution_overview:
