**Part 2: How to decide.**

Run a final checklist — person, thing, possession, contraction — on each sentence. When every relative's role matches the head noun and no leftover pronoun appears, mark the set true end to end.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Mia avoids talking on the phone while she cycles through traffic.
The twins enjoy to bake cinnamon rolls on rainy Sundays.
After the match, the coach decided postponing the next training session.
Noah refused to share his notes before the chemistry quiz.
Lara promised delivering the costumes for the school play by Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Mia avoids talking on the phone while she cycles through traffic.**

Avoid is one of the classic gerund verbs, so "avoids talking" is exactly the pattern you want. The rest of the sentence (cycling through traffic) does not change what avoid requires. Mia is simply naming the activity she stays away from.
**B) The twins enjoy to bake cinnamon rolls on rainy Sundays.**

enjoy needs a gerund, not a to-infinitive. Repair it to "enjoy baking cinnamon rolls," not "enjoy to bake." Like and love can be flexible in casual speech, but enjoy almost never takes to + verb when the object is an activity.
**C) After the match, the coach decided postponing the next training session.**

decide takes a to-infinitive, so the coach should have "decided to postpone," not "decided postponing." A bare gerund after decide is a frequent exam error.
**D) Noah refused to share his notes before the chemistry quiz.**

Refuse correctly pairs with a to-infinitive: "refuse to share." The meaning is a willful no — he will not share the notes — and English packages that refusal as refuse + to + verb.
**E) Lara promised delivering the costumes for the school play by Thursday.**

promise also wants to + verb: "promised to deliver the costumes," not "promised delivering." Commitment language after promise follows the same family as decide and refuse.
tasks.solution_overview:
You are sorting five everyday sentences by whether the verb after avoid, enjoy, decide, refuse, or promise is in the form that verb actually wants.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Avoid and enjoy take a gerund (-ing). Decide, refuse, and promise take a to-infinitive. The trap is mixing those two camps: putting to after a gerund verb, or -ing after an infinitive verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Circle the main verb that governs the second verb, then ask: is this an -ing verb or a to-verb? Match the complement to that list before you mark true or false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hiking club is considering organising a dawn walk next month.
Sofia enjoys reading graphic novels on the train.
The family decided to camp beside the lake this weekend.
The barista refused accepting tips during the charity day.
Jamal promised to text when his flight landed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The hiking club is considering organising a dawn walk next month.**

Consider takes a gerund, so "considering organising a dawn walk" is correct. The club is weighing an activity as an idea, which is exactly what consider + -ing expresses.
**B) Sofia enjoys reading graphic novels on the train.**

Enjoy + gerund is the standard pattern: "enjoy reading graphic novels." Reading is the liked activity, so -ing is required.
**C) The family decided to camp beside the lake this weekend.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to camp beside the lake." They made a future plan, and decide packages plans with to + base verb.
**D) The barista refused accepting tips during the charity day.**

refuse needs a to-infinitive — "refused to accept tips," not "refused accepting." The charity-day setting does not change the grammar.
**E) Jamal promised to text when his flight landed.**

Promise correctly takes a to-infinitive: "promised to text when his flight landed." That is a future commitment, which is the natural job of promise + to.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four of these lines already use the textbook complement; only one verb has crossed into the wrong pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Consider and enjoy want -ing. Decide, refuse, and promise want to + verb. Here the hiking club, Sofia, the family, and Jamal are fine; the barista's refuse line is the broken one.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for refuse first when the rest look polished — refuse is easy to contaminate with a gerund because avoid and enjoy sit nearby in your memory. Then confirm each remaining verb against its fixed list.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The librarian avoided to mention the overdue fines in front of the class.
Trainee chefs enjoy to practise knife skills on quiet mornings.
Management is considering to outsource the school canteen.
The band decided expanding their tour into two neighbouring towns.
The driver refused to open the boot without seeing ID.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The librarian avoided to mention the overdue fines in front of the class.**

avoid needs -ing — "avoided mentioning the overdue fines," not "avoided to mention." Do not borrow the to-infinitive from decide or promise just because they sound similar.
**B) Trainee chefs enjoy to practise knife skills on quiet mornings.**

enjoy takes a gerund — "enjoy practising knife skills," not "enjoy to practise." Trainee chefs still follow the same grammar rule as anyone else.
**C) Management is considering to outsource the school canteen.**

consider takes -ing — "considering outsourcing the school canteen," not "considering to outsource." If you can paraphrase as "the idea of …ing," you want a gerund.
**D) The band decided expanding their tour into two neighbouring towns.**

decide needs to + verb — "decided to expand their tour," not "decided expanding." Decide never takes a bare gerund as its direct complement.
**E) The driver refused to open the boot without seeing ID.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to open the boot without seeing ID." Refusal language almost always pairs with to + base verb, and this line does it right.
tasks.solution_overview:
This set is almost a wrong-pattern gallery: four sentences break the fixed complement, and only refuse survives cleanly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Avoid, enjoy, and consider must keep -ing; decide must keep to + verb. The only healthy line is refuse + to-infinitive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Flip every avoid/enjoy/consider error to a gerund and every decide error to to + verb. When refuse already has to, leave it alone.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We stopped to buy ice cream when we reached the pier.
Please stop to chew gum during the recital.
On the motorway they stopped talking and listened to the news.
She stopped to smoking after her doctor warned her.
He stopped typing when the fire alarm sounded.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We stopped to buy ice cream when we reached the pier.**

Stop + to-infinitive means they interrupted the journey in order to buy ice cream. That purpose reading fits the pier scene perfectly, so the sentence is grammatical.
**B) Please stop to chew gum during the recital.**

here you want quit the habit of chewing gum during the recital — "stop chewing," not "stop to chew." Stop to chew would oddly mean pause something else in order to start chewing.
**C) On the motorway they stopped talking and listened to the news.**

Stop + gerund means they quit talking and listened instead. On the motorway, the meaning is cessation of the same action, so -ing is the right form.
**D) She stopped to smoking after her doctor warned her.**

habit quitting needs the gerund alone — "stopped smoking," not "stopped to smoking." You cannot mix to and -ing in the same complement slot after stop.
**E) He stopped typing when the fire alarm sounded.**

Stop + gerund correctly means he quit typing when the fire alarm sounded. The typing itself ends; that is cessation, not purpose.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stop is special: the form after it changes the meaning, so you are choosing a sense of the verb as well as a pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Stop + to-infinitive means pause in order to do something else. Stop + gerund means quit / no longer do that activity. Hybrids like "stop to smoking" are never valid.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask which sense the sentence needs — purpose after a pause, or cessation of the same action — then pick to or -ing to match. Reject any string that glues to onto an -ing form.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Athletes often avoid eating heavy meals right before a race.
My grandparents enjoy gardening in the late afternoon.
Have you considered joining the community choir?
Elena decided studying abroad for one semester.
The museum promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Athletes often avoid eating heavy meals right before a race.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid eating heavy meals right before a race." Health and habit advice often uses this pattern, and athletes are a natural context for it.
**B) My grandparents enjoy gardening in the late afternoon.**

Enjoy + gerund names a liked activity: "enjoy gardening in the late afternoon." Enjoy almost never takes to + verb in standard exam English.
**C) Have you considered joining the community choir?**

Consider + gerund is correct: "considered joining the community choir." Consider means think about doing something, which takes -ing.
**D) Elena decided studying abroad for one semester.**

decide needs to + verb — "decided to study abroad," not "decided studying." Choose, refuse, and promise sit in the same to-infinitive family.
**E) The museum promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May.**

Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May." Commitments after promise use to + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
Clean models for avoid, enjoy, consider, and promise sit beside one decide error that uses the wrong complement.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep the -ing trio (avoid, enjoy, consider) separate from the to-infinitive trio (decide, refuse, promise). Only Elena's decide line breaks the rule here.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Verify each governing verb against its list. When four look textbook-correct, still check decide/refuse/promise carefully for a smuggled gerund.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tourists should avoid to swim near the rocks after dark.
Kids usually enjoy building sandcastles at low tide.
We are considering to rent bikes for the coastal path.
The jury refused to discuss the case outside the room.
Dad promised calling us as soon as the ferry docked.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tourists should avoid to swim near the rocks after dark.**

avoid takes -ing — "avoid swimming near the rocks," not "avoid to swim." Warnings with avoid always want the gerund.
**B) Kids usually enjoy building sandcastles at low tide.**

Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoy building sandcastles at low tide." Building is the liked activity, so -ing is required.
**C) We are considering to rent bikes for the coastal path.**

consider takes -ing — "considering renting bikes," not "considering to rent." Consider to + verb is a frequent exam trap.
**D) The jury refused to discuss the case outside the room.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to discuss the case outside the room." Refuse patterns with decide and promise, and this line keeps that to.
**E) Dad promised calling us as soon as the ferry docked.**

promise needs to + verb — "promised to call us," not "promised calling." Promise + -ing is not standard for future commitments.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two clean lines (enjoy, refuse) sit next to three pattern flips on avoid, consider, and promise.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch especially avoid/consider + to and promise + -ing — those are the crossed wires this set is fishing for. Enjoy and refuse already show the correct camps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Sort each verb into the -ing list or the to list, then check whether the written complement matches. Flip only the mismatches.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Runners stopped to stretch at the water station.
Please stop shouting; the neighbours can hear you.
We stopped for buying tickets at the kiosk.
She stopped to check the map because the path forked.
He stopped to listen music and missed the announcement.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Runners stopped to stretch at the water station.**

Stop to stretch = pause the run in order to stretch at the water station. Purpose after an interruption is exactly what stop + to-infinitive expresses.
**B) Please stop shouting; the neighbours can hear you.**

Stop shouting = quit the noisy behaviour. The neighbours can hear you, so the command is to cease that same action — gerund territory.
**C) We stopped for buying tickets at the kiosk.**

after stop, use to + verb for purpose, not for + -ing — "stopped to buy tickets," not "stopped for buying." For + -ing is not the purpose pattern you want here.
**D) She stopped to check the map because the path forked.**

Stop to check = interrupt travel in order to check the map because the path forked. Reason or purpose after a pause takes the to-infinitive.
**E) He stopped to listen music and missed the announcement.**

as written, both form and preposition fail. You need either "stopped listening to music" (quit) or "stopped to listen to music" (pause in order to) — and listen always keeps to before music.
tasks.solution_overview:
Deepen the stop contrast and catch side traps like for + -ing and a broken listen phrase.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Meaning still decides between stop to (purpose) and stop -ing (cessation). Also reject "stopped for buying" and any listen phrase that drops its to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label each stop as purpose or quit first. Then check that purpose uses to + verb (not for + -ing) and that any listen pattern keeps listen to.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I avoid checking social media before breakfast.
They enjoy to watch documentaries about deep-sea life.
Have you considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks?
The committee decided to cancel the outdoor picnic.
She refused helping with the dishes until her homework was done.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I avoid checking social media before breakfast.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid checking social media before breakfast." That is a habit she tries not to do, which is classic avoid + -ing.
**B) They enjoy to watch documentaries about deep-sea life.**

enjoy needs -ing — "enjoy watching documentaries," not "enjoy to watch." Enjoy to + verb is almost never right in carefully marked English.
**C) Have you considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks?**

Consider + gerund is correct: "considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks." Weighing an option takes -ing after consider.
**D) The committee decided to cancel the outdoor picnic.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to cancel the outdoor picnic." Decisions about future actions take to + verb.
**E) She refused helping with the dishes until her homework was done.**

refuse needs to + verb — "refused to help with the dishes," not "refused helping." Refuse + -ing is a classic false friend with avoid and enjoy.
tasks.solution_overview:
A mix of clean avoid/consider/decide lines and two flips: enjoy with to, and refuse with -ing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Group the verbs by pattern before scoring. Avoid and consider stay with -ing; decide stays with to; enjoy to and refuse -ing are the traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Mark each governing verb's camp first, then check the complement. The two false lines are the ones that borrowed the other camp's form.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: After years of late nights, he finally stopped drinking energy drinks.
We stopped to ask a local which tram went to the museum.
They stopped to arguing when the teacher walked in.
She never enjoys waiting in long airport queues.
The cast promised rehearsing every evening until opening night.
tactical_explanations:
**A) After years of late nights, he finally stopped drinking energy drinks.**

Stop + gerund = quit the habit of drinking energy drinks after years of late nights. Habit change is the cessation reading, so -ing is correct.
**B) We stopped to ask a local which tram went to the museum.**

Stop to ask = pause the journey in order to ask a local which tram went to the museum. Purpose after a pause takes stop + to.
**C) They stopped to arguing when the teacher walked in.**

** Never attach to directly to an -ing form after stop.

Trap: quit arguing needs the gerund alone — "stopped arguing," not "stopped to arguing." Do not glue to onto a gerund after stop.
**D) She never enjoys waiting in long airport queues.**

Enjoy + gerund is correct even when negated: "never enjoys waiting in long airport queues." Negation does not change the enjoy + -ing pattern.
**E) The cast promised rehearsing every evening until opening night.**

** Promise + to-infinitive for future commitments.

Trap: promise needs to + verb — "promised to rehearse every evening," not "promised rehearsing." Promise + -ing fails the commitment pattern.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stop meaning splits again, plus a hybrid "to arguing" error and a promise trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep purpose (stop to) versus cessation (stop -ing) sharply separate. Also reject glued hybrids like "to arguing," and remember promise wants to + verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each stop line, name the intended sense first. Then check enjoy's gerund and promise's infinitive independently.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Passengers should avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases.
Would you consider to volunteer at the food bank this winter?
The captain decided to turn back because of the fog.
My brother refuses admitting he lost the house keys.
Aunt Priya enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Passengers should avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases." Public notices often use avoid + -ing, and this one is textbook.
**B) Would you consider to volunteer at the food bank this winter?**

** Rewrite consider to + verb with -ing.

Trap: consider takes -ing — "consider volunteering at the food bank," not "consider to volunteer." Consider to is a frequent trap.
**C) The captain decided to turn back because of the fog.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to turn back because of the fog." Sudden decisions still take to + verb.
**D) My brother refuses admitting he lost the house keys.**

** Refuse + -ing → flip to to + verb.

Trap: refuse needs to + verb — "refuses to admit he lost the house keys," not "refuses admitting." Refuse + -ing wrongly mimics avoid.
**E) Aunt Priya enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family.**

Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family." Hobby verbs after enjoy always take -ing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Three solid models sit beside two crossed patterns: consider with to, and refuse with -ing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Sort each verb into the -ing list (avoid, consider, enjoy) or the to list (decide, refuse) before you answer. The false lines are the ones that swapped camps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm avoid/enjoy/decide first as clean anchors, then repair consider to → -ing and refuse -ing → to + verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We decided not to climb the ridge after the weather warning.
She avoids not to sit near the speakers at concerts.
They refused not to apologise, even though everyone expected it.
He promised not to spoil the ending of the film.
I enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We decided not to climb the ridge after the weather warning.**

Decide + not + to-infinitive is the correct negation: "decided not to climb the ridge." You negate the infinitive with not before to, not by switching to a gerund.
**B) She avoids not to sit near the speakers at concerts.**

** Avoid + -ing; do not add not to.

Trap: avoid already means "not do"; use "avoids sitting near the speakers," not "avoids not to sit." Do not stack an extra not + to onto avoid.
**C) They refused not to apologise, even though everyone expected it.**

** Refuse + to + verb; put not only when you truly mean "refuse to not do X."

Trap: the intended sense is almost always "refused to apologise" (would not apologise). "Refused not to apologise" is a double-negative mess unless you truly mean they insisted on apologising.
**D) He promised not to spoil the ending of the film.**

Promise + not + to-infinitive is correct: "promised not to spoil the ending." Negation sits before to in the infinitive pattern, same family as decide.
**E) I enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays.**

Enjoy + gerund works with negation inside the activity: "enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays." Enjoy still wants -ing even when the activity is a negative state.
tasks.solution_overview:
Negation tests the same fixed patterns: not to after decide/promise, plain -ing after avoid/enjoy, and careful handling of refuse.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Decide and promise negate with not before to. Avoid already means "not do," so it wants plain -ing, not a stacked not to. Refuse not to is usually a muddled double negation when the speaker meant refused to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find the governing verb, apply its usual complement, then place not only where that pattern allows — before to for infinitives, inside the gerund phrase for enjoy, and nowhere extra after avoid.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Midway through the hike we stopped drinking from the stream and switched to bottled water.
Midway through the hike we stopped to drink from our bottles.
The guide stopped us from approaching the cliff edge.
Please stop to interrupting the speaker with side comments.
They stopped singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Midway through the hike we stopped drinking from the stream and switched to bottled water.**

Stop + gerund = quit the activity of drinking from the stream and switch to bottled water. The same action ends, so -ing is correct.
**B) Midway through the hike we stopped to drink from our bottles.**

Stop to drink = pause walking in order to drink from our bottles. The purpose of the pause is the drink, so to-infinitive is correct.
**C) The guide stopped us from approaching the cliff edge.**

Stop someone from + -ing is a related but valid pattern: the guide prevented them from approaching the cliff edge. That is not the same as stop to or stop -ing, but it is grammatical.
**D) Please stop to interrupting the speaker with side comments.**

** Never attach to directly to an -ing form after stop.

Trap: quit interrupting needs "stop interrupting," not "stop to interrupting." Never attach to directly to an -ing form after stop.
**E) They stopped singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand.**

Stop + gerund = they quit singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand. Instant cessation of the same action takes -ing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Pair stop to / stop -ing with the prevent pattern stop someone from -ing, and reject the hybrid "to interrupting."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Same action ending → stop + -ing. Purpose of a pause → stop + to. Preventing someone → stop + object + from + -ing. Never write stop to + -ing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the intended meaning of stop in each line. Then match the structure: gerund, to-infinitive, or object + from + -ing — and kill the hybrid.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having considered moving house, they decided to stay another year.
She enjoys to be the first to arrive at rehearsals.
We avoided discussing politics at the family dinner.
He refused being photographed without his consent.
The mayor promised to fund the new skate park next spring.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having considered moving house, they decided to stay another year.**

Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive both follow their fixed patterns in one sentence: having considered moving, they decided to stay. Different verbs keep their own complements.
**B) She enjoys to be the first to arrive at rehearsals.**

** Enjoy + being / doing, never enjoy to be here.

Trap: enjoy needs -ing — "enjoys being the first to arrive," not "enjoys to be." Enjoy + being / doing, never enjoy to be in this sense.
**C) We avoided discussing politics at the family dinner.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided discussing politics at the family dinner." Sensitive topics often pair with avoid + -ing.
**D) He refused being photographed without his consent.**

** Passive infinitives still follow refuse + to.

Trap: refuse needs to + verb — "refused to be photographed without his consent," not "refused being." Passive infinitives still follow refuse + to.
**E) The mayor promised to fund the new skate park next spring.**

Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to fund the new skate park next spring." Public commitments use promise + to.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stacked verbs, a passive after refuse, and an enjoy trap — track each verb's complement independently.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Consider + -ing and decide + to can share one sentence without rewriting each other. Enjoy still wants -ing (including being). Refuse needs to even before a passive infinitive. Promise keeps to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline every verb that governs another verb form, then apply that verb's own rule. Do not let one correct pattern contaminate its neighbour.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I never stop to wonder how the magician hid the coin.
I never stop wondering how the magician hid the coin.
Doctors advised him to stop to smoke immediately.
They decided against postponing the wedding.
She is considering whether to accept the internship offer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I never stop to wonder how the magician hid the coin.**

** Never stop + -ing = keep doing something all the time.

Trap: the intended idiom is continuous curiosity — "never stop wondering" (gerund), not pause-in-order-to wonder. Stop to wonder would mean interrupt something else so you can wonder, which is not the usual reading.
**B) I never stop wondering how the magician hid the coin.**

Never stop + gerund correctly means the wondering continues without pause. Idiomatic "can't/never stop -ing" always wants the gerund.
**C) Doctors advised him to stop to smoke immediately.**

** Medical advice to quit → stop + -ing.

Trap: quit smoking needs "stop smoking"; "stop to smoke" would mean pause something else in order to smoke — the opposite of medical advice to quit.
**D) They decided against postponing the wedding.**

Decide against + gerund is a valid related pattern: "decided against postponing the wedding." You can also say decide to + verb; against + -ing is the negative sibling.
**E) She is considering whether to accept the internship offer.**

Consider whether + to-infinitive is grammatical when whether introduces the option: "considering whether to accept." Bare consider + verb still wants -ing; the whether-clause changes the frame.
tasks.solution_overview:
Idioms and near-neighbours: never stop -ing, stop smoking versus stop to smoke, decide against -ing, and consider whether to.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Never stop -ing" means keep doing something. Medical quit advice wants stop + -ing, not stop to. Decide against + gerund and consider whether + to are valid alternatives to the basic patterns.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read for idiom and structure, not just the first verb. Ask whether stop means cease or purpose, and whether decide/consider are using a legal alternative frame.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Rather than argue, they decided to sleep on the problem.
She avoids to be seen wearing the same outfit twice.
We enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues.
He refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa.
The club promised arranging free coaching for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Rather than argue, they decided to sleep on the problem.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to sleep on the problem." The opener "Rather than argue" does not change decide's to-pattern.
**B) She avoids to be seen wearing the same outfit twice.**

** Passive gerunds still follow avoid + -ing.

Trap: avoid needs -ing — "avoids being seen wearing the same outfit twice," not "avoids to be seen." Passive gerunds still follow avoid + -ing.
**C) We enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues.**

Enjoy + gerund (passive) is correct: "enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues." Enjoy + being + past participle is a common natural pattern.
**D) He refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa." Refuse to let / refuse to allow keep the to.
**E) The club promised arranging free coaching for beginners.**

** Promise + -ing is still wrong for offers.

Trap: promise needs to + verb — "promised to arrange free coaching," not "promised arranging." Promise + -ing is still wrong even with a kind offer.
tasks.solution_overview:
Passive gerunds after avoid/enjoy and a promise error — form (active/passive) does not rewrite the verb's complement rule.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Decide and refuse keep to. Avoid and enjoy keep -ing, including being + past participle. Promise still cannot take a bare gerund.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ignore active versus passive cosmetics and ask only what the governing verb demands. Repair avoid to be → being, and promise arranging → to arrange.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: What made them stop to check the tyre pressure was a strange vibration.
What made them stop checking their phones was the no-device rule.
Investors are considering selling a small stake in the start-up.
She decided that postponing the trip would be wiser.
He enjoys when friends drop by without calling first.
tactical_explanations:
**A) What made them stop to check the tyre pressure was a strange vibration.**

Stop to check = pause driving in order to check the tyre pressure after a strange vibration. The cleft "what made them…" still keeps stop's meaning split intact.
**B) What made them stop checking their phones was the no-device rule.**

Stop checking = quit the phone-checking habit because of the no-device rule. Same cleft frame, opposite stop pattern — meaning decides.
**C) Investors are considering selling a small stake in the start-up.**

Consider + gerund is correct: "considering selling a small stake in the start-up." Even in money contexts, consider still wants -ing.
**D) She decided that postponing the trip would be wiser.**

Decide that + clause is grammatical; the gerund postponing is the subject of the that-clause, not decide's complement. Decide to + verb OR decide that + clause — both work.
**E) He enjoys when friends drop by without calling first.**

Enjoy can take a when-clause as its object; no verb-complement conflict arises. Enjoy + noun/gerund/clause are fine — but not enjoy to + verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five are sound once you separate stop's two meanings and allow decide that / enjoy when as alternative structures.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Cleft frames do not rewrite stop to versus stop -ing. Consider still wants -ing. Decide that + clause and enjoy + when-clause are grammatical alternatives to decide to / enjoy + -ing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check stop by meaning first, then accept legal clause objects after decide and enjoy. Do not force every verb into only one complement shape.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far from avoiding to answer, she volunteered the awkward detail first.
They kept promising finishing the mural before the festival.
Only after refusing to compromise did the two sides walk out.
Having enjoyed to sail as children, they booked a dinghy again.
Stop to pretend you did not hear the question.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Far from avoiding to answer, she volunteered the awkward detail first.**

** Far from + -ing does not unlock avoid + to.

Trap: avoid still needs -ing — "avoiding answering," not "avoiding to answer." Far from + -ing does not license avoid + to.
**B) They kept promising finishing the mural before the festival.**

** Keep / start do not change promise's to-pattern.

Trap: promise needs to + verb — "promising to finish the mural," not "promising finishing." Keep / start do not change promise's to-pattern.
**C) Only after refusing to compromise did the two sides walk out.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct inside the inversion: "refusing to compromise." Inversion and emphasis leave the refuse + to pattern intact.
**D) Having enjoyed to sail as children, they booked a dinghy again.**

** Having enjoyed still takes -ing.

Trap: enjoy needs -ing — "enjoyed sailing as children," not "enjoyed to sail." The perfect participle having enjoyed still takes -ing.
**E) Stop to pretend you did not hear the question.**

** Commands to quit an act → stop + -ing.

Trap: quit pretending needs "stop pretending," not "stop to pretend" (which would mean pause in order to pretend). Commands to quit an act use stop + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Hard wrappers (far from, keep -ing, inversion, having -ed) still cannot rewrite avoid, enjoy, promise, or stop. Only refuse to survives cleanly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Far from + -ing does not license avoid + to. Keep promising still needs to finish. Inversion leaves refuse + to intact. Having enjoyed still takes -ing. Quit-commands need stop + -ing, not stop to pretend.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip the fancy wrapper mentally, apply the bare verb's complement rule, then put the wrapper back. Only the refuse line already matches.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She stopped to mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath.
If you stop meaning what you say, people stop trusting you.
We are still considering how to phrase the apology.
He decided on renting the attic flat above the bakery.
They refused their friends' offer of driving them home.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She stopped to mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath.**

** Stop to only works when the infinitive is a real purpose action.

Trap: nonsense meaning — stop to mean is not English for "intend." Use something like "She did not mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath." Stop to only works when the infinitive is a real purpose action.
**B) If you stop meaning what you say, people stop trusting you.**

Stop + gerund twice: quit meaning what you say / quit trusting you. Parallel stop + -ing structures keep the "cease" sense cleanly.
**C) We are still considering how to phrase the apology.**

Consider + how + to-infinitive is fine when how introduces the method: "considering how to phrase the apology." Consider + -ing OR consider + wh-word + to both work.
**D) He decided on renting the attic flat above the bakery.**

Decide on + gerund/noun is a valid alternative to decide to + verb: "decided on renting the attic flat." Decide to go OR decide on going — both grammatical.
**E) They refused their friends' offer of driving them home.**

Refuse can take a noun object ("refused their friends' offer"); the of + -ing belongs to offer, not to refuse. Refuse + noun and refuse + to + verb are both correct.
tasks.solution_overview:
Edge grammar: impossible stop to mean, parallel stop -ing, consider how to, decide on -ing, and refuse + noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Stop to only works when the infinitive is a real purpose action — "mean" is not one. Parallel stop + -ing keeps the cease sense. Consider how to, decide on -ing, and refuse + noun are all legal alternatives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Look past the first verb when the complement sits elsewhere (offer of driving). Reject nonsense purpose infinitives, and accept decide on / consider how / refuse + noun when they appear.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided interrupting the poet mid-line.
Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided to interrupt the poet mid-line.
They promised that they would water the plants while we were away.
He enjoys that his sister always remembers his birthday.
We stopped short of promising to host the entire reunion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided interrupting the poet mid-line.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided interrupting the poet mid-line." Fronted participle clauses (Not wishing to appear rude) do not change avoid's -ing rule.
**B) Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided to interrupt the poet mid-line.**

** Compare the pair; only the gerund version works.

Trap: same sentence with the wrong complement — avoid needs -ing, not to. Compare the pair; only the gerund version works.
**C) They promised that they would water the plants while we were away.**

Promise that + clause is a valid alternative to promise to + verb: "promised that they would water the plants." Promise to water OR promise that we will water.
**D) He enjoys that his sister always remembers his birthday.**

Enjoy that + clause is acceptable; the that-clause is the object of enjoy. Enjoy + -ing for activities; enjoy that for facts or situations.
**E) We stopped short of promising to host the entire reunion.**

Stop short of + -ing is an idiom meaning "almost but not quite"; promising keeps its own to inside the gerund phrase. Idioms can nest: stop short of + gerund, and inside it promise + to.
tasks.solution_overview:
Minimal pairs, that-clause alternatives, and the idiom stop short of -ing. Confirm which structure is actually complementing which verb.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Avoid keeps -ing even after a fronted participle clause; the to version is the false twin. Promise that and enjoy that are valid clause objects. Stop short of + -ing nests another verb's complement inside an idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Compare near-identical lines first. Then check whether that-clauses or idioms are carrying the object, so you do not over-apply the basic to/-ing rule to the wrong verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait for clearer skies.
She cannot help enjoying to win, even in friendly matches.
Whatever they refuse to discuss in public, they still avoid lying to each other.
To stop to worry is not the same as to stop worrying.
Only those who promise delivering results on time keep their places on the team.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait for clearer skies.**

Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive are both correct inside a conditional: had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait. Complex syntax still respects each verb's fixed complement.
**B) She cannot help enjoying to win, even in friendly matches.**

** Nested -ing does not license enjoy to.

Trap: enjoy needs -ing — "enjoying winning," not "enjoying to win." Cannot help + -ing is itself a gerund pattern and does not license enjoy to.
**C) Whatever they refuse to discuss in public, they still avoid lying to each other.**

Refuse + to and avoid + -ing are both correct in parallel clauses: whatever they refuse to discuss, they still avoid lying. Different verbs, different complements — both can be right at once.
**D) To stop to worry is not the same as to stop worrying.**

The contrast is precisely the teaching point: stop to worry is not the same as stop worrying. Infinitive subjects can showcase the stop meaning split cleanly, and both halves are grammatical as a contrast.
**E) Only those who promise delivering results on time keep their places on the team.**

** Relative clauses do not unlock promise + -ing.

Trap: promise needs to + verb — "promise to deliver results on time," not "promise delivering." Relative clauses do not unlock promise + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Final stress test: stacked patterns, cannot help + enjoy, parallel refuse/avoid, the stop meaning contrast as subject, and a last promise trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Complex syntax still respects each verb's fixed complement. Cannot help + -ing does not license enjoy to. Refuse to and avoid -ing can both be right at once. Infinitive subjects can showcase stop to versus stop -ing. Relative clauses do not unlock promise + -ing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Parse each governing verb on its own, even inside conditionals, clefts, and relative clauses. Mark true only when every stacked pattern is legal; the enjoy to and promise -ing lines fail.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The match starts at seven." → "She said the match started at seven."
Direct: "Where is the bus stop?" → "He asked where was the bus stop."
Direct: "We will bake bread tomorrow." → "They said they will bake bread tomorrow."
Direct: "Did you lock the bike?" → "She asked if I had locked the bike."
Direct: "I finished the essay yesterday." → "He said he had finished the essay yesterday."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "The match starts at seven." → "She said the match started at seven.".**

After a past reporting verb like said, present simple normally moves one step back to past simple. Here "starts" becomes "started," which is exactly the expected backshift for a factual present in the original line.

The report keeps the same content about the match time; only the tense moves with the reporting frame.
**B) Direct: "Where is the bus stop?" → "He asked where was the bus stop.".**

embedded wh-questions keep statement order — subject before the verb — so you need "where the bus stop was," not "where was the bus stop." The version with "where was" is still direct-question inversion after asked.

Repair: put the subject first inside the reported clause: He asked where the bus stop was.
**C) Direct: "We will bake bread tomorrow." → "They said they will bake bread tomorrow.".**

"will" normally backshifts to "would" after past said, and "tomorrow" usually becomes "the next day" (or "the following day"). Leaving both unshifted keeps the report locked in the original speaker's present.

Repair: They said they would bake bread the next day.
**D) Direct: "Did you lock the bike?" → "She asked if I had locked the bike.".**

Yes/no questions report with if or whether plus statement order, and past simple often deepens to past perfect. "Asked if I had locked the bike" does both jobs cleanly for "Did you lock…?"

The subject comes before the verb, and the lock action sits one step further back than the asking.
**E) Direct: "I finished the essay yesterday." → "He said he had finished the essay yesterday.".**

time markers shift with the tense. Once you backshift "finished" to "had finished," "yesterday" should become "the day before" (or "the previous day"), not stay as yesterday.

Repair: He said he had finished the essay the day before.
tasks.solution_overview:
Reported speech turns the original words into a past report — usually after said or asked — so tense, word order, and time words often all have to move together.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

After a past reporting verb, present simple usually becomes past simple. Embedded questions keep statement order (subject before the verb), not the inverted shape of a real question. Time markers like yesterday and tomorrow normally shift with the tense.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read each line as a report of the given direct speech. Check three things in order: did the tense backshift when it should, is any question still inverted, and did deictic time words stay stuck in the speaker's "now." Mark true only when all three fit.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I can swim across the lake." → "She said she can swim across the lake."
Direct: "When does the museum open?" → "He asked when the museum opened."
Direct: "We must pack today." → "She said they had to pack that day."
Direct: "I have watered the plants." → "He said he had watered the plants."
Direct: "Are the tickets ready?" → "She asked are the tickets ready."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "I can swim across the lake." → "She said she can swim across the lake.".**

ability "can" typically backshifts to "could" after a past reporting verb. Leaving "can" unchanged freezes the ability in the reporter's present instead of the reported past.

Repair: She said she could swim across the lake.
**B) Direct: "When does the museum open?" → "He asked when the museum opened.".**

The wh-word stays, the tense backshifts (does open → opened), and the clause keeps subject–verb statement order. "He asked when the museum opened" is the clean pattern.

You never reinstate "when does" or "when did" after asked.
**C) Direct: "We must pack today." → "She said they had to pack that day.".**

Obligation "must" often becomes "had to" in past reports, and "today" shifts to "that day." Both changes appear here, so the line is a solid report of "We must pack today."

Present obligation markers usually reshape once the reporting frame is past.
**D) Direct: "I have watered the plants." → "He said he had watered the plants.".**

Present perfect backshifts cleanly to past perfect after said: have watered → had watered. The report places the watering firmly before the speaking moment.

No extra inversion or deictic leftover is required here.
**E) Direct: "Are the tickets ready?" → "She asked are the tickets ready.".**

reported yes/no questions need if or whether plus statement order — not inverted "are the tickets ready." That shape is still a direct question after asked.

Repair: She asked whether the tickets were ready. (tense also backshifts are → were)
tasks.solution_overview:
This set mixes modal backshift with perfect tense moves and the if/whether pattern for yes/no reports.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Ability can typically becomes could after past said. Obligation must often surfaces as had to, with today → that day. Present perfect backshifts to past perfect. Reported yes/no questions need if/whether and statement order, never leftover inversion.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan each report for the verb class first (modal, perfect, or question). Then check whether the form moved one notch back and whether any question still looks inverted. Mark false as soon as either check fails.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The choir rehearses here tomorrow." → "He said the choir rehearsed here tomorrow."
Direct: "Why did the neighbour leave?" → "She asked why did the neighbour leave."
Direct: "I am reading the novel now." → "He said he was reading the novel then."
Direct: "Do not feed the stray cats." → "She told me do not feed the stray cats."
Direct: "We may hike next weekend." → "They said they may hike next weekend."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "The choir rehearses here tomorrow." → "He said the choir rehearsed here tomorrow.".**

place and time markers usually shift with a past report. Keeping "here" and "tomorrow" leaves the choir rehearsal anchored in the original speaker's location and day even though said pushes the frame back.

Repair: He said the choir rehearsed there the following day.
**B) Direct: "Why did the neighbour leave?" → "She asked why did the neighbour leave.".**

embedded why-questions need statement order and usually past-perfect backshift for a finished past event — not "why did the neighbour leave," which still looks like a direct question with do-support.

Repair: She asked why the neighbour had left.
**C) Direct: "I am reading the novel now." → "He said he was reading the novel then.".**

Present continuous backshifts to past continuous, and "now" becomes "then." "He said he was reading the novel then" is the textbook mapping for "I am reading… now."

Both the aspect and the time word move with the reporting verb.
**D) Direct: "Do not feed the stray cats." → "She told me do not feed the stray cats.".**

negative commands in reports use told/asked + object + not + to-infinitive. Leaving "do not feed" keeps an imperative shape that does not belong after told.

Repair: She told me not to feed the stray cats.
**E) Direct: "We may hike next weekend." → "They said they may hike next weekend.".**

"may" for possibility often becomes "might," and "next weekend" should become "the following weekend." Leaving both unshifted under-reports the past frame.

Repair: They said they might hike the following weekend.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four traps stack unshifted place/time words, leftover do-support, a bare negative command, and an unmoved may/next — only the continuous now→then line is clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Deictics usually move: here → there, tomorrow → the following day, now → then. Embedded why-questions need statement order and often past-perfect backshift. Negative commands report as told/asked + object + not + to-infinitive. Possibility may commonly becomes might.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, ask whether any "here/now/tomorrow" survived unchanged, whether a question still uses did/do inversion, and whether a command stayed as bare do not. Only mark true when tense, order, and deictics all match the reporting frame.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Please text me the address." → "He asked me to text him the address."
Direct: "Who watered the garden?" → "She asked who had watered the garden."
Direct: "I will have finished by Friday." → "He said he would have finished by Friday."
Direct: "This recipe needs more salt." → "She said that recipe needed more salt."
Direct: "Have you seen my keys?" → "He asked had I seen his keys."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "Please text me the address." → "He asked me to text him the address.".**

Polite requests report as asked + object + to-infinitive. "Please text me the address" becomes "He asked me to text him the address," with the pronoun also shifting to the new viewpoint.

The imperative disappears; the to-clause carries the instruction.
**B) Direct: "Who watered the garden?" → "She asked who had watered the garden.".**

Subject questions keep who as the subject of the reported clause; the tense still backshifts. "She asked who had watered the garden" is statement-like and correctly shifted from "Who watered…?"

There is no do-support to delete because who is already the subject.
**C) Direct: "I will have finished by Friday." → "He said he would have finished by Friday.".**

Future perfect "will have finished" backshifts to "would have finished" after past said. The "by Friday" deadline can stay when it is still a named calendar point relative to the report.

Only the will piece moves to would inside the perfect stack.
**D) Direct: "This recipe needs more salt." → "She said that recipe needed more salt.".**

"This" often becomes "that" after a past report, with present → past: needs → needed. "She said that recipe needed more salt" bundles both shifts cleanly.

Demonstratives move with the reporting viewpoint just like here/now.
**E) Direct: "Have you seen my keys?" → "He asked had I seen his keys.".**

yes/no perfect questions need if or whether plus statement order — not "had I seen…" inversion. That shape still looks like a direct question after asked.

Repair: He asked whether I had seen his keys.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four solid reports cover polite requests, subject questions, future perfect backshift, and this→that; the trap is leftover question inversion after asked.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Please-requests become asked + object + to-infinitive. Subject who-questions keep who as subject but still backshift. Will have finished becomes would have finished. Demonstratives often move (this → that). Yes/no perfect questions need if/whether, not "had I…" inversion.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Identify the speech act (request, subject question, statement, yes/no). Apply the matching structure, then check tense and demonstratives. Mark false the moment you still see question inversion after asked.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The soup is too salty." → "Mia told that the soup was too salty."
Direct: "How long have you lived here?" → "She asked how long I had lived there."
Direct: "We shall meet at noon." → "He said they should meet at noon."
Direct: "I saw the fox last night." → "She said she had seen the fox the night before."
Direct: "Can you join the hike?" → "He asked could I join the hike."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "The soup is too salty." → "Mia told that the soup was too salty.".**

"tell" needs a personal object — tell someone that… — so bare "Mia told that…" is ungrammatical. Without an object, use "said that…"

Repair: Mia said that the soup was too salty. (or Mia told us that…)
**B) Direct: "How long have you lived here?" → "She asked how long I had lived there.".**

Present perfect → past perfect, "here" → "there," and statement order after how long all appear together. "She asked how long I had lived there" is a complete report of the original question.

Bundle tense, place, and order rather than fixing only one layer.
**C) Direct: "We shall meet at noon." → "He said they should meet at noon.".**

Formal "shall" for future often reports as "should" (or sometimes "would") after past said. "He said they should meet at noon" treats shall like a future marker that backshifts.

The subject also shifts from we to they with the reporting viewpoint.
**D) Direct: "I saw the fox last night." → "She said she had seen the fox the night before.".**

Past simple → past perfect and "last night" → "the night before" work as a pair. "She said she had seen the fox the night before" places the sighting before the speaking and rewrites the relative night.

Relative past time phrases shift just like yesterday/tomorrow.
**E) Direct: "Can you join the hike?" → "He asked could I join the hike.".**

modal yes/no reports need if or whether + subject + could, not "could I join…" inversion. The inverted modal is still direct-question order after asked.

Repair: He asked if I could join the hike.
tasks.solution_overview:
Say versus tell joins the usual backshift package here. Watch for a missing object after tell and for inverted modals after asked.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Tell needs a personal object (told someone that…); without one, use said that…. Bundle tense, place, and order shifts on long wh-questions. Formal shall for future often reports as should. Past simple plus last night → past perfect plus the night before. Modal yes/no reports need if/whether + subject + could.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First check the reporting verb (said vs told). Then verify backshift and whether any yes/no line still inverts. Mark true only when verb choice, tense, and order all pass.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Bring a spare towel." → "She told us to bring a spare towel."
Direct: "I may be late." → "He said he might be late."
Direct: "Where have they put the map?" → "She asked where they had put the map."
Direct: "We were discussing the film." → "He said they had been discussing the film."
Direct: "I leave for Lisbon tonight." → "She said she was leaving for Lisbon that night."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "Bring a spare towel." → "She told us to bring a spare towel.".**

Imperatives report as tell/ask + object + to-infinitive. "Bring a spare towel" becomes "She told us to bring a spare towel" — the command verb drops and the to-clause carries the instruction.

The addressee appears as the object of told.
**B) Direct: "I may be late." → "He said he might be late.".**

Possibility "may" commonly becomes "might" in past reports. "He said he might be late" is the safe mapping for "I may be late."

No further change is required beyond that modal step.
**C) Direct: "Where have they put the map?" → "She asked where they had put the map.".**

Wh-word + statement order + present perfect → past perfect: "She asked where they had put the map." There is no auxiliary before the subject.

The put-action sits before the asking, which is why past perfect fits.
**D) Direct: "We were discussing the film." → "He said they had been discussing the film.".**

Past continuous often becomes past perfect continuous after a past reporting verb when you need a further step back: were discussing → had been discussing.

That form keeps the ongoing sense while lining the discussion up before he said.
**E) Direct: "I leave for Lisbon tonight." → "She said she was leaving for Lisbon that night.".**

Present simple for a near arrangement can report as past continuous, with "tonight" → "that night." "She said she was leaving for Lisbon that night" is a natural report of a planned departure.

Timetabled or arranged futures often surface as was/were + -ing in reports.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five lines are clean reports: commands with to-infinitive, modal may→might, embedded perfect questions, past continuous deepening, and arranged-future reporting.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Imperatives report as tell/ask + object + to-infinitive. Possibility may commonly becomes might. Wh-questions keep statement order with present perfect → past perfect. Past continuous often becomes past perfect continuous when sequence needs a further step back. Present simple for a near arrangement can surface as was/were + -ing, with tonight → that night.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm each speech-act pattern first, then check that every tense and time word moved exactly one appropriate step. Here every line already does — use them as models for later traps.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I must have left my scarf at the café." → "He said he must have left his scarf at the café."
Direct: "Will the library renew the card?" → "She asked would the library renew the card."
Direct: "These clouds are gathering." → "He said those clouds were gathering."
Direct: "I used to cycle to school." → "She said she used to cycle to school."
Direct: "Don't forget the tickets." → "He reminded me not to forget the tickets."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "I must have left my scarf at the café." → "He said he must have left his scarf at the café.".**

Deduction "must have" often stays unchanged because it already refers to a past conclusion. "He said he must have left his scarf at the café" keeps the logical guess intact under said.

Logical deduction with must have need not backshift further.
**B) Direct: "Will the library renew the card?" → "She asked would the library renew the card.".**

yes/no with will needs if or whether + would + subject, not "would the library renew…" inversion. That order is still a direct question after asked.

Repair: She asked whether the library would renew the card.
**C) Direct: "These clouds are gathering." → "He said those clouds were gathering.".**

"These" → "those" and present continuous → past continuous: "He said those clouds were gathering." Demonstratives and tense move together with the reporting viewpoint.

The gathering is reported as ongoing relative to the past speaking moment.
**D) Direct: "I used to cycle to school." → "She said she used to cycle to school.".**

"Used to" already marks past habit and normally stays as used to after said. No further backshift is required, and inventing "had used to" would sound wrong.
