Passive past yes/no → whether + past perfect passive + last→previous. Would prefer + object + not to keeps its skeleton while pronouns and this→that adjust. Rare dare questions can report as if + dared + bare infinitive. Will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing. What if… hypotheticals often keep what if and simply backshift the following verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm voice/stack retention where needed and only the layers that truly move (will→would, last→previous, this→that). Every line already does — use the set as a high-difficulty model bank.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Seldom have we seen such fog." → "She said seldom had they seen such fog."
Direct: "I was to have signed before noon." → "He said he was to have signed before noon."
Direct: "Who should we notify first?" → "She asked who should we notify first."
Direct: "The bread will still be warm tomorrow morning." → "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning."
Direct: "Might the shop extend its hours?" → "They asked might the shop extend its hours."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "Seldom have we seen such fog." → "She said seldom had they seen such fog.".**

Negative inversion can survive inside the reported clause after said, with pronoun and tense already matching. "She said seldom had they seen such fog" keeps the inverted rhetorical shape.

Reporting rare inverted rhetoric may keep that shape when the rest aligns.

**Tip:** ** Flashy inversion is optional but grammatical if tenses/pronouns fit.
**B) Direct: "I was to have signed before noon." → "He said he was to have signed before noon.".**

"Was to have + past participle" (unfulfilled plan) typically remains was to have…. This past-scheduled perfect form needs no further shift under said.

"He said he was to have signed before noon" keeps the missed-plan meaning intact.

**Tip:** ** Leave was to have + pp unchanged.
**C) Direct: "Who should we notify first?" → "She asked who should we notify first.".**

Repair: She asked who we should notify first.

Trap: embedded object questions need statement order — "who we should notify first," not "who should we notify first." Modal should still follows the subject after asked.
**D) Direct: "The bread will still be warm tomorrow morning." → "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning.".**

Future will → would, and tomorrow morning → the next morning. "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning" moves both pieces after past said.

Will and time words travel together.
**E) Direct: "Might the shop extend its hours?" → "They asked might the shop extend its hours.".**

Repair: They asked whether the shop might extend its hours.

Trap: yes/no might needs if or whether + subject + might, not "might the shop extend…" Bare modal inversion is still a direct question after asked.
tasks.solution_overview:
Inverted who-should and bare might-yes/no fail. Surviving rhetorical inversion, was-to-have, and would + next-morning time shifts are acceptable.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Negative inversion can survive inside a reported clause after said when pronouns and tenses already match. Was to have + past participle (unfulfilled plan) typically remains. Embedded object questions need statement order: who we should notify. Will → would with tomorrow morning → the next morning. Yes/no might needs if/whether + subject + might.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow rare rhetorical inversion and frozen was-to-have; still force statement order on ordinary who/might questions. Mark false on who should we and bare might the shop.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I'd rather you didn't spoil this." → "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that."
Direct: "How come the cake collapsed?" → "He asked how come the cake had collapsed."
Direct: "We used not to skip breakfast." → "They said they used not to skip breakfast."
Direct: "Will you have finished by the time I call?" → "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called."
Direct: "Suppose we freeze the leftovers." → "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "I'd rather you didn't spoil this." → "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that.".**

Would rather + past clause for preference about someone else keeps that past shape; this→that adjusts. "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that" does not force past perfect inside the rather-clause.

Preferential rather-clauses are not automatically deepened further.
**B) Direct: "How come the cake collapsed?" → "He asked how come the cake had collapsed.".**

Informal how come reports with statement order and optional past perfect for a prior failure. "He asked how come the cake had collapsed" keeps how come and deepens the collapse.

Pattern: asked how come + subject + (had) + past participle.

**Tip:** ** how come stays; tense may backshift.
**C) Direct: "We used not to skip breakfast." → "They said they used not to skip breakfast.".**

"Used not to" (or didn't use to) for past habit can remain used not to. Habitual used-to patterns are already past-oriented, so further backshift is unnecessary.

"They said they used not to skip breakfast" keeps the old habit meaning.
**D) Direct: "Will you have finished by the time I call?" → "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called.".**

Future perfect in a yes/no question → if + would have, and the time-clause present→past. "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called" shifts both the main future perfect and the by-the-time clause.

Both layers move together under past asked.
**E) Direct: "Suppose we freeze the leftovers." → "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers.".**

Suppose-ideas often become suggested that + base (or past) form in formal reports. "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers" is exam-friendly for "Suppose we freeze…"

Mandative or tentative freeze after suggested that is acceptable.
highlights: how come the cake had collapsed
tasks.solution_overview:
All five are advanced but valid: rather + past clause, how come, used not to, nested would-have with by-the-time, and suggested that.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Would rather + past clause for preference about someone else keeps that past shape; this→that adjusts. Informal how come reports with statement order and optional past perfect. Used not to for past habit can remain. Future perfect in a yes/no question → if + would have, and the by-the-time clause present→past. Suppose-ideas often become suggested that + base form.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Retain already-past preference and habit patterns; still shift futures and demonstratives; allow suggested that for suppose. Every line passes — treat the set as a finishing model.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Not only is the path steep, but the wind is fierce." → "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce."
Direct: "I needn't have packed every jumper." → "He said he needn't have packed every jumper."
Direct: "Where should the chairs sit?" → "She asked where should the chairs sit."
Direct: "By next March we will have been leasing the studio for a decade." → "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade."
Direct: "Was anyone monitoring the feed then?" → "She asked was anyone monitoring the feed then."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "Not only is the path steep, but the wind is fierce." → "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce.".**

Correlative not only…but also can keep inversion after said while tenses sit in the past. "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce" is optional but grammatical when pronouns and tenses align.

Reporting flashy inversion is allowed if the rest of the clause matches the past frame.
**B) Direct: "I needn't have packed every jumper." → "He said he needn't have packed every jumper.".**

Needn't have for unnecessary past action stays needn't have. Perfect absence-of-need does not become hadn't need under said.

"He said he needn't have packed every jumper" keeps the "did it but didn't need to" meaning.
**C) Direct: "Where should the chairs sit?" → "She asked where should the chairs sit.".**

Repair: She asked where the chairs should sit.

Trap: statement order required — "where the chairs should sit," not "where should the chairs sit." Modal should follows the subject in embedded wh-questions.
**D) Direct: "By next March we will have been leasing the studio for a decade." → "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade.".**

Next→the following and will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing. "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade" changes only will→would in the long stack.

Long future-perfect-continuous stacks shift the will piece and the next calendar word.
**E) Direct: "Was anyone monitoring the feed then?" → "She asked was anyone monitoring the feed then.".**

Repair: She asked whether anyone was monitoring the feed then.

Trap: yes/no past continuous needs if or whether + statement order — "whether anyone was monitoring…" — never bare "was anyone…" after asked.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two order failures remain: should after where, and bare was-anyone after asked. Inverted not only, needn't have, and future perfect continuous reports are fine.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Correlative not only…but can keep inversion after said while tenses sit in the past. Needn't have for unnecessary past action stays needn't have. Embedded wh + modal needs statement order: where the chairs should sit. Next→the following and will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing. Yes/no past continuous needs if/whether + statement order.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow rhetorical not-only inversion and frozen needn't have; still refuse bare inversion after asked on ordinary questions. Mark false on where should and asked was anyone.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She packed a apple in her lunchbox for the hike.
He bought an umbrella before the outdoor concert.
We need an new bicycle for the weekend trip.
The coach approved an plan for the relay team.
Please send me an email with the rehearsal times.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She packed a apple in her lunchbox for the hike.**

"apple" begins with a vowel sound, so English needs "an apple," not "a apple." Repair it to "an apple" and leave the rest of the lunchbox sentence alone. Matching a/an to the letter you see instead of the sound you hear is the classic mistake here.
**B) He bought an umbrella before the outdoor concert.**

"Umbrella" starts with a vowel sound, so "an umbrella" is the correct first-mention form. The sentence introduces one countable item before the concert, which is exactly where a/an belongs. Nothing else in the line needs fixing.
**C) We need an new bicycle for the weekend trip.**

"new" begins with a consonant sound (/n/), so English needs "a new bicycle," not "an new bicycle." The adjective does not change the a/an rule — you still listen to the sound right after a/an. Repair only the article before new.
**D) The coach approved an plan for the relay team.**

"plan" begins with a consonant sound, so use "a plan," not "an plan." The coach, the approval, and the relay team can stay exactly as written; only the form before plan is wrong. Think consonant sound → a.
**E) Please send me an email with the rehearsal times.**

"Email" begins with a vowel sound (/iː/), so "an email" is correct. Saying the next word aloud confirms the vowel onset immediately. This is a clean, standard first-mention pattern.
tasks.solution_overview:
You are packing lunch, shopping for outdoor gear, and emailing rehearsal times — everyday scenes where a and an sit right before a singular countable noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This task is only about matching a versus an to the sound that follows, not to the first letter on the page. An adjective between the article and the noun still counts: listen to the first sound of that adjective. First-mention countable nouns take a/an; the wrong shape of that article is what makes a line fail.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Say the word right after a/an aloud. If it starts with a vowel sound, choose an; if it starts with a consonant sound, choose a. Spelling alone (apple, umbrella, email, new, plan) can mislead you — sound wins every time.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide asked for an honest answer about the trail conditions.
They hired a European tutor for their French exchange.
She completed a MBA while volunteering at the library.
We reserved an hotel near the festival grounds.
He is an university student in biology.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The guide asked for an honest answer about the trail conditions.**

"Honest" starts with a silent h, so the spoken form begins with a vowel sound and takes "an." The spelling still shows h, which is why this feels like a trap until you hear it. Silent letters decide a/an by sound, not by the letters you see.
**B) They hired a European tutor for their French exchange.**

"European" begins with a /j/ sound (like "you"), which counts as a consonant sound, so "a European" is correct. The eu- spelling looks vowel-first, but the glide at the start blocks an. Treat that "y" onset like any other consonant sound.
**C) She completed a MBA while volunteering at the library.**

"MBA" is normally read letter by letter, starting with /em/, a vowel sound, so it needs "an MBA." Repair "a MBA" to "an MBA"; the volunteering clause can stay. With abbreviations, base a/an on how you pronounce the first letter name.
**D) We reserved an hotel near the festival grounds.**

In standard modern pronunciation, "hotel" keeps the /h/, so "a hotel" is the usual form, not "an hotel." Prefer a before clearly sounded h-words in contemporary English. Older "an hotel" usage is not the safe exam default here.
**E) He is an university student in biology.**

"University" starts with a /j/ sound, so the correct form is "a university student." If you can hear a "y" glide at the start, choose a — the written u does not unlock an. Repair only the article before university.
tasks.solution_overview:
Trail talk, a French exchange tutor, an MBA, a hotel near the festival, and a biology student: the same a/an choice, but sound and spelling pull in different directions.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

These lines turn on pronunciation traps — silent h, the "y" glide in European and university, letter-name openings in abbreviations, and whether hotel keeps a sounded /h/. Spelling is only a hint; the spoken onset decides a versus an.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Say the next word (or abbreviation) the way you would in careful speech. Silent letters, initialisms starting with vowel-letter names, and /j/-glides are the three places people guess wrong — check those first on every line.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I read a novel yesterday; the novel kept me awake until dawn.
Please close a window; it is freezing in here.
She joined the choir as a junior soprano in 2022.
Could you pass me a salt from the tray?
They opened an café on the corner last spring.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I read a novel yesterday; the novel kept me awake until dawn.**

First mention uses "a novel"; the second mention switches to "the novel" because the same book is now identified. That a → the handoff is exactly how English tracks reference across two clauses. Nothing in the chain is accidental.
**B) Please close a window; it is freezing in here.**

In this situation the window is a specific one in the room, so English expects "the window," not "a window." When both speakers can identify the thing from context, prefer the. Repair to "Please close the window…"
**C) She joined the choir as a junior soprano in 2022.**

Roles after "as" commonly take a/an for one role among many: "as a junior soprano." The choir is already definite with the, and the role is introduced as a class member with a. Occupations and voice parts follow this pattern cleanly.
**D) Could you pass me a salt from the tray?**

At the table, "salt" is a specific shared item, so "the salt" is the natural choice. Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting take the, not a. Repair to "pass me the salt from the tray."
**E) They opened an café on the corner last spring.**

"Café" begins with a consonant sound (/k/), so use "a café," not "an café." A vowel letter in the spelling does not override a consonant sound. Repair only the article before café.
tasks.solution_overview:
A novel at midnight, a freezing room, a choir role, salt on the tray, and a corner café — these lines mix first mention, shared objects, roles, and one a/an sound trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on whether the noun is newly introduced or already clear to both speakers. First mention often takes a/an; a second mention of the same thing switches to the. Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting also prefer the, while roles after "as" commonly keep a/an.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask: Can both people already point to this exact thing? If yes, lean toward the. If the noun is one of a class being introduced — including a role among many — lean toward a/an. Then double-check café-type sound matches so a misspelled an does not sneak through.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sun was still low when the runners started.
Moon looks unusually bright tonight over the harbour.
She is only person who finished the crossword.
This is same recipe we used last winter.
He is the tallest player on the school team.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The sun was still low when the runners started.**

Unique celestial bodies take "the": "the sun." The runners are also definite in this race context, so the before runners fits as well. One-of-a-kind natural referents almost always need the.
**B) Moon looks unusually bright tonight over the harbour.**

"Moon" in this sense needs "the moon"; leaving it bare is not standard. Pair the with unique natural landmarks and celestial objects the same way you do with the sun. Repair to "The moon looks unusually bright…"
**C) She is only person who finished the crossword.**

"Only" before a singular noun requires "the only person." Patterns with only, same, next, and last usually need the locked in before the noun. Repair to "the only person who finished the crossword."
**D) This is same recipe we used last winter.**

The fixed pattern is "the same recipe," not bare "same recipe." "Same" almost never stands without the in this comparative use. Insert the before same and the relative clause can stay.
**E) He is the tallest player on the school team.**

Superlative forms take "the": "the tallest player." If you see -est (or most + adjective) for a unique ranking in a set, expect the. The school-team frame makes that unique ranking clear.
tasks.solution_overview:
Sunrise races, a bright harbour moon, a crossword finisher, a winter recipe, and a school-team ranking — these lines hunt for the with unique, exclusive, or superlative reference.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unique things (the sun, the moon), superlatives (the tallest), and words like only and same strongly prefer the. The noun must point to one identifiable item in the world or in a set; if that exclusivity marker is missing the, the line fails.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for uniqueness markers first: celestial one-offs, only, same, and -est / most rankings. If you see one of those, expect the before the noun. Bare Moon, only person, or same recipe without the is almost always the error.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hikers received useful advice from the ranger.
She gave me an advice about packing for cold weather.
We still need more informations before we choose a route.
The lab ordered new equipment for the science fair.
They bought an furniture for the guest room.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The hikers received useful advice from the ranger.**

"Advice" is uncountable, so it appears with zero article here and is modified by "useful," not by a/an. Uncountable abstract nouns often take zero article when used in a general sense. The line models the pattern you want to protect.
**B) She gave me an advice about packing for cold weather.**

"Advice" cannot take "an"; say "some advice" or "a piece of advice." If you need a countable unit, use a piece/bit/item of + the uncountable noun. Specific packing tips still do not unlock an advice.
**C) We still need more informations before we choose a route.**

"Information" has no plural form in standard English; use "more information," not "informations." Watch for false plurals on uncountable nouns — the -s ending is the whole problem here. Keep more and drop the illegal plural.
**D) The lab ordered new equipment for the science fair.**

"Equipment" is uncountable and correctly appears without a/an; "new" simply describes the mass noun. Zero article + adjective + uncountable noun is a common correct pattern. The science-fair purpose does not suddenly make equipment countable.
**E) They bought an furniture for the guest room.**

"Furniture" is uncountable, so "an furniture" is impossible; use "furniture" or "a piece of furniture." Do not place a/an directly before classic uncountables like furniture, equipment, or advice. Strip an, or quantify with a piece of.
tasks.solution_overview:
Ranger tips, packing advice, route information, science-fair equipment, and guest-room furniture — classic uncountable nouns that push back against a/an and false plurals.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Uncountable nouns reject a/an and usually reject plural -s. General reference prefers zero article (useful advice, new equipment), while a quantifying phrase such as a piece of is the way to carve out a unit when you need one.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the noun is a mass/abstract (advice, information, equipment, furniture). If yes, ban a/an directly before it and check plural endings too. Prefer zero article for general talk, or a piece/bit/item of when you need a countable unit.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Progress on the mural has been slower than expected.
The news were surprising for the whole neighbourhood.
Research shows that morning light can improve mood.
We lack an evidence to support that claim.
Traffic was heavy on the way to the airport.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Progress on the mural has been slower than expected.**

"Progress" is uncountable and correctly used with zero article for a general process underway. Zero article is normal with progress, research, and similar abstracts. The mural phrase narrows topic without forcing a/an.
**B) The news were surprising for the whole neighbourhood.**

"News" is uncountable and takes a singular verb: "The news was surprising." The determiner "the" can stay; the verb must agree. "News" looks plural but behaves as singular — that mismatch is the whole trap.
**C) Research shows that morning light can improve mood.**

General research findings use zero article: "Research shows…" When you mean research as a field or body of work in general, omit a/the. The that-clause content does not change the bare subject pattern.
**D) We lack an evidence to support that claim.**

"Evidence" is uncountable, so "an evidence" is wrong; use "evidence" or "a piece of evidence." Specificity about a claim does not make evidence countable with a/an. Drop an, or quantify with a piece of.
**E) Traffic was heavy on the way to the airport.**

"Traffic" is uncountable and takes zero article in this general statement about conditions. Mass nouns for weather, traffic, and similar conditions usually need no a/an. The airport trip supplies setting, not a countable unit.
tasks.solution_overview:
A mural's progress, neighbourhood news, mood research, courtroom-style evidence, and airport traffic — everyday mass nouns that look countable until agreement or a/an goes wrong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Several everyday nouns are uncountable even when they end in -s or feel countable. Keep zero article for general reference and avoid a/an before evidence, progress, and traffic. News takes singular agreement despite its plural look.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Test number first: news/progress/research/evidence/traffic usually refuse plural verbs and refuse a/an as a direct determiner. Prefer zero article for general statements; allow the when a specific body of news is framed, but still keep singular was, not were.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Children need clear routines at home.
The neighbours expect quieter evenings during exam week.
Water is still scarce after the long drought.
She drinks the coffee every morning before class.
Teachers should explain key ideas carefully.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Children need clear routines at home.**

Plural nouns in a general sense take zero article: "Children need…" General plurals usually omit the because no definite set of kids has been named. The home setting stays general too.
**B) The neighbours expect quieter evenings during exam week.**

Here "the neighbours" can refer to the known people next door, so the is acceptable and natural. The + plural is fine when the group is definite in context. Exam week just supplies the time frame.
**C) Water is still scarce after the long drought.**

Uncountable "water" used generically takes zero article. Materials and substances in general statements often need no determiner. The drought explains why, without turning water into a definite bottle or tap.
**D) She drinks the coffee every morning before class.**

Habitual general coffee-drinking uses zero article: "She drinks coffee every morning," not "the coffee," unless a specific coffee is meant. Do not force the onto uncountables used in a general habitual sense. Repair by dropping the before coffee.
**E) Teachers should explain key ideas carefully.**

Plural "Teachers" in a general professional statement correctly takes zero article. Job-title plurals meaning "teachers in general" stay bare. The advice is about the profession as a class, not one named staff list.
tasks.solution_overview:
Kids' routines, quieter exam-week evenings, scarce water, morning coffee, and careful teachers — general plurals and general uncountables versus a forced the.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

General plurals and general uncountables prefer zero article. Use the only when the group or substance is already limited to a known set. Habitual coffee as a substance is bare; the coffee usually means a specific brew already identified.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each plural or mass noun, ask whether the speaker means "in general" or "this known set." General → usually zero (Children, Water, Teachers). Known neighbours next door → the neighbours is fine. Habitual substance use → drop the unless a specific serving is meant.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He goes to work by bus on most weekdays.
She travelled to Lisbon by a train last Friday.
They sent the parcels by courier overnight.
I usually go to the home after the evening class.
We went to school together in the same district.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He goes to work by bus on most weekdays.**

Fixed patterns "go to work" and "by bus" both use zero article. Memorise by + transport and go to work/school/bed as zero-article chunks. The weekday habit fits the institutional-purpose reading perfectly.
**B) She travelled to Lisbon by a train last Friday.**

The transport pattern is "by train," not "by a train." After by for means of transport, do not insert a/an. Repair to "by train last Friday" and keep Lisbon as the destination.
**C) They sent the parcels by courier overnight.**

"By courier" follows the same zero-article transport/delivery pattern. By + service/means is typically bare. The parcels can stay definite with the; the means phrase still stays bare.
**D) I usually go to the home after the evening class.**

The fixed expression is "go home," never "go to the home" in this meaning. Home after go/arrive/get normally takes no to and no the. Repair to "go home after the evening class."
**E) We went to school together in the same district.**

"Go to school" with zero article means attendance as a student, which fits this sentence. Purpose-of-institution uses often drop the. The same district just locates that shared schooling.
tasks.solution_overview:
Commuting by bus, a Friday train to Lisbon, overnight courier parcels, going home after class, and schooling in the same district — frozen chunks where articles do not follow ordinary logic.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Several high-frequency chunks freeze the determiner choice: by bus/train, go to work/school, and go home. Treat them as fixed patterns rather than building them word by word with "logical" a/the.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Whenever you see by + transport or go to work/school/home, recall the memorised frame first. by train stays bare; go home drops both to and the in this meaning; go to school (attendance) stays bare. If someone inserted a or the inside those frames, that is usually the fault.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Her brother is still in hospital after the operation.
We drove past the hospital on our way to the lake.
Three activists are in the prison for peaceful protest.
The prison on the hill dates from the nineteenth century.
She stayed in bed until noon because of a migraine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Her brother is still in hospital after the operation.**

British English uses zero article in "in hospital" when the person is there as a patient. Purpose (patient/prisoner/student) often means zero article with the institution. The operation supplies why without turning the phrase into a building tour.
**B) We drove past the hospital on our way to the lake.**

When the building itself is meant as a location landmark, "the hospital" is correct. Switch to the when you mean the building, not the institutional purpose. The lake trip makes the physical pass-by reading obvious.
**C) Three activists are in the prison for peaceful protest.**

** Purpose reading → zero; building reading → the.

Trap: As inmates, the natural British pattern is "in prison," not "in the prison." Purpose reading → zero; building reading → the. Repair to "in prison for peaceful protest."
**D) The prison on the hill dates from the nineteenth century.**

Post-operation recovery, driving past a hospital, activists and a hillside prison, and a migraine day in bed — institution nouns flipping between purpose and building.

Name the head noun first and ask whether you could count separate units. If yes, reject much and little; if no, reject many and few. Then confirm the quantifier matches that class before you tick true or false.

**A) The amount of litter on the beach has fallen since spring.**

"Litter" is a mass of rubbish, not a countable row of items, so "amount of" is the right frame. Singular "has fallen" agrees with that mass reading. Use this as the clean beachside model for amount + uncountable.
**B) The number of cyclists has risen sharply.**

"Cyclists" are countable people, so "number of" is required. The phrase "the number of…" is grammatically singular, which is why "has" is correct even though cyclists is plural. Lock verb agreement to number, not to the people inside the of-phrase.
**C) The amount of cyclists has decreased this month.**

cyclists are countable, so "amount of cyclists" is the classic mix-up — repair to "the number of cyclists." Amount stays with masses you measure; number stays with units you count.
**D) A large number of neighbours joined the street clean-up.**

"A large number of" correctly introduces plural countable neighbours for the street clean-up. This construction roughly means "many neighbours," so a plural verb like "joined" is natural. Contrast it mentally with singular "the number of".
**E) There was a large amount of fog over the harbour.**

"Fog" is weather-as-mass, so "amount of fog" and singular "was" both fit. You would not say "many fogs" in this harbour scene. Keep amount + uncountable as your default for fog, traffic, and similar masses.
tasks.solution_overview:
This card is all beach litter, cyclists, neighbours, and harbour fog — still the same amount-versus-number decision underneath.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If the units are discrete (cyclists, neighbours), choose number. If you are measuring a mass (litter, fog), choose amount. "The number of" then pulls a singular verb even when the noun after of is plural.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline the noun after of or after amount/number. Ask whether you would answer with a headcount or with a mass measure. Pick the matching noun phrase, then check that the verb follows the head of the quantifier phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: All of the equipment is new.
The equipments in the lab need updating.
We bought three new pieces of equipment.
There are many evidences against the claim.
The evidence supports the detective's conclusion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) All of the equipment is new.**

"Equipment" stays uncountable even when you mean several machines, so the verb is singular "is". "All of the equipment" therefore behaves like a single mass subject. This is the safe detective-lab pattern exams love to test.
**B) The equipments in the lab need updating.**

"equipments" is not standard — keep "equipment" and, if you must count, write "pieces of equipment". The plural -s here is the whole error; the lab scene does not license a countable plural form.
**C) We bought three new pieces of equipment.**

"Pieces of equipment" is the approved counting scaffold: piece unlocks a number while equipment itself stays uncountable. Three pieces is therefore grammatical buying language. Memorise piece/item of for any mass noun you need to count.
**D) There are many evidences against the claim.**

"evidence" is uncountable, so "many evidences" fails on both the pluralisation and the countable quantifier. Repair to "much evidence" or "several pieces of evidence," and drop the -s on evidence.
**E) The evidence supports the detective's conclusion.**

Uncountable "evidence" takes a singular verb, here "supports". Even if the detective weighs several facts, the noun still behaves as one mass. Keep information, research, and evidence in the same singular-mass family.
tasks.solution_overview:
Lab kit and detective evidence dominate this set — classic uncountable nouns that learners over-pluralise.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Equipment and evidence do not take a plural -s in exam English. Count them only with piece/item of, and keep the verb singular when the bare noun is the subject. "Many evidences" and "equipments" are near-automatic false marks.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see -s on equipment or evidence, reject it. If the sentence already uses pieces of…, accept the count scaffold. Otherwise demand singular agreement with the mass noun itself.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Less information was available than we expected.
Fewer matches were cancelled this week.
Less noise was reported after the new windows arrived.
There is little doubt about the team's formation.
There is little doubt about the festival schedule.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Less information was available than we expected.**

"Information" is uncountable, so "less" is the precise comparative. Singular "was" matches that mass subject. Keep this as your clean less + uncountable baseline.
**B) Fewer matches were cancelled this week.**

"Matches" is a countable plural, so "fewer" is the form exams prefer. You could answer "how many matches?" with a number, which locks the choice. Treat fewer as the default for cancelled fixtures, tickets, and similar plurals.
**C) Less noise was reported after the new windows arrived.**

"Noise" is a mass, so "less noise" is correct after the new windows. You are reducing volume of sound, not counting separate noises. Mass nouns like noise, traffic, and waste almost always take less, not fewer.
**D) There is little doubt about the team's formation.**

"Doubt" here is uncountable, and "there is little…" is the matching pattern with singular "is". The sports formation topic does not change the grammar. Remember little = not much of a mass.
**E) There is little doubt about the festival schedule.**

Same grammatical frame again: uncountable "doubt" with "little" and singular "is". Repeating the pattern with a festival schedule helps you feel how stable the rule is. Use there is/are only after you know the noun's count class.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five lines are intentionally clean — information, cancelled matches, window noise, team formation, and festival schedules — so you can lock less/little versus fewer before the later traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Less and little partner with uncountables (information, noise, doubt). Fewer partners with countable plurals (matches). Singular there is fits little + uncountable.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each sentence, classify the noun, then choose less/little or fewer accordingly. Because this card has no planted errors, use it as a positive model rather than hunting for damage.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We still need much more data before we publish the survey.
How many volunteers attended the beach clean-up?
How much volunteers attended the beach clean-up?
Only a few bakers entered the pie contest.
Only a little bakers entered the pie contest.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We still need much more data before we publish the survey.**

In careful exam English, "data" is treated as uncountable, so "much more data" is acceptable. The survey-publishing context does not turn data into a countable plural here. Keep much/little as your default with data on this paper.
**B) How many volunteers attended the beach clean-up?**

Volunteers are people you can number, so "how many" is the correct question frame. The beach clean-up theme still obeys the countable rule. If the answer could be "twelve people," you needed many, not much.
**C) How much volunteers attended the beach clean-up?**

"volunteers" are countable, so "how much volunteers" is wrong — repair to "how many volunteers". How much asks about mass or quantity of an uncountable, not a headcount of people.
**D) Only a few bakers entered the pie contest.**

"A few" correctly quantifies plural countable bakers and carries a neutral or mildly positive "some" feel. The pie contest remains a countable scene. Contrast a few (some) with bare few (almost none) later, but grammar here is solid.
**E) Only a little bakers entered the pie contest.**

"a little" belongs with uncountables, but "bakers" is plural countable — repair to "a few bakers". Think "a little flour" versus "a few bakers" and the mix-up becomes obvious.
tasks.solution_overview:
Survey data, beach volunteers, and a pie contest bake the how much/how many and a few/a little contrasts into one card.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

How many asks about countable sets of people or items; how much asks about masses. A few partners with countables; a little partners with uncountables. Exam English often treats data as a mass noun with much.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For questions, imagine the answer type: a headcount needs many, a mass needs much. For a few/a little, check whether the noun can take a plural -s as separate units. Reject any cross-pairing before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of the novel was unfinished.
Much of the novels was unfinished.
Many of the novels were unfinished.
Several of the chapters were cut.
A great deal of research has been published on sleep.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Much of the novel was unfinished.**

"Much of" plus a singular unit ("the novel") is natural and takes singular "was". You are talking about a large part of one book, not counting books. Treat much of + singular/mass as a stock pattern.
**B) Much of the novels was unfinished.**

after plural "novels," you need "many of the novels were," not "much of… was". Much of wants a singular or mass noun; the plural forces many of and a plural verb.
**C) Many of the novels were unfinished.**

This is the repaired plural version: many of + plural countable + plural "were". Of-phrases still demand agreement with the counted noun's number. Use it as the contrast twin of A.
**D) Several of the chapters were cut.**

"Several" always implies more than two countable units, here chapters, with plural "were". The editing scene does not change the rule. If you cannot pluralise the noun, several cannot apply.
**E) A great deal of research has been published on sleep.**

"A great deal of" behaves like much and pairs with uncountable "research" plus singular "has". Sleep research stays a mass topic in exam English. Prefer studies only when you need an explicit countable plural.
tasks.solution_overview:
Novels, chapters, and sleep research put the of-phrase rules under the spotlight: much of, many of, several of, and a great deal of.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Look at the noun after of. Singular or mass nouns take much of / a great deal of with singular verbs. Plural countables take many of / several of with plural verbs. Mixing much of with a bare plural is the planted trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Circle the noun after of, classify it, then choose the quantifier and verb together. Do not let the word much distract you when the noun is already plural — switch to many and plural agreement.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She gave me some useful advice on the audition.
She gave me some useful advices on the audition.
We need more detailed information from the guide.
We need more detailed informations from the guide.
The news was announced after the match ended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She gave me some useful advice on the audition.**

"Advice" is uncountable, so "some useful advice" is the natural audition tip. You never add -s for ordinary exam English. If you must count, switch to "a piece of advice".
**B) She gave me some useful advices on the audition.**

"advices" is the classic over-pluralisation — keep "advice" or count with "pieces of advice". The audition context cannot rescue the -s ending.
**C) We need more detailed information from the guide.**

"Information" likewise stays uncountable and takes no plural -s. "More detailed information" is exactly how a guide briefing should read. Treat information like advice: mass form only.
**D) We need more detailed informations from the guide.**

"informations" is ungrammatical — keep "information," or say "bits/pieces of information" if you need a count. The false plural is the whole story here.
**E) The news was announced after the match ended.**

"News" looks plural but is uncountable and takes singular "was". After the match, the announcement is still "the news is/was," never "are/were" in careful use. Remember the -s is spelling, not a plural marker.
tasks.solution_overview:
Audition advice, guide information, and post-match news are high-frequency uncountables that learners love to pluralise wrongly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Advice, information, and news stay singular as masses. Reject -s forms and keep singular verbs with news. Piece/bit of is the only clean counting route.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Spot any -s on advice or information and mark false. For news, ignore the deceptive spelling and demand a singular verb. Accept the unmarked mass forms as true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is too much homework in this module.
There are too many homeworks in this module.
We have made little progress on the mural.
We have made few progress on the mural.
Only a little time remains before the concert starts.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There is too much homework in this module.**

"Homework" is a mass of study work, so "too much" plus singular "is" is correct. Modules feel heavy in volume, not in countable "homeworks". Keep much/little with this school mass noun.
**B) There are too many homeworks in this module.**

"homeworks" is not standard — keep "homework" uncountable with much/is. If it feels like a pile of study work, treat it as a mass, not a countable set.
**C) We have made little progress on the mural.**

"Progress" is uncountable, so "little progress" correctly reports a small amount of mural advancement. You would not say "few progresses" in this sense. Little keeps the slightly negative "not much" tone.
**D) We have made few progress on the mural.**

"few" needs a plural countable, but "progress" is uncountable — repair to "little progress". The mural topic does not turn progress into a countable noun.
**E) Only a little time remains before the concert starts.**

"Time" as remaining duration is uncountable, so "a little time" is right before the concert. A little is the positive "some" twin of bare little. Duration questions almost always want much/little, not many/few.
tasks.solution_overview:
Module homework, mural progress, and concert countdown time are everyday mass nouns that take much/little, not many/few.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Homework, progress, and time (duration) stay uncountable. Reject homeworks and few progress. Notice the tone split between little and a little, but do not let tone override countability.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the noun names a pile, process, or duration rather than separate countable units. If it does, choose much/little and singular agreement; reject many/few immediately.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Fewer runners than expected finished the half marathon.
Less runners than expected finished the half marathon.
The café used less sugar in the lemonade this summer.
The café used fewer sugar in the lemonade this summer.
There were fewer typos in the revised draft.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Fewer runners than expected finished the half marathon.**

"Runners" is countable plural, so "fewer" is the precise comparative for the half marathon. Exams still reward fewer with people and other countable plurals. Read this as the gold standard less-versus-fewer line.
**B) Less runners than expected finished the half marathon.**

** exams still reward fewer + countable plural.

Trap: plural people take "fewer," not "less" — repair to "fewer runners". Informal speech sometimes blurs the line, but exam marking stays strict here.
**C) The café used less sugar in the lemonade this summer.**

"Sugar" is a mass ingredient in the lemonade, so "less sugar" is correct. You are reducing quantity of a substance, not counting sugar crystals as units. Switch to fewer only if you count spoons or bags.
**D) The café used fewer sugar in the lemonade this summer.**

** fewer only works if the noun is plural and countable.

Trap: mass "sugar" takes "less," not "fewer". Fewer only works when the noun is plural and countable, which sugar is not in this café scene.
**E) There were fewer typos in the revised draft.**

"Typos" are countable errors, so "fewer typos" is exact. If you can put a number in front (ten typos), use fewer. Draft-editing language is a reliable countable domain.
tasks.solution_overview:
Half-marathon runners, café lemonade sugar, and draft typos are the classic less-versus-fewer battlefield.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Plural countables (runners, typos) want fewer. Mass quantities (sugar) want less. Informal "less people" is still a trap on this exam track.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip the scene down to the noun and ask "can I count these as separate units?" Yes → fewer; no → less. Apply that same test to both the race lines and the café lines.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A large amount of evidence was presented in court.
A large number of evidence was presented in court.
Several pieces of evidence were disclosed yesterday.
The equipment have already been installed.
Most of the furniture was damaged in transit.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A large amount of evidence was presented in court.**

"Evidence" is uncountable, so "amount of evidence" with singular "was" is courtroom-safe. You measure the mass of evidence, not a number of evidences. Keep amount for evidence, equipment, and furniture.
**B) A large number of evidence was presented in court.**

** number of + plural countables only.

Trap: "number of" needs a plural countable, but "evidence" is not one — repair to "amount of evidence" or "a large number of pieces of evidence". Never write number of evidence.
**C) Several pieces of evidence were disclosed yesterday.**

"Pieces of evidence" correctly builds countable units, so plural "were" follows. This is how you count when the base noun must stay uncountable. Piece of is your courtroom unlock key.
**D) The equipment have already been installed.**

** all the equipment is … / has been …

Trap: uncountable "equipment" needs singular "has," not "have". Say "the equipment has already been installed" even if many devices were fitted. Agreement tracks the mass noun, not the imagined items.
**E) Most of the furniture was damaged in transit.**

"Furniture" is uncountable and takes singular "was" when damaged in transit. Luggage and equipment share the same pattern. Do not invent "furnitures" or force a plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
Court evidence, installed equipment, and damaged furniture stay uncountable even when you mean several items.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Use amount or pieces of with evidence; keep singular verbs with equipment and furniture. Number of + evidence is an automatic fail unless you insert pieces.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First decide whether the head noun is a mass. If yes, ban bare number of and plural verbs. Only accept plural agreement when piece/item creates real countable units.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is not much time left to revise the essay.
There are not many times left to revise the essay.
We have plenty of chances to reschedule the picnic.
We have plenty of chancs to reschedule the picnic.
Hardly any of the guests supported the playlist change.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There is not much time left to revise the essay.**

Here "time" means remaining duration, which is uncountable, so "much" and singular "is" are correct. Essay revision left on the clock is a mass, not a countable set. Read not much time as little time remaining.
**B) There are not many times left to revise the essay.**

** many times = frequency; much time = duration.

Trap: "many times" usually means frequency ("often"), which twists the intended remaining-duration meaning — repair to "much time". For countdown-to-deadline language, stay with uncountable time.
**C) We have plenty of chances to reschedule the picnic.**

"Chances" is a countable plural, and "plenty of" works happily with countables. Picnic rescheduling options can be numbered. Plenty of also works with uncountables, but here the plural noun already fits.
**D) We have plenty of chancs to reschedule the picnic.**

** watch irregular -y → -ies and silent-e plurals on countables.

Trap: the plural spelling must be "chances," not "chancs". Even though plenty of is fine, the misshapen countable plural sinks the sentence. Watch silent-e and -y → -ies plurals on countables.
**E) Hardly any of the guests supported the playlist change.**

"Hardly any of" plus plural countable guests is a natural negative quantifier pattern. It means almost none of the guests liked the playlist change. Negative quantifiers still require the right noun type underneath.
tasks.solution_overview:
Essay-revision time, picnic chances, and playlist guests mix duration, countable opportunities, and negative quantifiers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Time as duration is uncountable (much time), while chances and guests are countable. Hardly any still needs a compatible noun after of. Spelling errors on countable plurals count as false.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate duration from frequency when you see time/times. Confirm countable plurals are spelled correctly after plenty of. Then check that negative of-phrases sit on the right noun class.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A few of the students raised lighting concerns.
Few of the students raised lighting concerns, which surprised the tutor.
Little of the flour remains for the final batch.
A little of the flour remains for the final batch.
Few of the flour remains for the final batch.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A few of the students raised lighting concerns.**

"A few of" plus plural countable students correctly signals a small but real number. The lighting-concern scene stays countable throughout. Tone is neutral or positive: some students spoke up.
**B) Few of the students raised lighting concerns, which surprised the tutor.**

Bare "few of" is also grammatical; it stresses scarcity and a more negative tone. The tutor's surprise fits "almost none," but the countable requirement is unchanged. Few versus a few is tone, not a grammar fork, when the noun is countable.
**C) Little of the flour remains for the final batch.**

"Little of" plus uncountable "flour" correctly stresses that almost none remains for the batch. Baking language is a natural mass domain. Little of the + uncountable is the mirror of few of the + plural.
**D) A little of the flour remains for the final batch.**

"A little of" is equally grammatical and more positive: some flour remains. Again the noun is uncountable flour, so a little is licensed. Tone shifts; count class does not.
**E) Few of the flour remains for the final batch.**

** few of the bags/cups; little of the flour/milk.

Trap: "few of" demands a countable plural, but "flour" is a mass — repair to "little of the flour" (or "few of the bags/cups"). Crossing the countable line with food masses is the exact trap this card is built to catch.
tasks.solution_overview:
Classroom lighting feedback and bakery flour show that a few/few and a little/little are all fine — until you swap them across the countable line.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A few/few need plural countables (students). A little/little need uncountables (flour). Tone differences are real, but they do not excuse mixing few with a mass noun.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Classify the noun after of first. If it is a plural countable, accept few/a few; if it is a mass, accept little/a little. Reject the crossed pairing even when the rest of the sentence looks fluent.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of remote learners is increasing every year.
The number of remote learners are increasing every year.
A number of remote learners are requesting evening classes.
A number of remote learners is requesting evening classes.
The amount of remote learners is increasing every year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of remote learners is increasing every year.**

"The number of" makes a singular subject even though learners is plural, so "is" is correct. Remote-learning growth is still about one rising figure. Lock the verb to number, not to learners.
**B) The number of remote learners are increasing every year.**

** lock the verb to number (singular), not to learners.

Trap: plural "are" after "the number of" is wrong — keep singular "is". Do not let the nearby plural noun steal the agreement.
**C) A number of remote learners are requesting evening classes.**

"A number of" means several and normally takes a plural verb, here "are requesting". Evening-class demand from several learners fits that plural reading. Contrast a number (plural) with the number (singular).
**D) A number of remote learners is requesting evening classes.**

** contrast the number (singular) vs a number (plural).

Trap: with "a number of learners," prefer plural "are," not singular "is". The article a versus the flips the agreement rule, and this line gets that flip wrong.
**E) The amount of remote learners is increasing every year.**

** amount of work; number of learners.

Trap: learners are countable people, so use "number of," not "amount of". Amount of work would be fine; amount of learners is not.
highlights: A number of remote learners are
A number of remote learners is
tasks.solution_overview:
Remote learners requesting evening classes stack two traps at once: the number versus a number, and amount versus number.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"The number of" is singular; "a number of" is plural in sense. People must be counted with number, not amount. Verb agreement follows the determiner before number.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the word before number first (the/a), choose the verb, then check whether people should be under number at all. Reject amount of + people immediately.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of what the coach recommended has already been tried.
Many of what the coach recommended has already been tried.
None of the evidence points to intentional foul play.
None of the evidences point to intentional foul play.
Both of the equipment need replacing before the trip.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Much of what the coach recommended has already been tried.**

"Much of what…" treats the coach's advice-content as an uncountable mass and takes singular "has". You are not counting separate tips in this wording. Much of what / much of the advice is a reliable singular pattern.
**B) Many of what the coach recommended has already been tried.**

** many of those drills / many of the tips.

Trap: "what the coach recommended" is not framed as a plural countable set, so "many of what" is unnatural — prefer "many of those drills" or "many of the tips". Keep many of for explicit plurals.
**C) None of the evidence points to intentional foul play.**

With uncountable evidence, "none of the evidence" commonly takes singular "points" in careful formal English. The foul-play sports frame does not change the mass noun. Prefer singular agreement here on exam papers.
**D) None of the evidences point to intentional foul play.**

** none of the evidence / none of the pieces of evidence.

Trap: "evidences" is wrong; keep evidence uncountable. Write "none of the evidence" or "none of the pieces of evidence" if you insist on counting units.
**E) Both of the equipment need replacing before the trip.**

** both needs two countable units.

Trap: "both" needs two countable units, but "equipment" is uncountable — repair to "both pieces of equipment need replacing". Before the trip, count with piece/item or name two devices.
tasks.solution_overview:
Coach recommendations, foul-play evidence, and trip equipment push of-phrases into advanced territory: much of what, none of, and both.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Much of what… works as a mass; many of what does not. None of the evidence stays singular and uncountable. Both only attaches to countable pairs, never to bare equipment.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask what kind of noun the quantifier expects, then inspect the material after of. If the quantifier demands count units and the noun is a mass, insert piece/item or reject the line.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We have received a great deal of positive feedback.
We have received a great number of positive feedback.
There was a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.
There were a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.
Only a small proportion of listeners chose the jazz option.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We have received a great deal of positive feedback.**

"A great deal of" means roughly much and correctly quantifies uncountable "feedback". Survey or performance feedback stays a mass on this paper. Keep deal for uncountables and number for plural countables.
**B) We have received a great number of positive feedback.**

** a great number of comments/emails; a great deal of feedback.

Trap: feedback is uncountable, so "a great number of feedback" fails — repair to "a great deal of feedback" or "a great number of comments/emails". Number wants things you can pluralise.
**C) There was a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.**

"Quantity of" with mass "rainwater" and singular "was" is correct for the tank. Quantity and amount often take singular agreement with mass nouns. The weather-collection scene is pure uncountable measuring.
**D) There were a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.**

** there was a large quantity of …

Trap: singular "quantity" as the grammatical subject needs "was," not "were". There was a large quantity of… is the fixed frame here.
**E) Only a small proportion of listeners chose the jazz option.**

"Proportion of" plus plural countable listeners is standard survey language, and "chose" fits the plural sense. Jazz-option polling is a natural home for proportion/percentage of. Reports use this pattern constantly.
tasks.solution_overview:
Feedback, rainwater tanks, and jazz-poll listeners look similar under deal/number/quantity/proportion — but each head selects a different noun type and verb.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Deal pairs with uncountables like feedback; number needs plural countables. Quantity with a mass often takes singular there was. Proportion of listeners is fine with a plural countable.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match the quantifier to countability first, then force the verb to agree with the real head of the phrase. Reject number of + feedback and plural were with singular quantity.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Research shows that morning light can improve alertness.
Researches show that morning light can improve alertness.
Several researches have confirmed the same pattern.
Several studies have confirmed the same pattern.
A piece of research published last year challenged the consensus.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Research shows that morning light can improve alertness.**

Uncountable "research" correctly takes singular "shows". Morning-light alertness is presented as a body of research, not as counted papers. Keep research is / research shows as your default.
**B) Researches show that morning light can improve alertness.**

** use studies/projects when you need a plural countable.

Trap: do not pluralise academic "research" as "researches" in this sense — switch to studies or projects when you need a countable plural. The -es form is the error.
**C) Several researches have confirmed the same pattern.**

** several needs a countable plural.

Trap: "several" needs a countable plural, and "researches" is unidiomatic — prefer "several studies" or "several research projects". Several cannot rescue a bad mass pluralisation.
**D) Several studies have confirmed the same pattern.**

"Studies" is the countable counterpart that "several" was looking for. This is the clean repair of the researches lines. Distinguish research (mass) from studies (count).
**E) A piece of research published last year challenged the consensus.**

"A piece of research" is an acceptable formal count expression for one study. Piece of again unlocks counting without pluralising research itself. Last year's challenge to the consensus fits that single-unit frame.

**Tip:** ** piece of research / item of research in formal prose.
tasks.solution_overview:
Morning-light research behaves like evidence: keep the mass form, switch to studies for several, or use a piece of research for one unit.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Reject researches and several researches. Accept research shows, several studies, and a piece of research. Several always signals that you need a true countable plural.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the sentence needs one mass claim, keep research singular. If it needs multiple units, replace research with studies or add piece of. Never invent a plural -es on research for this exam sense.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far fewer runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.
Far less runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.
Considerably less clutter is left after the spring clean.
Considerably fewer clutter is left after the spring clean.
There has been far too much gossip and far too few facts.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Far fewer runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.**

"Far" merely intensifies "fewer," and runners remain countable. Qualifying-time athletics still wants fewer for people. Intensifiers never switch the countable rule.

**Tip:** ** far/much/considerably can modify fewer/less.
**B) Far less runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.**

** far fewer people; far less interest.

Trap: plural countable runners still need "fewer," even after "far" — repair to "far fewer runners". Far less interest would be fine; far less runners is not.
**C) Considerably less clutter is left after the spring clean.**

"Clutter" is uncountable, so "considerably less clutter" is correct after the spring clean. Considerably is only an intensifier sitting on less. Boxes would take fewer; clutter takes less.

**Tip:** ** intensifiers do not change the countable rule.
**D) Considerably fewer clutter is left after the spring clean.**

** fewer boxes; less clutter.

Trap: uncountable clutter cannot take "fewer" — repair to "less clutter". Strip considerably and the error is obvious.
**E) There has been far too much gossip and far too few facts.**

The parallel contrast is deliberate: much + uncountable gossip, few + countable facts. Mixed quantifiers in one sentence still obey each noun's type. Too and far only strengthen the same choices.
tasks.solution_overview:
Qualifying-time runners, spring-clean clutter, gossip, and facts show that intensifiers (far, considerably, too) only dress up the same less/fewer and much/few choices.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Strip the adverb and decide from the noun alone. Countable plurals keep fewer/few; uncountables keep less/much. Parallel sentences can mix quantifiers safely when each half matches its noun.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Mentally delete far/considerably/too, classify the noun, then put the intensifier back on the correct base quantifier. Reject any line where the intensifier is sitting on the wrong partner.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Each item of equipment must be labelled before the hike.
Each equipment must be labelled before the hike.
No further evidence is required at this stage.
No further evidences are required at this stage.
A substantial amount of sunlight has already flooded the atrium.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Each item of equipment must be labelled before the hike.**

"Each" needs a singular countable noun, and "item of equipment" supplies that unit before the hike. Equipment itself stays uncountable underneath the counting scaffold. This is the model repair for each + mass nouns.
**B) Each equipment must be labelled before the hike.**

** each piece/item of equipment.

Trap: "each equipment" fails because equipment is uncountable — repair to "each piece/item of equipment". The hike labelling task cannot license bare each + mass.
**C) No further evidence is required at this stage.**

"Evidence" stays uncountable with singular "is". "No further evidence is…" is standard formal English at this stage of a case. Do not pluralise evidence to force a plural verb.
**D) No further evidences are required at this stage.**

** further pieces of evidence if you insist on counting.

Trap: avoid plural "evidences" and the plural verb that follows — keep "evidence is," or say "further pieces of evidence" if you must count. The -s and are travel together as one error bundle.
**E) A substantial amount of sunlight has already flooded the atrium.**

"Amount of sunlight" treats sunlight as an uncountable mass with singular "has". Atrium flooding by light is measured, not counted as separate sunlights. Rainwater and fog often behave the same way.
tasks.solution_overview:
Pre-hike labelling, case evidence, and atrium sunlight show how determiners like each and no further expose uncountable nouns immediately.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Each demands a countable unit, so insert item/piece of before equipment. Evidence stays uncountable under no further. Amount of sunlight is a clean mass measure.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check whether the determiner presupposes countable units. If it does and the noun is a mass, require piece/item of or reject the sentence. Otherwise keep singular mass agreement.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Scarcely any of the luggage was recovered after the delay.
Scarcely any of the luggages were recovered after the delay.
A surprising number of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
A surprising amount of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
Too little attention has been paid to hydration on long walks.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Scarcely any of the luggage was recovered after the delay.**

"Luggage" is uncountable, so "scarcely any of the luggage was" is correct after the delay. Like furniture and baggage, it rejects a plural -s. Singular agreement follows the mass noun.
**B) Scarcely any of the luggages were recovered after the delay.**

** pieces of luggage if you need a count.

Trap: "luggages" is non-standard — keep luggage uncountable with singular agreement, or say "pieces of luggage". The travel-delay story does not create a countable plural form.
**C) A surprising number of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.**

"Criteria" is already plural, so "a surprising number of the criteria were" matches countability and plural verb. Remember criterion (singular) versus criteria (plural). Inconsistent standards are counted, not measured as a mass.
**D) A surprising amount of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.**

** amount of inconsistency; number of criteria.

Trap: prefer "number of the criteria"; amount is for mass nouns, not plural criteria. You might say amount of inconsistency, but criteria themselves take number.
**E) Too little attention has been paid to hydration on long walks.**

"Attention" is uncountable, so "too little attention" with singular "has" is correct for hydration advice on long walks. Little attention / much attention; few comments if you switch to a countable.
tasks.solution_overview:
Delayed luggage, inconsistent criteria, and walk hydration mix an uncountable, a plural countable learned noun, and another uncountable in one card.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Luggage stays mass and singular. Criteria are plural countable and want number of, not amount of. Attention takes little/much. Identify each head noun's class before choosing any/number/amount/little.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label luggage, criteria, and attention independently, then pick the quantifier that matches that label. Reject luggages and amount of criteria on sight.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The jury found insufficient evidence to convict.
The jury found insufficient evidences to convict.
There remains a large number of unresolved questions in the chapter.
There remains a large amount of unresolved questions in the chapter.
Fewer than ten percent of the equipment have been calibrated.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The jury found insufficient evidence to convict.**

"Insufficient evidence" correctly keeps evidence uncountable in the courtroom sense. Sufficient/insufficient naturally partner with mass nouns like evidence and information. This is the lone fully clean line on the hardest card.
**B) The jury found insufficient evidences to convict.**

** insufficient pieces of evidence if counting is required.

Trap: "evidences" is wrong in this legal/academic sense — keep "evidence," or use "insufficient pieces of evidence" if counting is required. The jury scene does not license the plural.
**C) There remains a large number of unresolved questions in the chapter.**

** there remain + plural; there remains + singular/mass.

Trap: "a large number of unresolved questions" is plural in sense, so prefer "there remain," not singular "remains". There remain + plural; there remains + singular/mass. The chapter's open questions need plural agreement.
**D) There remains a large amount of unresolved questions in the chapter.**

** number of questions remain; amount of uncertainty remains.

Trap: questions are countable, so "amount of unresolved questions" is off, and singular "remains" still clashes. Prefer "a large number of unresolved questions remain" or "an amount of uncertainty remains".
**E) Fewer than ten percent of the equipment have been calibrated.**

** percent of + uncountable → singular; fewer needs countable units.

Trap: double error — equipment is uncountable, so "fewer… have" is wrong; prefer "less than ten percent of the equipment has been calibrated" or "fewer than ten pieces of equipment have…". Percent of + uncountable takes singular; fewer needs countable units.
tasks.solution_overview:
The final card mixes courtroom evidence, chapter questions with there remain(s), and percent-of agreement with equipment — only one sentence survives.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Evidence stays uncountable. Number of questions wants plural remain, not remains, and never amount of questions. Percent of equipment is singular mass agreement; fewer needs countable pieces.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Resolve countability first, then force verb agreement to follow that decision. When two errors stack (wrong quantifier plus wrong verb), mark false even if one half almost looks repairable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.
My sister's flat is larger than mine.
Of the three trails, this path is the worse.
The new bus stop is closer than the old one.
She sings more better than she did at the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.**

"Heavier" already includes the comparative ending -er, so pairing it with "more" doubles the mark. Repair: drop "more" and write simply "heavier than the one I packed last summer." One comparative marker is enough for a clean two-item contrast.
**B) My sister's flat is larger than mine.**

One-syllable "large" correctly becomes "larger" before "than." This is the standard short-adjective pattern for comparing two flats, and nothing extra is needed.
**C) Of the three trails, this path is the worse.**

"worse" is the comparative (two items), but "of the three trails" ranks a group of three. Repair: use the superlative "the worst." Among three or more options, -est / worst / best is the form you want.
**D) The new bus stop is closer than the old one.**

"Close" is short, so "closer than" correctly compares the new stop with the old one. Two named places → comparative, not superlative.
**E) She sings more better than she did at the school concert.**

"better" is already the irregular comparative of "well/good," so "more better" doubles the mark. Repair: sing "better than she did at the school concert." Never stack "more" on an irregular comparative.
tasks.solution_overview:
Suitcases, flats, trails, bus stops, and a school concert — everyday scenes asking whether each comparison is marked correctly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This opener targets double marking and the two-versus-many rule. Short adjectives usually take -er / -est; irregulars like better and worse already carry the comparative meaning, so stacking "more" on top is always wrong.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, ask two questions: Is the adjective already comparative or superlative? And does the sentence compare two things or rank a whole group? Mark true only when both the form and the grade of comparison fit.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.
That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.
