Under no circumstances + may + subject is correct modal inversion. After this phrase, expect may/will/should before the subject - and here may is correctly placed.

**Tip:** ** Policy English still follows the same modal-before-subject rule.
**C) Seldom has a community garden produced such a crop of tomatoes.**

Seldom + present perfect inversion is correct: seldom has + subject + past participle. Frequency negative and perfect line up.
**D) Only by rearranging the furniture can the sofa fit through the door.**

Only by + -ing, then modal inversion in the main clause: can the sofa fit. Only by / only with / only through all invert the following clause.

**Tip:** ** Invert after the by-phrase; leave the -ing clause as is.
**E) Hardly had the babysitter arrived than the toddler woke up crying.**

** Hardly/scarcely/barely → when; no sooner → than.

Trap: perfect inversion is fine, but hardly takes when, not than. Repair: Hardly had the babysitter arrived when the toddler woke up crying. Even with perfect inversion, a wrong correlative still fails the item.
tasks.solution_overview:
Top-band items stay inside negative/restrictive inversion: not until, under no circumstances, seldom, only by, hardly. Judge each line by whether the auxiliary moved - and whether than/when is the right partner.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Not until → invert the main clause. Under no circumstances + may. Seldom + present perfect. Only by + -ing → modal inversion in the main clause. Hardly + had still fails if than replaces when.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Run two passes: (1) auxiliary before subject after every fronted trigger; (2) correlative audit on hardly/no sooner. A line can pass pass one and still fail pass two.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Under no circumstances is smoking permitted near the playground.
No sooner had the ferry docked than foot passengers streamed ashore.
Not only were tickets refunded, but free drinks were offered as well.
Seldom does a weekday market feel this crowded before noon.
Little did neighbours expect the street party to last past midnight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Under no circumstances is smoking permitted near the playground.**

Under no circumstances + is + subject is correct. Be-main verbs invert be after this phrase; no extra do is needed.

**Tip:** ** Invert is/are/was/were when be carries the sentence.
**B) No sooner had the ferry docked than foot passengers streamed ashore.**

No sooner… than with past perfect is exact. Had + subject + than remains the gold standard, and both pieces are here.
**C) Not only were tickets refunded, but free drinks were offered as well.**

Not only were… but… correctly inverts were. Plural subject → were before it after not only; the second clause completes the contrast.

**Tip:** ** With were/was, invert be; no do-support.
**D) Seldom does a weekday market feel this crowded before noon.**

Seldom does… is clean do-support inversion: frequency negative + does/do + subject + base verb.
**E) Little did neighbours expect the street party to last past midnight.**

Little did… is the classic restrictive inversion: little + did + subject + base verb. Meaning "not at all," it fronts like a negative.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five are model answers across the core triggers - playground rules, ferries, ticket refunds, weekday markets, and street parties. Treat this task as a checklist of shapes you should be able to produce under exam pressure.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Under no circumstances + is (be). No sooner + had + than. Not only + were + but. Seldom + does. Little + did. Every line should already show the auxiliary immediately after the front.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm each opener, confirm the swap, confirm any correlative. With no misses in this set, every statement is TRUE - store them as production models.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after the gym closed members were allowed to collect belongings.
Not until the vet confirmed the results did the owners relax.
Barely had the campsite been booked when a storm warning arrived.
On no account should unfinished cakes leave the kitchen counter.
Never the caretaker had unlocked every classroom before dawn.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Only after the gym closed members were allowed to collect belongings.**

** Only after + clause → invert the main clause.

Trap: main clause still subject-first (members were). Repair: Only after the gym closed were members allowed to collect belongings. Invert be in the main clause after the only-after time clause.
**B) Not until the vet confirmed the results did the owners relax.**

Not until… did… is correctly inverted in the main clause. Keep the not-until clause in normal order - as this line does.
**C) Barely had the campsite been booked when a storm warning arrived.**

Barely had… when… is right. Passive past perfect still inverts had: Barely had the campsite been booked…. The correlative when matches.

**Tip:** ** Barely = hardly for inversion and when.
**D) On no account should unfinished cakes leave the kitchen counter.**

On no account should… is correct modal inversion. Should/must/may belong before the subject after on no account.

**Tip:** ** On no account = under no circumstances for ordering.
**E) Never the caretaker had unlocked every classroom before dawn.**

** Move had left of the subject; keep unlocked after it.

Trap: never + subject before had. Repair: Never had the caretaker unlocked every classroom before dawn. Never + past perfect → Never had + subject + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two lines forget to invert after only after and never. The others show not until, barely, and on no account in full working order - gym closing, vet results, campsite booking, kitchen rules, and dawn unlocks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Only after + clause → invert the main clause. Not until… did…. Barely had… when… (including passive past perfect). On no account + should. Never + past perfect → Never had + subject.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Jump to the main clause after only after / not until and demand the auxiliary first. After never + past perfect, demand had before the subject. Match the three correct templates to the two repairs.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does it mention the Monday trail closure.
Not only did the hostel refill the kettle, but it also left fresh towels.
Hardly had the blackout ended when the street lights flickered back on.
Under no circumstances the landlord will enter without written notice.
No sooner had the suitcases been labelled than the taxi pulled up.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does it mention the Monday trail closure.**

Nowhere… does it mention… correctly inverts after a negative place adverbial. Nowhere / no place at the front → does/do/did + subject.
**B) Not only did the hostel refill the kettle, but it also left fresh towels.**

Not only did… but also… is fully inverted and parallel. Match verb forms across both halves after not only / but also - and both halves here do.

**Tip:** ** Parallel verbs after the correlative pair.
**C) Hardly had the blackout ended when the street lights flickered back on.**

Hardly had… when… is the standard pattern. When after hardly; had before the subject - both present and correct.
**D) Under no circumstances the landlord will enter without written notice.**

** Opener → will/may/should → subject.

Trap: subject before will after under no circumstances. Repair: Under no circumstances will the landlord enter without written notice. Final check on every under-no-circumstances item: modal before subject.
**E) No sooner had the suitcases been labelled than the taxi pulled up.**

No sooner had… than… closes the set correctly, including passive past perfect. Than after no sooner; had before the subject.
highlights: Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does
tasks.solution_overview:
Four model inversions and one classic miss: under no circumstances without modal-subject swap. Hiking leaflets, hostel service, blackouts, landlord notice, and labelled suitcases wrap the final checklist.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Nowhere… does…. Not only did… but also…. Hardly had… when…. Under no circumstances → will before the subject. No sooner had… than….

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you catch the under-no-circumstances pattern every time - modal before subject - this topic is exam-ready. Use the four true lines as production models and fix the one order miss the same way.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Walking through the market, the spices smelled amazing.
Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena carried the fragile vase home.
Hoping for clear skies, the hikers set out before dawn.
Burned on one side, the toast still tasted fine with jam.
Running late for practice, the gym bag was left by the door.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Walking through the market, the spices smelled amazing.**

The spices were not walking through the market — a person was. As written, the opener attaches to "the spices," which creates a dangling participial phrase. Repair by naming the walker: "Walking through the market, we noticed that the spices smelled amazing," or similar.
**B) Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena carried the fragile vase home.**

Lena was not packed carefully in tissue paper; the vase was. The participle "Packed…" currently modifies "Lena," so the attachment is backwards. Put the fragile object next: "Packed carefully in tissue paper, the vase travelled home with Lena."
**C) Hoping for clear skies, the hikers set out before dawn.**

The hikers hoped for clear skies, and "the hikers" is the subject that follows — so the -ing opener attaches cleanly. No dangling modifier here: the same people who hope are the ones setting out.
**D) Burned on one side, the toast still tasted fine with jam.**

The toast was burned on one side, and "the toast" is exactly the subject that follows. Past participles often describe a state of the subject, which is the natural reading here — and it tastes fine with jam anyway.
**E) Running late for practice, the gym bag was left by the door.**

The gym bag was not running late for practice; the athlete was. An -ing opener about being late needs a person (or agent) as subject, not the bag left by the door.
highlights: Walking through the market, the spices
Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena
Hoping for clear skies, the hikers
Burned on one side, the toast
Running late for practice, the gym bag
tasks.solution_overview:
Participial openers can make everyday scenes (markets, toast, gym bags) feel vivid — and they also create classic dangling-modifier traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A participial phrase at the start of the sentence (-ing or -ed) is meant to describe the grammatical subject that comes right after the comma. If spices walk through a market or a gym bag runs late, the opener has attached to the wrong noun. Past participles (burned, packed) often describe a state; present participles (walking, hoping, running) usually describe an action someone is doing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, ask: who or what is really doing or undergoing the participle? That answer must be the subject of the main clause. When the subject fails the test, the sentence is false — rewrite by naming the logical doer first.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tired after the long flight, Maya collapsed onto the sofa.
Covered in mud after the match, the boots needed a thorough scrub.
Having lost the map, the trail suddenly seemed endless.
Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma filled the kitchen.
Excited about the museum trip, the children packed their sketchbooks.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tired after the long flight, Maya collapsed onto the sofa.**

Maya was tired after the long flight, and she is the subject after the comma, so the past-participle opener attaches correctly. Collapsing onto the sofa is a natural next action for that tired traveller.
**B) Covered in mud after the match, the boots needed a thorough scrub.**

The boots were covered in mud after the match, and "the boots" is the subject — a clean condition-of-a-thing attachment. No person is wrongly said to be muddy unless you put that person next.
**C) Having lost the map, the trail suddenly seemed endless.**

The trail did not lose the map; the hikers did. "Having + past participle" still requires the logical agent as the subject of the main clause.
**D) Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma filled the kitchen.**

An aroma cannot stir soup; the cook who is stirring is missing from the subject slot. Active -ing openers need a person (or agent) who performs the action.
**E) Excited about the museum trip, the children packed their sketchbooks.**

The children were excited about the museum trip, and they are the subject — so the opener attaches cleanly. Emotion adjectives built from participles belong with people, not with sketchbooks or museums.
highlights: Tired after the long flight, Maya
Covered in mud after the match, the boots
Having lost the map, the trail
Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma
Excited about the museum trip, the children
tasks.solution_overview:
This set mixes tired/excited states, muddy boots, and "having + past participle" forms with a couple of active -ing traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Past participles and emotion adjectives (tired, covered, excited) still need a matching subject: the person who is tired, or the thing that is covered. "Having lost…" and "Stirring…" look polished, but they still demand the logical agent next — trails and aromas cannot lose maps or stir soup.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the agent of the opener, then check that it appears as the subject after the comma. Condition-of-a-thing participles belong with that thing; intentional actions belong with people (or other agents).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Looking out the train window, the countryside rushed past in a blur.
Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar ducked under a café awning.
Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card was hard to read.
Waiting for the ferry, seagulls circled above the pier.
Finished with homework, Priya started a new puzzle.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Looking out the train window, the countryside rushed past in a blur.**

The countryside was not looking out the train window; the passenger was. Sight and perception -ing phrases almost always need a person as subject.
**B) Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar ducked under a café awning.**

Omar was soaked by the sudden shower, and "Omar" follows the comma — correct attachment. Past participles like soaked, drenched, or frozen naturally modify the person who got wet or cold.
**C) Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card was hard to read.**

The recipe card was written in tiny handwriting, so the past participle correctly describes the card. This is the passive sense of the participle pointing at the object described — hard to read, but grammatically clean.
**D) Waiting for the ferry, seagulls circled above the pier.**

Seagulls were not waiting for the ferry; the travellers were. Location scenes tempt dangling openers because wildlife and scenery are already in the shot — still check who waited.
**E) Finished with homework, Priya started a new puzzle.**

Priya finished her homework, and "Finished with homework" correctly modifies her before she starts a new puzzle. The pattern works when the subject is the person who finished.
highlights: Looking out the train window, the countryside
Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar
Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card
tasks.solution_overview:
Travel and home scenes still obey one attachment rule: the participle’s logical subject must be the sentence subject.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Sight and waiting openers (-ing) almost always need a person. Passive-feeling past participles (soaked, written, finished) often describe what happened to the subject — Omar, a recipe card, Priya. Landscape and wildlife after an -ing opener are frequent danglers.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the subject can literally look, wait, be soaked, be written, or finish homework. If the countryside is "looking" or seagulls are "waiting for the ferry," mark false and reattach the opener to the traveller.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having packed the tent, the campsite looked ready for the night.
Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans urged the team forward.
Left overnight in the fridge, the dough rose beautifully.
Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze turned the pages.
Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed stood out among the trees.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having packed the tent, the campsite looked ready for the night.**

The campsite did not pack the tent; the campers did. "Having packed…" always needs the packer as subject.
**B) Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans urged the team forward.**

The fans were cheering loudly from the stands, and they are the subject who urge the team forward — clean attachment. Crowd actions belong with people, not with the score or the pitch.
**C) Left overnight in the fridge, the dough rose beautifully.**

The dough was left overnight in the fridge, so the past participle correctly modifies "the dough" that then rose. Food-prep sentences often use past participles for what happened to the ingredient.
**D) Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze turned the pages.**

A breeze does not read on the balcony; the reader is missing. If the opener is an intentional human action, the subject must be human (or another agent that can read).
**E) Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed stood out among the trees.**

The garden shed was painted bright yellow last spring, and that shed is the subject — no dangling modifier. "Painted/repaired/built…" usually modifies the object that received the action.
highlights: Having packed the tent, the campsite
Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans
Left overnight in the fridge, the dough
Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze
Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed
tasks.solution_overview:
Camping, sports, kitchen prep, and a garden shed: same participle test, everyday props.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having packed…" needs the packer. Crowd -ing openers need fans or people. Past participles on dough or a shed (left overnight, painted) correctly modify those objects. A breeze that "reads" is a classic intentional-action dangler.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate human actions from object states. If the opener is something a person does on purpose, the subject must be that person; if it describes what was done to an object, that object should follow the comma.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Jogging along the canal path, Sam spotted a heron in the reeds.
Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film felt twice as cosy.
Having trained all week, the final whistle still came as a shock.
Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions sweetened the sauce.
Standing in the doorway, the hallway light cast long shadows.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Jogging along the canal path, Sam spotted a heron in the reeds.**

Sam was jogging along the canal path and spotted a heron — the same person does both actions, so the -ing opener is safely attached. When one agent performs opener and main verb, this pattern is usually reliable.
**B) Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film felt twice as cosy.**

The film was not wrapped in a thick blanket; the viewer was. Comfort and clothing participles modify people or bodies, not the entertainment on screen.
**C) Having trained all week, the final whistle still came as a shock.**

The final whistle did not train all week; the player or team did. "Having trained…" must be followed by the athlete (or team), not by a result or signal.
**D) Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions sweetened the sauce.**

The onions were chopped finely and fried gently, so stacked past participles correctly modify the ingredient that then sweetened the sauce. Cooking sequences often use this pattern before the food noun.
**E) Standing in the doorway, the hallway light cast long shadows.**

The hallway light was not standing in the doorway. Posture verbs (standing, sitting, leaning) need a person or object that can hold that pose as subject.
highlights: Jogging along the canal path, Sam
Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film
Having trained all week, the final whistle
Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions
Standing in the doorway, the hallway light
tasks.solution_overview:
Difficulty steps up: some wrong lines sound natural until you ask who wrapped, trained, or stood.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When the same person does both the opener and the main verb (jogging + spotting), -ing is usually safe. Comfort/clothing and "having trained" must stay with people, not films or whistles. Cooking past participles stack cleanly before the ingredient. Posture verbs need a body that can hold the pose.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check agent match first, then whether an abstract result (whistle, hallway light) has stolen the subject slot. Only Sam and the onions keep a clean logical pairing here.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks were easy to find.
Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath needed warm water.
Hoping to improve her serve, Nina practised against the garage wall.
Filled with fresh berries, Tom carried the bowl to the picnic table.
Turning the page slowly, the mystery finally made sense.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks were easy to find.**

Quiet study desks did not arrive early at the library; the student did. Time-of-arrival openers need a person as subject, not the place or the furniture.
**B) Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath needed warm water.**

The birdbath was frozen solid after the cold night, so the past participle correctly describes that object. Weather effects on outdoor objects are natural past-participle modifiers.
**C) Hoping to improve her serve, Nina practised against the garage wall.**

Nina hoped to improve her serve, and she practised — purpose/hope -ing phrases should be followed by the person with that goal. The attachment here is exact.
**D) Filled with fresh berries, Tom carried the bowl to the picnic table.**

Tom was not filled with fresh berries; the bowl was. "Filled/loaded/packed with…" modifies the container, not the person carrying it (unless you literally mean something else).
**E) Turning the page slowly, the mystery finally made sense.**

The mystery did not turn the page. Reading actions belong with the reader: put that person after the comma, then let the mystery make sense.
highlights: Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks
Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath
Hoping to improve her serve, Nina
Turning the page slowly, the mystery
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch container versus carrier, and arrival versus furniture — two of the most common participial mix-ups.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Time-of-arrival openers need a person, not desks. Weather past participles on objects (frozen birdbath) are fine. Hope/purpose -ing belongs with the athlete who hopes. "Filled with…" modifies the bowl, not Tom carrying it. Page-turning needs a reader, not "the mystery."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each opener, decide: person acting, or object in a state? Then verify the noun after the comma matches that role. Shuffle roles and you get a dangler even if the scene still "makes sense" narratively.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having watered the plants, the windowsill looked bright again.
Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we missed the opening kick-off.
Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough became smooth and elastic.
Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence settled over the group.
Repaired with strong tape, the torn map lasted the rest of the hike.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having watered the plants, the windowsill looked bright again.**

The windowsill did not water the plants. "Having watered…" requires the gardener as subject before you describe how bright the sill looked.
**B) Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we missed the opening kick-off.**

We were stuck in traffic near the stadium, and "we" is the subject — so the participle modifies the right people (who then missed kick-off). "Stuck/caught/trapped…" with a human subject is a common correct pattern.
**C) Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough became smooth and elastic.**

The bread dough was kneaded for ten minutes, and that dough is the subject that became smooth. Baking steps as past participles usually modify the dough, batter, or loaf.
**D) Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence settled over the group.**

Silence was not watching the sunset from the ridge; the hikers were. Abstract subjects (silence, calm, tension) rarely perform -ing actions in openers.
**E) Repaired with strong tape, the torn map lasted the rest of the hike.**

The torn map was repaired with strong tape, so the past participle correctly modifies the map that lasted the rest of the hike. "Repaired/mended/patched…" modifies the damaged object.
highlights: Having watered the plants, the windowsill
Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we
Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough
Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence
Repaired with strong tape, the torn map
tasks.solution_overview:
Home gardening, traffic, baking, ridgelines, and trail maps recycle the same attachment test.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having watered…" needs the gardener. "Stuck in traffic…" with "we" is a clean human-state pattern. Kneaded dough and a repaired map take past participles naturally. Abstract nouns like "silence" almost never perform watching or similar -ing actions.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask who did the -ing/-ed action, then insist that noun is the subject. Furniture and mood nouns after active openers are nearly always false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration proved difficult.
Dried on the washing line, the sheets smelled of sunshine.
Having booked the earliest train, Lara reached the coast by noon.
Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk needed clearing.
Scoring the winning goal, the stadium erupted in cheers.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration proved difficult.**

Concentration did not skip breakfast before the exam; the student did. Result nouns (concentration, success, fatigue) cannot be the agent of the opener.
**B) Dried on the washing line, the sheets smelled of sunshine.**

The sheets were dried on the washing line, and they are the subject — correct attachment. "Dried/hung/aired…" naturally modifies laundry or similar objects.
**C) Having booked the earliest train, Lara reached the coast by noon.**

Lara booked the earliest train, so "Having booked…" correctly modifies her before she reached the coast. Travel logistics with "having + past participle" need the traveller as subject.
**D) Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk needed clearing.**

The desk was cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, so the past participle matches the surface that needed clearing. "Cluttered/covered/littered with…" modifies the space, not a person walking by.
**E) Scoring the winning goal, the stadium erupted in cheers.**

The stadium did not score the winning goal; the player did. Sports highlights often dangle when the venue follows a player’s action.
highlights: Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration
Dried on the washing line, the sheets
Having booked the earliest train, Lara
Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk
Scoring the winning goal, the stadium
tasks.solution_overview:
Study habits, laundry, travel booking, a cluttered desk, and a stadium goal — three attachments succeed, two fail loudly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Result nouns (concentration) cannot skip breakfast. Laundry past participles modify the sheets. "Having booked…" needs the traveller. "Cluttered with…" modifies the desk. Sports action openers need the player, not the venue that erupts afterward.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject subjects that are effects, places, or venues when the opener describes a human action. Accept object-state participles only when the subject truly carries that state.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea sounded irresistible.
Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes were unusually sweet.
Having finished the crossword, Eli started a new novel.
Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote finally turned up.
Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps flickered on one by one.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea sounded irresistible.**

Hot tea was not shivering in the queue for tickets. Sensory desires as subjects after bodily -ing phrases usually create danglers — put the cold person first.
**B) Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes were unusually sweet.**

The tomatoes were grown in the neighbour’s garden, so the past participle correctly modifies the produce that tasted sweet. "Grown/picked/harvested…" modifies the crop.
**C) Having finished the crossword, Eli started a new novel.**

Eli finished the crossword, and "Having finished…" attaches clearly to him before he starts a novel. "Having finished X" + person subject is a reliable non-dangling pattern.
**D) Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote finally turned up.**

The remote was hidden behind the sofa cushions, so the past participle fits the lost-and-found item that finally turned up. Household finds often take "hidden/buried/tucked…".
**E) Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps flickered on one by one.**

Streetlamps were not cycling through the park at dusk. Motion openers need the cyclist, walker, or runner as subject — not the scenery lighting up.

Trap: "Cycling through the park at dusk, she watched streetlamps flicker on one by one."
highlights: Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea
Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes
Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote
Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps
tasks.solution_overview:
Mid-difficulty danglers look vivid: shivering queues and dusk cycling can hypnotise you into accepting the wrong subject.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Bodily -ing openers followed by sensory desires ("hot tea") usually dangle. Produce and lost-item past participles (grown, hidden) attach well to tomatoes and remotes. "Having finished…" + person is reliable. Motion openers need the cyclist, not the streetlamps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep asking whether this subject could literally shiver, grow, finish, hide, or cycle. Related scene props (tea, lamps) are not enough.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies disappeared fast.
Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps became clear.
Having lost his gloves, Noah kept his hands in his pockets.
Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots waited for the weekend.
Crossing the busy square, a street musician started a lively tune.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies disappeared fast.**

The cookies were burned at the edges but soft in the centre, and that food noun is the subject — a clean descriptive past-participle attachment. Food states before the food noun are usually correct.
**B) Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps became clear.**

Recipe steps do not listen to podcasts. "Listening/watching/reading…" needs a person (or animal) subject who can pay attention.

Trap: "Listening carefully to the podcast, she found the recipe steps became clear."
**C) Having lost his gloves, Noah kept his hands in his pockets.**

Noah lost his gloves, so "Having lost…" correctly modifies him before he keeps his hands in his pockets. Possession loss with "having lost" must be followed by the owner.
**D) Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots waited for the weekend.**

The hiking boots were stacked neatly beside the door, so the arrangement participle modifies the arranged items waiting for the weekend. Stacked/lined/arranged patterns belong with the things in that arrangement.
**E) Crossing the busy square, a street musician started a lively tune.**

Who crossed the busy square? Grammatically, "a street musician" is said to be crossing while starting a tune — but the intended crosser is usually a passer-by, not the performer already in place. Reattach the opener to the walker, or drop it.
highlights: Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies
Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps
Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots
Crossing the busy square, a street musician
tasks.solution_overview:
Cookies and boots look solid; listening and crossing create the traps you need to catch at this level.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Food-state past participles before the food noun are usually correct. Perception verbs (listening) need a person. "Having lost…" needs the owner. Arrangement participles modify the arranged items. "Crossing…" must be followed by whoever crossed — not a musician who may already be performing in the square.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reattach any -ing opener that describes intentional human behaviour to a human subject. Keep past-participle state descriptions on the objects that underwent them.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic smelled of old cedar.
Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves stayed crisp.
Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket stayed packed indoors.
Sliding into third base, the umpire called him safe.
Printed on recycled paper, the flyer advertised the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic smelled of old cedar.**

The attic did not climb the spiral staircase. "Having climbed…" needs the climber as subject before you mention how the attic smelled.

Trap: "Having climbed the spiral staircase, we noticed the attic smelled of old cedar."
**B) Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves stayed crisp.**

The salad leaves were rinsed under cold water, so the past participle correctly modifies the food that stayed crisp. Prep verbs on ingredients (rinsed, peeled, sliced) modify the food.
**C) Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket stayed packed indoors.**

The picnic basket was not worried about the weather forecast; the hosts were. Emotion participles (worried, delighted, annoyed) modify people, not objects that stay packed indoors.
**D) Sliding into third base, the umpire called him safe.**

The umpire did not slide into third base; the runner did. Sports action openers must be followed by the player who performed the move.

Trap: "Sliding into third base, the runner heard the umpire call him safe."
**E) Printed on recycled paper, the flyer advertised the school concert.**

The flyer was printed on recycled paper, so the past participle correctly describes the notice advertising the concert. "Printed/published/posted…" usually modifies the document.
highlights: Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic
Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves
Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket
Sliding into third base, the umpire
Printed on recycled paper, the flyer
tasks.solution_overview:
Emotion and sports danglers are easy to miss when the scenery feels connected to the action.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having climbed…" needs the climber, not the attic. Prep verbs on ingredients (rinsed) modify the food. Emotion participles (worried) modify people, never picnic baskets. Sliding belongs with the runner, not the umpire. "Printed on…" correctly modifies the flyer.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Mental states and athletic moves stay with people. Object subjects are fine only for make/print/prep states that truly describe those objects.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Folded into neat squares, the napkins brightened the dinner table.
Having studied until midnight, the exam questions still felt unfamiliar.
Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel filled quickly.
Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook recommended three streets nearby.
Exhausted but pleased, the choir packed away the music stands.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Folded into neat squares, the napkins brightened the dinner table.**

The napkins were folded into neat squares, so the past participle matches the fabric items that brightened the table. Household "folded/ironed/pressed…" modifies the textile.
**B) Having studied until midnight, the exam questions still felt unfamiliar.**

Exam questions did not study until midnight. "Having studied…" must be followed by the student who still finds the questions unfamiliar.
**C) Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel filled quickly.**

The rain barrel was not dripping from the eaves; the water was. Make sure the participle’s subject is what drips, hangs, or falls — not only the container if the opener describes the runoff.

Trap: "Dripping from the eaves after the storm, rain filled the barrel quickly," or name the water explicitly.
**D) Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook recommended three streets nearby.**

The guidebook was not searching for a quiet café. Search/look-for openers need a traveller as subject, not the book that lists streets.
**E) Exhausted but pleased, the choir packed away the music stands.**

The choir was exhausted but pleased, and that animate group is the subject packing away the stands. Paired emotion adjectives still require a human (or animate) subject.
highlights: Folded into neat squares, the napkins
Having studied until midnight, the exam questions
Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel
Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook
tasks.solution_overview:
Only napkins and a choir keep solid matches; study, weather, and travel lines shuffle agents onto questions, barrels, and guidebooks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Household "folded…" modifies fabric. "Having studied…" needs the student. "Dripping from the eaves…" describes water, not the barrel as the thing that drips. Search openers need a person. Paired emotion adjectives (exhausted but pleased) still require an animate subject — the choir works.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the opener is a human mental action or motion, reject furniture, guides, and result nouns as subjects. If it is a fabric or body state that the subject can hold, accept it.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seasoned generously with herbs, the roast chicken came out of the oven golden.
Having missed the last bus, the walk home took nearly an hour.
Balanced carefully on the windowsill, the orchid tilted toward the light.
Cheering for their classmates, the relay baton felt heavier than usual.
Written by a local poet, the short story won the school prize.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Seasoned generously with herbs, the roast chicken came out of the oven golden.**

The roast chicken was seasoned generously with herbs, so the past participle correctly modifies the dish coming out golden. Seasoned/marinated/basted modifies the food.
**B) Having missed the last bus, the walk home took nearly an hour.**

The walk home did not miss the last bus; the traveller did. "Having missed…" needs a person subject, not the resulting journey that took an hour.
**C) Balanced carefully on the windowsill, the orchid tilted toward the light.**

The orchid was balanced carefully on the windowsill, so the position participle correctly modifies the plant tilting toward the light. Position participles can modify plants and objects that sit or rest.
**D) Cheering for their classmates, the relay baton felt heavier than usual.**

The relay baton was not cheering for classmates. Spectator -ing openers need people (fans, classmates), not equipment that suddenly feels heavy.

Trap: "Cheering for their classmates, the runners felt the relay baton heavier than usual."
**E) Written by a local poet, the short story won the school prize.**

The short story was written by a local poet, so "Written by…" correctly modifies the text that won the prize. That pattern almost always points at the work, not the author as subject after the comma.
highlights: Seasoned generously with herbs, the roast chicken
Having missed the last bus, the walk home
Balanced carefully on the windowsill, the orchid
Cheering for their classmates, the relay baton
Written by a local poet, the short story
tasks.solution_overview:
Higher difficulty: results ("the walk") and gear ("the baton") look related to the scene but cannot perform the participle.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Seasoned chicken and "written by…" stories take past participles cleanly. "Having missed…" needs the traveller, not the resulting walk. Position participles can modify an orchid on a sill. Spectator -ing openers need people, not relay equipment.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Never let a consequence phrase or a piece of kit steal the subject after "having…" or cheering. Put the person who missed the bus or cheered first.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tangled in the blackberry bushes, the path seemed to disappear.
Having tuned the guitar carefully, the first chord rang clear.
Glazed with honey and nuts, the pastry cooled on a wire rack.
Running to catch the tram, her scarf slipped from her shoulders.
Stored in a cool cupboard, the spices kept their aroma for months.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tangled in the blackberry bushes, the path seemed to disappear.**

The path was not tangled in the blackberry bushes; a hiker (or animal) might have been. If "tangled" describes a person’s predicament, make that person the subject — do not assign the snare to the path itself.
**B) Having tuned the guitar carefully, the first chord rang clear.**

The first chord did not tune the guitar. "Having tuned…" needs the musician as subject before the chord rings clear.
**C) Glazed with honey and nuts, the pastry cooled on a wire rack.**

The pastry was glazed with honey and nuts, so the past participle correctly modifies the baked good cooling on the rack. Baking finishes (glazed, dusted, iced) modify the treat.
**D) Running to catch the tram, her scarf slipped from her shoulders.**

Classic dangler: the scarf was not running to catch the tram; she was. A possessive subject after an -ing opener wrongly says the scarf ran and then slipped.

Trap: name the person first — "Running to catch the tram, she felt her scarf slip from her shoulders."
**E) Stored in a cool cupboard, the spices kept their aroma for months.**

The spices were stored in a cool cupboard, so the past participle correctly modifies the stored items that kept their aroma. Storage participles belong with what was stored.
highlights: Tangled in the blackberry bushes, the path
Having tuned the guitar carefully, the first chord
Glazed with honey and nuts, the pastry
Running to catch the tram, her scarf
Stored in a cool cupboard, the spices
tasks.solution_overview:
Nature and music danglers grow subtle; the scarf line is a classic possessive trap after an -ing opener.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Tangled…" describing a path wrongly assigns a hiker’s predicament to the path. "Having tuned…" needs the musician, not the chord. Glazed pastry and stored spices correctly take past participles. "Running…, her scarf…" makes the scarf the runner — a famous dangling pattern with possessives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Prefer naming the person before possessives or results. Accept object-state participles only when the object underwent that treatment.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having stirred the sauce for twenty minutes, a silky texture finally appeared.
Pinned to the noticeboard, the timetable showed every club meeting.
Leaning over the garden fence, neighbours swapped seeds and tips.
Defeated in the first set, the second set still offered hope.
Carved from a single piece of wood, the salad bowl felt smooth to the touch.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having stirred the sauce for twenty minutes, a silky texture finally appeared.**

A silky texture did not stir the sauce for twenty minutes. Cooking "having + past participle" openers need the cook as subject before you mention the result.
**B) Pinned to the noticeboard, the timetable showed every club meeting.**

The timetable was pinned to the noticeboard, so the past participle correctly modifies the notice showing club meetings. "Pinned/posted/taped…" modifies the paper or notice.
**C) Leaning over the garden fence, neighbours swapped seeds and tips.**

Neighbours were leaning over the garden fence and swapping seeds — the -ing opener attaches to people who perform both actions. Shared activities work when the subject group does what the opener describes.
**D) Defeated in the first set, the second set still offered hope.**

The second set was not defeated in the first set; the player was. Match outcome participles (defeated, exhausted) to the competitor, not the next phase of the match.
**E) Carved from a single piece of wood, the salad bowl felt smooth to the touch.**

The salad bowl was carved from a single piece of wood, so the craft participle correctly modifies the finished object that felt smooth. Make/craft participles modify what was made.
highlights: Having stirred the sauce for twenty minutes, a silky texture
Pinned to the noticeboard, the timetable
Leaning over the garden fence, neighbours
Defeated in the first set, the second set
Carved from a single piece of wood, the salad bowl
tasks.solution_overview:
Results and next stages (a silky texture, a second set) tempt danglers after cooking and sports openers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Cooking "having + past participle" needs the cook. Notices pinned up, neighbours leaning, bowls carved from wood are legitimate object/person matches. "Defeated in the first set…" must modify the competitor, not the next phase of the match.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep agents human for intentional prep and emotional outcomes; let objects take only make/state participles that truly describe them.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Wading into the cold lake, goosebumps rose along her arms.
Annotated in the margins, the textbook looked well used.
Having repaired the puncture, the bicycle was ready for the trail.
Sipping tea on the porch, evening birdsong filled the garden.
Buried under last year’s leaves, the garden path was hard to find.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Wading into the cold lake, goosebumps rose along her arms.**

Goosebumps were not wading into the cold lake. Bodily reactions as subjects after motion openers almost always dangle — use "she" (or the swimmer) as subject.

Trap: "Wading into the cold lake, she felt goosebumps rise along her arms."
**B) Annotated in the margins, the textbook looked well used.**

The textbook was annotated in the margins, so the past participle correctly modifies the well-used book. Study participles (annotated, highlighted, dog-eared) modify the book.
**C) Having repaired the puncture, the bicycle was ready for the trail.**

Here the intended reading is object-focused: after the puncture repair, the bicycle is what stands ready for the trail. Many style guides still prefer "Having repaired the puncture, she found the bicycle ready," but for this bank we treat the bike’s post-repair readiness as acceptable.

**Tip:** ** Prefer the person who repaired it for the safest formal reading; object readiness after repair can still pass when that is the intended focus.
**D) Sipping tea on the porch, evening birdsong filled the garden.**

Evening birdsong was not sipping tea on the porch. Leisure -ing openers need a person subject enjoying the tea while the garden fills with sound.
**E) Buried under last year’s leaves, the garden path was hard to find.**

The garden path was buried under last year’s leaves, so the past participle correctly modifies the path that was hard to find. "Buried/hidden/covered…" can modify places and paths.
highlights: Wading into the cold lake, goosebumps
Annotated in the margins, the textbook
Having repaired the puncture, the bicycle
Sipping tea on the porch, evening birdsong
Buried under last year’s leaves, the garden path
tasks.solution_overview:
Body reactions and nature sounds create vivid danglers; object-focused past participles on books, bikes, and paths can still be clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Goosebumps do not wade; birdsong does not sip tea. Annotated textbooks and buried paths take past participles well. "Having repaired the puncture, the bicycle…" is accepted here as object-focused readiness after repair (the bike is what is ready for the trail).

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject bodily reactions and ambient sounds as agents of motion or leisure openers. Allow past participles when the subject is the thing annotated, repaired-for-use, or buried.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having tasted every sample at the food fair, the decision became impossible.
Polished until it shone, the trophy sat on the top shelf.
Dashing through the rain toward the pavilion, umbrellas were useless against the wind.
Layered with cream and strawberries, the cake barely fitted in the fridge.
Confused by the trail markers, the map seemed to contradict itself.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having tasted every sample at the food fair, the decision became impossible.**

The decision did not taste every sample at the food fair. "Having tasted…" needs the eater as subject before choosing becomes impossible.
**B) Polished until it shone, the trophy sat on the top shelf.**

The trophy was polished until it shone, so the past participle correctly modifies the object sitting on the top shelf. "Polished/cleaned/buffed…" modifies the object treated.
**C) Dashing through the rain toward the pavilion, umbrellas were useless against the wind.**

Umbrellas were not dashing through the rain toward the pavilion. Motion openers need the people running; equipment cannot be the agent here even if umbrellas appear in the scene.

Trap: "Dashing through the rain toward the pavilion, we found umbrellas useless against the wind."
**D) Layered with cream and strawberries, the cake barely fitted in the fridge.**

The cake was layered with cream and strawberries, so the construction participle correctly modifies the dish that barely fitted in the fridge. Food construction participles (layered, filled, topped) modify the dish.
**E) Confused by the trail markers, the map seemed to contradict itself.**

The map was not confused by the trail markers; the hiker was. Mental-state participles modify people — even when a map is mixed up in the confusion.

Trap: "Confused by the trail markers, she felt the map seemed to contradict itself."
highlights: Having tasted every sample at the food fair, the decision
Polished until it shone, the trophy
Dashing through the rain toward the pavilion, umbrellas
Layered with cream and strawberries, the cake
Confused by the trail markers, the map
tasks.solution_overview:
Hard danglers hide behind related nouns: decisions, umbrellas, and maps that sit near the real agent.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having tasted…" needs the eater, not "the decision." Polished trophies and layered cakes undergo the participle directly. "Dashing through the rain…" needs people, not umbrellas. "Confused by…" is a mental state — it belongs with the hiker, even if trail markers and a map are involved.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the subject performs or receives the participle’s action. Nearby props and abstract results almost always fail that test.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Twisting the radio dial slowly, a faint station finally came through.
Packed the night before, the suitcase stood ready by the door.
Having overwatered the ferns, yellow leaves began to drop.
Stretching after yoga class, the wooden floor felt warm underfoot.
Signed by every teammate, the jersey became a keepsake.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Twisting the radio dial slowly, a faint station finally came through.**

A faint station did not twist the radio dial. Instrument/action openers need the person handling the object before the station comes through.

Trap: "Twisting the radio dial slowly, she finally caught a faint station."
**B) Packed the night before, the suitcase stood ready by the door.**

The suitcase was packed the night before, so the past participle correctly modifies the bag standing ready by the door. Travel "packed/zipped/labelled…" modifies the case.
**C) Having overwatered the ferns, yellow leaves began to drop.**

Yellow leaves did not overwater the ferns. "Having overwatered…" needs the gardener; then you can mention leaves dropping in a separate clause.

Trap: "Having overwatered the ferns, she watched yellow leaves begin to drop."
**D) Stretching after yoga class, the wooden floor felt warm underfoot.**

The wooden floor was not stretching after yoga class. Exercise -ing openers require the person stretching, not the surface underfoot.
**E) Signed by every teammate, the jersey became a keepsake.**

The jersey was signed by every teammate, so the past participle correctly modifies the keepsake that received the signatures. "Signed/inscribed/embroidered…" modifies the marked item.
highlights: Twisting the radio dial slowly, a faint station
Packed the night before, the suitcase
Having overwatered the ferns, yellow leaves
Stretching after yoga class, the wooden floor
Signed by every teammate, the jersey
tasks.solution_overview:
Hobbies and home care produce near-miss subjects: radio stations, yellow leaves, and warm floors.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Twisting a dial and stretching after yoga are human actions — stations and floors cannot do them. Packed suitcases and signed jerseys correctly take past participles. "Having overwatered…" needs the gardener; leaf drop is a result, not the agent.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Instrument and exercise openers demand the person handling the action. Storage/signing past participles stay with the bag or jersey that received the treatment.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Flying low over the marsh, a sudden gust rocked the small plane.
Simmered for hours with garlic and thyme, the stew filled the kitchen with warmth.
Having forgotten her locker key, the PE kit stayed behind the door.
Crouched beside the stream, the photographer waited for the kingfisher.
Scattered across the rug, building blocks made evening clear-up slow.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Flying low over the marsh, a sudden gust rocked the small plane.**

A sudden gust was not flying low over the marsh; the plane (or pilot) was. After "Flying…," the next noun should be the aircraft or pilot, not the weather that rocks it.
**B) Simmered for hours with garlic and thyme, the stew filled the kitchen with warmth.**

The stew was simmered for hours with garlic and thyme, so the past participle correctly modifies the dish filling the kitchen with warmth. Long cooking processes as past participles modify the food.
**C) Having forgotten her locker key, the PE kit stayed behind the door.**

The PE kit did not forget her locker key. "Having forgotten…" needs the person; then mention the kit left behind separately.
**D) Crouched beside the stream, the photographer waited for the kingfisher.**

The photographer was crouched beside the stream and waiting — posture plus person subject is a reliable non-dangling pattern while the kingfisher is still elusive.
**E) Scattered across the rug, building blocks made evening clear-up slow.**

Building blocks were scattered across the rug, so the past participle correctly modifies the toys that made clear-up slow. "Scattered/strewn/spread…" modifies the items in that state.
highlights: Flying low over the marsh, a sudden gust
Simmered for hours with garlic and thyme, the stew
Having forgotten her locker key, the PE kit
Crouched beside the stream, the photographer
Scattered across the rug, building blocks
tasks.solution_overview:
Nature and school scenes: weather and PE kits cannot fly or forget.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

After "Flying…," the next noun should be the aircraft or pilot, not a gust. Simmered stew, a crouched photographer, and scattered blocks attach correctly. "Having forgotten…" needs the person who forgot the key, not the kit left behind.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match flight and posture to flyer or person; match cooking and arrangement states to the dish or toys; refuse forgotten-key openers that put clothing or gear in the subject slot.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having measured the ingredients twice, a perfect loaf seemed guaranteed.
Mended with invisible thread, the costume survived the whole play.
Peeking through the kitchen blinds, the smell of fresh bread drifted in.
Drenched after the charity run, the volunteers shared orange slices.
Built into the hillside, the cabin stayed cool even in midsummer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having measured the ingredients twice, a perfect loaf seemed guaranteed.**

A perfect loaf (or the guarantee) did not measure the ingredients twice. "Having measured…" needs the baker as subject before confidence about the loaf creeps in.
**B) Mended with invisible thread, the costume survived the whole play.**

The costume was mended with invisible thread, so the past participle correctly modifies the repaired clothing that survived the play. Repair participles modify the mended item.
**C) Peeking through the kitchen blinds, the smell of fresh bread drifted in.**

A smell cannot peek through kitchen blinds. Perception -ing openers need a person looking or listening while the aroma drifts in.

Trap: "Peeking through the kitchen blinds, we caught the smell of fresh bread drifting in."
**D) Drenched after the charity run, the volunteers shared orange slices.**

The volunteers were drenched after the charity run, so the past participle correctly modifies the people sharing orange slices. Weather/state past participles (drenched, chilled) with people subjects are clean.
**E) Built into the hillside, the cabin stayed cool even in midsummer.**

The cabin was built into the hillside, so the construction participle correctly modifies the building that stayed cool. Construction participles (built, nestled, carved) often modify buildings and places.
highlights: Having measured the ingredients twice, a perfect loaf
Mended with invisible thread, the costume
Peeking through the kitchen blinds, the smell
Drenched after the charity run, the volunteers
Built into the hillside, the cabin
tasks.solution_overview:
Final set: abstract results and sensory nouns after active openers fail; costume, volunteers, and cabin succeed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having measured…" needs the baker, not a "perfect loaf" or guarantee. Mended costumes, drenched volunteers, and hillside cabins take the right past-participle attachments. "Peeking through…" needs a person looking — smells cannot peek.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Always verify that the subject after the comma is what the participle really describes. Results and aromas after -ing/-having openers are false; treated objects and people in that state are true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike.
The soup was enough hot to warm us after the hike.
It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk.
It was so a noisy café that we could barely talk.
The trail was too steep for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike.**

Hot enough places enough after the adjective, which is the standard slot before a to-infinitive. The soup was hot enough to warm us reads as natural, living English and matches the sufficiency pattern you want after a hike.
**B) The soup was enough hot to warm us after the hike.**

Enough cannot sit before the adjective here. Flip to hot enough (or switch the meaning to too hot if you mean excess).
**C) It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk.**

Such a + adjective + singular countable noun + that-clause is the classic result pattern. Such a noisy café that… correctly intensifies the whole noun phrase, not just the adjective alone.
**D) It was so a noisy café that we could barely talk.**

So does not combine with a before a noun. Repair to such a noisy café that…, or drop the noun and write so noisy that…
**E) The trail was too steep for beginners.**

Too + adjective (+ for…) correctly marks excess relative to a purpose or audience. Too steep for beginners is exactly the shape you want when the trail goes past what beginners can handle.
tasks.solution_overview:
These five lines swap so, such, too, and enough around everyday food, cafés, and hiking talk. You are deciding whether each sentence is grammatical as written—not whether you like the word choice.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The focus is partnering each intensifier with the right kind of word, and keeping enough after adjectives. So wants an adjective or adverb; such wants a noun phrase; too marks excess before an adjective; enough after an adjective signals "sufficient for a purpose." Easy misspellings of the pattern are really word-order errors: so a… and enough + adjective.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each letter, spot the intensifier first, then check what sits immediately after it. If the partner type or order is wrong, mark false; if the classic pattern holds (adj + enough, such a + noun, too + adj), mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in harbour.
There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
There was so excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
He is not tall enough for the roller coaster.
He is not enough tall for the roller coaster.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in harbour.**

So + adjective + that-clause intensifies the quality and links a clear result. So thick that the ferry stayed in harbour keeps the adjective alone in so's slot and lets that introduce what followed.
**B) There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early.**

Such + uncountable noun (excitement) + that needs no article. There was such excitement that… correctly treats excitement as a mass noun under such.
**C) There was so excitement that the crowd started cheering early.**

So cannot modify a bare noun. Repair to such excitement or so much excitement that…
**D) He is not tall enough for the roller coaster.**

Tall enough places enough after the adjective and before for. He is not tall enough for the roller coaster is the everyday sufficiency pattern under negation.
**E) He is not enough tall for the roller coaster.**

Enough tall reverses the required order. Flip to tall enough; only when a noun follows (enough time) can enough come first.
tasks.solution_overview:
Fog, ferry delays, crowd noise, and a roller-coaster height check — each sentence turns on so, such, or enough. Judge only the grammar of the intensifier pattern, not how dramatic the scene sounds.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Pair each intensifier with its partner: so with adjectives (and result that-clauses), such with nouns, and enough after adjectives before for / to…. When so sits bare before a noun with no much/many, the structure collapses.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan left to right for so / such / enough, then ask what word class follows. Correct partners stay true; so + bare noun or enough + adjective flips to false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty.
It was so an early train that half the carriages were empty.
The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone.
The lecture was too much technical for first-year students.
She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty.**

Such an before a vowel-sound adjective + noun is correct — early begins with a vowel sound, so an is right. Such an early train that… builds the full noun phrase under such and adds a result clause.
**B) It was so an early train that half the carriages were empty.**

So an is ungrammatical. Replace with such an early train that…, or restructure as so early that… without parking the noun after so.
**C) The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone.**

Too + adjective + to-infinitive expresses excess that blocks a result. The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone means the weight stops a solo lift — a clean too…to pattern.
**D) The lecture was too much technical for first-year students.**

Do not insert much between too and a single adjective. Write too technical; reserve too much for nouns (too much noise).
**E) She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent.**

So + adverb + that-clause parallels so + adjective. She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent intensifies manner and states the result without dragging a noun into so's slot.
tasks.solution_overview:
Early trains, heavy suitcases, technical lectures, and a quiet hall after a song — the sentences lean on such, so, and too. Your job is to accept clean patterns and reject article or much mistakes.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch article choice with such (such an before a vowel sound) and the too much trap before a lone adjective. So an… is never a substitute for such an…, and so + adverb + that is fine when you intensify manner.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see so / such before an article + noun, ask whether such owns that noun phrase. If too is followed by much + adjective (not a noun), mark false; keep too + adj + to and so + adverb + that as true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural.
The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes.
She typed so quickly notes that nobody could read them.
The film was such gripping that we stayed until the credits.
The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural.**

Enough + noun is correct when enough quantifies a noun. We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural treats daylight as the thing of which there was a sufficient amount.
**B) The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes.**

So + adjective + that correctly builds cause and result. The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes keeps icy in the adjective slot after so.
**C) She typed so quickly notes that nobody could read them.**

So quickly notes mixes the adverb pattern with a noun sitting where that or an infinitive should be. Repair to so quickly that… or such quick notes that…
**D) The film was such gripping that we stayed until the credits.**

Such needs a noun phrase: such a gripping film that…, not such gripping alone before that. Without a noun head, such has nothing to intensify.
**E) The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge.**

Adjective + enough + for + noun phrase is grammatical. The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge places enough after large and licenses the for-complement.
tasks.solution_overview:
Daylight for photography, icy paths, typing speed, a gripping film, and kitchen space — again so / such / enough decide truth. Separate quantity enough from adjective enough before you judge hybrids.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Enough + noun quantifies (enough daylight); adjective + enough describes sufficiency of a quality. Hybrid errors stack words from different patterns: so + adverb + noun, or such + bare adjective with no noun head.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether enough is quantifying a noun or finishing an adjective. Then check that so's next word is adj/adv only, and that such still has a noun phrase before that.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned.
There were so many volunteers that the charity ran out of badges.
The recipe is too vaguely to follow without a video.
The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back.
It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned.**

So much + uncountable noun (+ that) is the correct so + noun pattern. There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned pairs much with uncountable rain and states the result.
**B) There were so many volunteers that the charity ran out of badges.**

So many + plural countable noun is parallel to so much. There were so many volunteers that… correctly chooses many for a plural count noun.
**C) The recipe is too vaguely to follow without a video.**

Too must modify an adjective after be when you mean the recipe itself: too vague to follow, not too vaguely. The -ly form is wrong for a subject complement here.
**D) The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back.**

Generous enough to… places enough correctly after the adjective. The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back is the standard not + adj + enough to… exam shape.
**E) It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early.**

Such + adjective + uncountable noun (weather) needs no article. It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early is textbook such + mass noun phrasing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Rain, volunteers, a vague recipe, a job offer, and bad weather — quantity so much/many and such with uncountables sit beside a too + adverb slip. Count the noun before you choose much or many.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When so modifies quantity, check much (uncountable) versus many (plural countable). When too follows be, prefer an adjective describing the subject. Such before an uncountable noun phrase usually drops the article.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Identify whether the intensifier is grading quantity, quality, or excess. So much / so many + matching noun stays true; too + -ly after be when you mean the thing itself is false; adj + enough and such + adj + uncountable noun stay true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes.
The photos were such blurry that we deleted the whole roll.
We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf.
It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross.
The library was enough quiet for evening revision.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes.**

Too + adverb + to-infinitive correctly marks excess manner blocking a purpose. The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes parallels too small to… with an adverb instead of an adjective.
**B) The photos were such blurry that we deleted the whole roll.**

Such blurry lacks a noun head. Use such blurry photos that… or so blurry that…
**C) We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf.**

Enough + uncountable noun (flour) is correct before to. We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf quantifies the ingredient, not an adjective.
**D) It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross.**

So + adjective + a + noun (+ that) is a formal but grammatical pattern. It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross matches such a narrow bridge in meaning while keeping the article after the adjective.
**E) The library was enough quiet for evening revision.**

Quiet is an adjective, so use quiet enough, not enough quiet. Flip enough to the post-adjective slot for evening revision.
tasks.solution_overview:
Slow apps, blurry photos, baking flour, a narrow bridge, and a quiet library — patterns range from everyday too…to… to the formal so + adj + a + noun. Do not mark a rarer formal pattern false just because such a… is more common.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch for such + bare adjective (needs a noun) and enough + adjective (must flip). Too + adverb + to is fine when manner is excessive, and enough + uncountable noun is the quantity slot.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check each intensifier's partner word class. Accept so narrow a bridge as a formal twin of such a narrow bridge; fail enough quiet and such blurry that…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot.
It was so clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late.
The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train.
Such were the crowds that the museum opened an extra wing.
The essay is too much short for a full literature review.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot.**

Adjective + enough + that-clause is acceptable alongside enough to…. The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot still means "sufficiently tight," with that spelling out the consequence.
**B) It was so clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late.**

So clever puzzle misses the article/noun patterning needed with a countable singular. Use such a clever puzzle that… or so clever that…
**C) The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train.**

Too + adverb/adjective + for + object + to-infinitive is a solid excess pattern. The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train means we could not catch it in time.
**D) Such were the crowds that the museum opened an extra wing.**

Inversion such were the crowds that… is formal but grammatical. Such + be + noun phrase + that intensifies the noun phrase with literary word order — still correct on a true/false grammar check.
**E) The essay is too much short for a full literature review.**

Too much short wrongly inserts much before an adjective. Use too short; save too much for nouns.
tasks.solution_overview:
Deadlines, puzzles, late couriers, museum crowds, and short essays — most items still hinge on so/such/too word order, but one formal inversion with such is legitimately correct. Unusual word order is not automatically wrong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep policing partners of so and the too much + adjective error. Adj + enough + that is acceptable, and such were the crowds that… is literary inversion, not a slip. So + adj + countable noun without a remains a classic miss.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept tight enough that… and the inverted such were…. Fail so clever puzzle (missing article patterning) and too much short (much before an adjective).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist.
They made so rapid progress that the language course finished early.
They made such rapid progress that the language course finished early.
The backpack is too heavily to carry up the ridge.
We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist.**

Not + adjective + enough + for + noun + to-infinitive is fully grammatical. The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist licenses the for…to… complement after enough.
**B) They made so rapid progress that the language course finished early.**

So + adjective + uncountable noun (progress) without a is acceptable because progress is uncountable. They made so rapid progress that… contrasts with countable so clever puzzle, which needs an article.
**C) They made such rapid progress that the language course finished early.**

Such + adjective + uncountable noun is the safer textbook twin of the previous pattern. They made such rapid progress that… is the exam-safe default many teachers prefer.
