**D) The backpack is too heavily to carry up the ridge.**

Too heavily is an adverb where an adjective is needed after be. Write too heavy to carry… (or restructure with a different verb if you truly need an adverb).
**E) We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival.**

Enough + adjective + plural noun quantifies how many of that type you have. We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival means a sufficient number of that kind — noun phrase after enough, not the illegal enough + bare adjective flip.
tasks.solution_overview:
Misty hiking maps, language progress, overloaded backpacks, and spare batteries — countable versus uncountable after so/such matters, and be still wants an adjective after too. Enough before a noun phrase is not the enough + adjective error.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Distinguish countable vs uncountable after so/such, and adjective vs adverb after linking be. So + adj + uncountable noun (so rapid progress) can work; such rapid progress is the safer twin. Too heavily after be is the wrong word class.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the noun is uncountable, both so adj + noun and such adj + noun may be true. Fail adverbials after be where an adjective describes the subject; accept not + adj + enough for…to… and enough + noun phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The view was such stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry.
It was too a complicated route for a first visit.
There has been such an upsurge in tickets that the box office stayed open late.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.**

So + adjective + as to + infinitive is a formal result pattern parallel to so…that. The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence means the view was stunning enough that it stopped us.
**B) The view was such stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.**

** Such pairs with nouns; so…as to pairs with adjectives.

Trap: Such does not take as to after a bare adjective. Use so stunning as to… or such a stunning view that…
**C) The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry.**

Not + adjective + enough + to… is correct. The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry places enough after hot before the purpose infinitive.
**D) It was too a complicated route for a first visit.**

** Too + adj + a + noun is possible (too complicated a route), but too a… never is.

Trap: Too a complicated wrongly puts the article right after too. Use too complicated a route or such a complicated route — never too a…
**E) There has been such an upsurge in tickets that the box office stayed open late.**

Such an + noun (+ that) correctly intensifies a countable singular. There has been such an upsurge in tickets that… chooses an because upsurge is countable singular.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stunning views, pastry, complicated routes, and ticket surges — formal so…as to… enters alongside ordinary enough and such. Treat the elevated pattern as fair game when the pieces fit.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective + as to + infinitive parallels so…that for result. Such does not take as to after a bare adjective, and too never precedes the article directly (too a…). Such an + countable singular remains standard.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept so stunning as to… and hot enough / such an upsurge. Fail such stunning as to… and too a complicated…; remember the repair too complicated a route is possible, but too a… never is.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend.
Fans left because the queue was such long.
We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage.
The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap.
She is enough experienced to lead the climbing group.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend.**

Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is a formal pattern matching so adj a noun. The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend means an excessively dense book for that timeframe.
**B) Fans left because the queue was such long.**

** Bare such + adjective without noun is incomplete.

Trap: Such long needs a noun: such a long queue, or else so long that…. Bare such + adjective without a noun is incomplete.
**C) We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage.**

Adverb early + enough + to-infinitive is correct — enough follows the adverb just as it follows adjectives. We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage is everyday event English.
**D) The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap.**

So + adjective + that after a reporting verb is clean. The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap keeps so on the adjective in the object complement.
**E) She is enough experienced to lead the climbing group.**

** Same flip rule as enough hot.

Trap: Experienced is an adjective, so write experienced enough, not enough experienced. Same flip rule as enough hot.
tasks.solution_overview:
Dense novels, long queues, early arrivals, rushed warm-ups, and climbing experience — formal too/so + adj + a + noun shapes appear beside the usual enough and such traps. Article placement after the adjective is the tell.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Accept too/so + adjective + a + noun when the article lands after the adjective. Reject such + bare adjective and enough + adjective, which recycle the same order mistakes from easier tasks.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see too/so + adj + a + noun + for/that, treat it as formal but true. Fail such long without a noun, and flip enough experienced to experienced enough.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The storm was so fierce as that ferries cancelled sailings.
The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings.
We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call.
It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns.
The hills are too steep for the juniors finish before dusk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The storm was so fierce as that ferries cancelled sailings.**

** Never stack as and that after so.

Trap: So…as that mixes two patterns. Choose so…that or so…as to, not both markers stacked.
**B) The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings.**

Clean so + adjective + that result clause. The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings uses one linker only.
**C) We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call.**

Enough + noun (evidence) before a to-infinitive is correct. We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call quantifies an uncountable noun under enough.
**D) It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns.**

Such a + adverb + adjective + noun is fine when the adverb modifies the adjective inside the noun phrase. It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns — the whole noun phrase still sits after such.
**E) The hills are too steep for the juniors finish before dusk.**

** For + object needs to before the verb.

Trap: Missing to before the infinitive: write too steep for the juniors to finish before dusk. For + object needs to before the verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
Fierce storms, referee disputes, poorly printed maps, and steep hills for juniors — blended result markers and a missing to after for + object are the hard catches. Such can still head a heavily modified noun phrase.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hunt stacked linkers after so (as that mixes two patterns) and missing to in too…for X [to] V. Enough + noun before to remains the quantity pattern; such a + adverb + adjective + noun is fine when everything modifies the noun head.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Choose exactly one result linker after so: that or as to, never as that. Keep enough evidence and such a poorly printed map; add to before finish in the juniors line.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Practice stopped because the heat became so intense.
Practice stopped because the heat became such intense.
The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion.
There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane.
The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Practice stopped because the heat became so intense.**

So + adjective can stand without a that-clause when the result is implied by context. Practice stopped because the heat became so intense — that-clause is common but not obligatory.
**B) Practice stopped because the heat became such intense.**

** After become, prefer so + adjective.

Trap: Such intense needs a noun (such intense heat) or a switch to so intense. After become, prefer so + adjective for a subject complement.
**C) The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion.**

Carefully enough places enough after the adverb modifying how the clause is worded. The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion works like adj + enough + to…
**D) There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane.**

Too few + plural noun expresses insufficiency — an excess of scarcity. There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane is grammatical and means roughly not enough lifeguards.
**E) The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty.**

So few + plural noun + that is grammatical and parallel to so many. The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty pairs few with a plural count noun under so.
tasks.solution_overview:
Intense heat stopping practice, careful wording, short staffing of lifeguards, and a sparse gallery wall — result that-clauses are optional here. The real test is whether such has a noun and whether few sits correctly after so/too.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective can stand alone when context implies the result. Such still needs a noun head after become. Too few / so few + plural noun are grammatical quantity patterns, not the too much + adjective error.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If such + adjective has no noun, mark false. Accept bare so intense, carefully enough to…, too few lifeguards, and so few paintings that…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour.
The rule is so that latecomers wait for the next tour.
Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race.
She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass.
The trail is not enough marked for night walking.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour.**

Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern without an adjective after such. The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour means the nature of the rule produces that outcome.
**B) The rule is so that latecomers wait for the next tour.**

** So that ≠ such that; different jobs.

Trap: So that expresses purpose ("in order that"), not the "of a kind that" reading. Here such that is required if you mean the rule's character.
**C) Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race.**

Too + adjective + to-infinitive inside a participial absolute is still grammatical. Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race keeps the too…to shape in a reduced clause.
**D) She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass.**

Enough of a + singular countable noun is idiomatic. She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass — of a(n) before the singular count noun is the natural frame.
**E) The trail is not enough marked for night walking.**

** Flip enough after adjectives even with not.

Trap: Marked is adjectival here, so write not marked enough, not not enough marked. Flip enough after the adjective even under negation.
tasks.solution_overview:
Tour rules, muddy race courses, bike gaps, and marked trails — harder items separate such that (nature/result) from so that (purpose), and test enough of a… plus adjective–enough order under negation.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern. So that marks purpose ("in order that") and cannot swap in for that reading. Enough of a + singular countable noun is idiomatic; enough still follows adjectives even with not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the clause describes the nature of the rule (such that) or a purpose (so that). Accept too…to inside reduced clauses and enough of a gap; flip not enough marked to not marked enough.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Attendance fell so low as volunteers began cancelling shifts.

tactical_explanations:
**A) Attendance fell so low as volunteers began cancelling shifts.**

** So adj as + finite clause is not standard for result.

Trap: So…as without to needs a different reading; here a result clause should use that (or so low as to cause…). So adj as + finite clause is not standard for result.
**B) Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts.**

So + adjective + that correctly states the result. Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts is the default result pattern.
**C) The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student.**

Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is grammatical formal English. The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student ≈ an excessively costly requirement.
**D) We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists.**

Such…as meaning "the kind that" with a relative-like clause is correct. We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists = the spices that the recipe lists.
**E) The rebuild was enough extensive that the gallery closed for a year.**

** Enough never precedes the adjective in this frame.

Trap: Enough extensive reverses order; need extensive enough that…. Enough never precedes the adjective in this frame.
tasks.solution_overview:
Falling attendance, costly visas, listed spices, and a long rebuild — result linkers after so, formal too adj a noun, and such…as all appear. Enough + adjective is still illegal.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate result that from faulty so…as + finite clause. Formal such…as ("the kind that") and too + adjective + a + noun are acceptable. Keep policing enough before adjectives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Default result linker after so is that (or as to + infinitive). Accept too costly a requirement and such spices as…; fail so low as volunteers… and enough extensive…

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale.
Cash on hand is barely enough for bus fare, let alone a taxi.
It was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.
There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.
The dish became such favourite with locals that tourists queued daily.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale.**

So + past participle/adjective + as to + infinitive expresses designed result. The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale = arranged in such a way that it built toward the finale.
**B) Cash on hand is barely enough for bus fare, let alone a taxi.**

Enough for + noun works; barely intensifies sufficiency without breaking grammar. Cash on hand is barely enough for bus fare, let alone a taxi keeps enough in its quantity/sufficiency role.

**Tip:** ** Modifiers like barely/almost can precede enough.
**C) It was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.**

** Watch dummy it with quantity noun phrases.

Trap: It was too little time is awkward/wrong for this quantity reading. Prefer there was / we had too little time, or too little time remained.
**D) There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.**

There was too little + uncountable noun (+ to…) is the natural existential pattern. There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act frames the shortage cleanly.

**Tip:** ** Prefer there-insertion with too little/much + noun.
**E) The dish became such favourite with locals that tourists queued daily.**

** Countable singular after such almost always needs a/an.

Trap: Needs an article: such a favourite with… (or so popular with…). Countable singular after such almost always needs a/an.
tasks.solution_overview:
Playlists, bus fare, rehearsal time, and a local favourite dish — existential framing with too little + noun and articles after such decide several letters. Surface similarity can hide a missing there or a/an.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Judge there was / we had with too little + noun, article requirements after such with countable singulars, and formal so…as to…. Barely can intensify enough without breaking the pattern.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Prefer there-insertion with too little/much + noun; fail dummy it was too little time…. Accept so arranged as to… and barely enough for…; add a before favourite.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant.
The experiment is designed so that temperature stays constant.

We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant.**

Designed such that… means "in such a way that" and is standard in scientific English. The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant is a normal lab-register pattern.

**Tip:** ** Verb + such that ≈ configured so that.
**B) The experiment is designed so that temperature stays constant.**

Designed so that… expressing purpose/result is also grammatical. Here so that and such that can both work, with so that leaning slightly more toward intended purpose.
**C) The dough proved elastic enough that it stretched without tearing.**

Adjective + enough + that-clause is acceptable. The dough proved elastic enough that it stretched without tearing = sufficiently elastic that it stretched without tearing.
**D) He spoke with so a confident tone that doubts faded.**

** So a… returns as a trap even in longer NPs.

Trap: So a confident tone is wrong; use such a confident tone or so confidently that…. So a… returns as a trap even inside longer noun phrases.
**E) We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break.**

Adjective + enough + not to-infinitive correctly encodes avoidance. We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break = sufficiently short to avoid overrunning.
tasks.solution_overview:
Lab temperature control, elastic dough, confident speaking, and a short talk — after verbs of designing, both so that and such that can be right. The old so a… trap still fails.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Designed such that… ("in such a way that") and designed so that… (purpose/result) are both grammatical with slightly different nuance. Adj + enough + that and enough not to… are valid; so a… is not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow both designing linkers when the sentence is well formed. Fail so a confident tone; accept elastic enough that… and short enough not to…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains.
The tent proved insufficiently sturdy enough to survive the gale.
Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed.
The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started.
They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains.**

Inversion with seldom does not break the inner so…that pattern. Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains — evaluate the so…that core as true.

**Tip:** ** Judge the so/such/too/enough core even inside inversion shells.
**B) The tent proved insufficiently sturdy enough to survive the gale.**

** One sufficiency tool per adjective phrase.

Trap: Insufficiently sturdy enough doubles the sufficiency marker. Use insufficiently sturdy or not sturdy enough — not both in one adjective phrase.
**C) Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed.**

Not so much X as Y is an established correlative; so is required in this idiom. Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed is grammatical even though this is not ordinary so + adjective intensification.
**D) The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started.**

Such that introducing a counterfactual continuation is formal and correct. The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started — such that can host complex follow-ons, including inverted conditionals.
**E) They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly.**

Too + adverb + for + noun + to-infinitive marks excess manner or cost. They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly parallels too steep for X to V, with the adverb modifying the verb priced.

**Tip:** ** Too steeply for X to V parallels too steep for X to V (adv vs adj depends on what is modified).
tasks.solution_overview:
Eroded coastlines, gale-hit tents, timed complaints, delayed concerts, and steep ticket prices — advanced packaging wraps familiar so/such/too cores in inversion and idioms. Reject double intensifiers; keep legitimate so idioms.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Inversion shells and correlative not so much…as… still hide a clean so/such/too/enough core you can judge. Insufficiently…enough doubles sufficiency marking. Too + adverb + for…to… remains available for excess manner or cost.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Judge the inner pattern even when seldom opens the sentence. Fail stacked insufficiently sturdy enough; accept not so much…as…, such that with a counterfactual continuation, and too steeply for students to…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18

**B) No other runner moved such swiftly as to claim the lead overnight.**

** Such → noun phrases only (or such that).

Trap: Such does not modify adverbs; such swiftly is impossible. Switch to so swiftly as to… or restructure with a noun phrase under such.

Adverb/adjective + enough + that remains grammatical in careful register. The rule is drawn tightly enough that substitutions need consent = sufficiently tightly that…

tasks.solution_overview:
Overnight race leads, tightly drawn rules, thin daylight, and intuitive interfaces — stress-test so…as to… with adverbs and demand the right linker after so adj a noun. Degree modifiers before too are allowed.

So + adverb + as to + infinitive works; such does not modify adverbs. Adv/adj + enough + that remains fine in careful register. Rather too… is idiomatic; so adj a noun needs that or as to, not bare as + finite clause.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

Kayaking on a high river, biased samples, thin supplies, and perfectionists — article placement separates so adj a noun (correct) from such adj a noun (incorrect). The idiom too much of a… to… is also in play.

So + adjective + a + noun keeps the article after the adjective; such wants such a + adjective + noun. Embedded enough patterns survive inversion. Enough and too can contrast in one sentence; too much of a + noun + to… is a fixed evaluative idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept high enough inside only then did…, so biased a sample, healthy enough / too thin, and too much of a perfectionist to…. Fail such biased a sample (article must precede the adjective after such).

Icy lakes, long rehearsals, poster promises, early booking automation, and abrupt replies — the final set mixes conditionals, formal too adj a noun, and result-linker discipline after so. Keep such that versus so that distinct.

Accept thick enough in the inverted conditional, swift enough to…, and too early a stage…. Fail so protracted as nobody… and was so that we… (use such that or so + adj + that).

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success depends of careful practice before the recital.
She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.
They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.
Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.
He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Success depends of careful practice before the recital.**

Depend never partners with of in standard English. The locked pattern is depend on (or upon) plus a noun or gerund for the thing that controls the outcome.
**B) She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.**

Responsible takes for when you name a duty or job. Responsible of is not an English ownership/duty frame.
**C) They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.**

Interest as an adjective locks to in: interested in learning / interested in Portuguese.
**D) Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.**

Despite is a single preposition; it never takes of. You can write Despite the rain or In spite of the rain — but not Despite of.
**E) He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.**

Accuse (and be accused) locks to of plus a wrongdoing noun or gerund. Here accused of cheating is exactly the exam pattern.

Nothing to repair — keep of and the -ing form together.
tasks.solution_overview:
Before a recital or a neighbour-sitting favour, English often locks a verb or adjective to one preposition — and the wrong partner sounds almost right if you translate from another language.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This task is all about fixed dependency and responsibility patterns: depend on, responsible for, interested in, despite (no of), and accused of. The classic false friends are of after depend/responsible/despite, and on after interested.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline the head word and the preposition right after it. Ask whether that pair is the textbook lock for this meaning. If you can swap in the standard preposition and the sentence suddenly sounds native, mark the original false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.
Her recipe differs of last year's version.
We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.
The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.
She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.**

Insist on plus a gerund is the fixed forcefulness pattern: he insisted on seeing the sheets, not a bare infinitive.

The form matches the lock, so the line stands.
**B) Her recipe differs of last year's version.**

Differ compares one thing with another using from. Differs of is a transfer error, not a variant.
**C) We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.**

Careful exam English wants apologise for a fault or inconvenience. Apologised about is weaker and often marked wrong even when it is heard in speech.
**D) The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.**

Focus and concentrate take on, never to, when they name a topic of attention.
**E) She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.**

Participate in correctly names involvement in an event or activity. The workshop line uses the right lock.
tasks.solution_overview:
These lines mix everyday insist, differ, apologise, focus, and participate — verbs that almost all students know, but that each demand one locked preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch insist on + -ing, differ from, apologise for, focus on, and participate in. The traps swap of/about/to into slots that English does not allow for those heads.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the verb, then name the preposition that textbooks glue to it. If the sentence uses a different satellite, it is false even when the meaning is clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.
The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.
She is good in swimming long distances.
We look forward to meeting your cousins.
He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.
tactical_explanations:
**A) They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.**

Object takes to, not against: objected to the new quiet-hours rule. Protest against is a different verb with a different preposition.
**B) The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.**

Capable of plus a gerund is the standard ability frame, and handling the front desk fits it cleanly.

Do not confuse it with able to + infinitive — different head, different pattern.
**C) She is good in swimming long distances.**

Skills and activities take good at in exam English: good at swimming. Good in is reserved (at best) for school subjects in some varieties, and even there at is safer for a sport/skill.
**D) We look forward to meeting your cousins.**

Look forward to is a multi-word unit; to is a preposition here, so it takes a noun or gerund (meeting), not a bare infinitive.

The cousins line is correctly formed.
**E) He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.**

Succeed in plus -ing reports achievement. Succeeded to repair copies manage to, which is the wrong head for this verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
Object, capable, good, look forward, and succeed all look friendly — until the wrong preposition or infinitive slips in after them.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The fixed frames here are object to, capable of + -ing, good at (skills), look forward to + -ing, and succeed in + -ing. Mixing against/in/to-infinitives against those locks is the trap set.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check two layers: which preposition the head wants, and whether what follows should be a gerund rather than a bare or to-infinitive.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.
This jacket belongs to my older brother.
You can rely of her to bring the tent.
They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.
A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.**

Consist of lists the ingredients or parts. Consist from has no place in this frame (be made from is a different pattern).
**B) This jacket belongs to my older brother.**

Belong to marks ownership cleanly: the jacket belongs to my older brother.

Never write belong of.
**C) You can rely of her to bring the tent.**

Rely, depend, and count all take on for trust. Rely of is the same transfer trap as depend of.
**D) They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.**

You complain about a problem (noise, service) and complain to a person. Complain for is non-standard for this meaning.
**E) A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.**

Prevent someone from + gerund is the restraint lock. The locked-gate line uses it correctly.

Do not replace from with to after prevent.
tasks.solution_overview:
Ownership, composition, trust, complaint, and prevention verbs are tightly glued to one preposition each in everyday English.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Target consist of, belong to, rely on, complain about, and prevent from. Swapping from/of/for into those slots is enough to fail the item.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the preposition names parts, possession, support, a grievance topic, or a blocked action — then match the lock listed above.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.
This trail is similar with the one near the lake.
My playlist is different than yours in every genre.
She has been married with her partner for twelve years.
The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.**

Famous for plus a feature is the standard reputation pattern, and tiled façades fit that slot.

Famous as would name a role, not a tourist trademark.
**B) This trail is similar with the one near the lake.**

Similar, identical, and comparable take to, not with.
**C) My playlist is different than yours in every genre.**

In careful exam English prefer different from (or different to in some BrE); different than is often marked down even where American speech allows it.
**D) She has been married with her partner for twelve years.**

Married to a person is the lock. Married with copies other languages and belongs instead in frames like live with.
**E) The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.**

Afraid of plus a noun (thunderstorms) is correct and natural.

Frightened of follows the same of pattern.
tasks.solution_overview:
Adjective + preposition pairs feel flexible when you translate, but exam English treats famous for, similar to, different from, married to, and afraid of as closed locks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set checks reputation (famous for), comparison (similar to / different from), marriage (married to), and fear (afraid of). With, than, and from transfers are the usual failures.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the preposition and ask which one the adjective textbooks require. If your guess differs from what is on the page, the sentence is false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We arrived to the station just before midnight.
Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.
They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.
Look at the mural behind the café.
We talked the film for almost an hour.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We arrived to the station just before midnight.**

Arrive at a station or building and arrive in a city or country — not arrive to. Get to is the pattern that keeps to.
**B) Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.**

Listen to plus an object is obligatory. Hear can take a direct object; listen cannot in standard exam English.

The podcast line is correctly locked.
**C) They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.**

Wait for someone or something. Wait cannot take the bus as a bare object here.
**D) Look at the mural behind the café.**

Look at directs visual attention to a target. The mural line uses the right preposition.

Watch can take a bare object; look usually needs at.
**E) We talked the film for almost an hour.**

Talk about a topic (or talk to a person). Talk the film drops the required about.
tasks.solution_overview:
Arrive, listen, wait, look, and talk are easy verbs — and easy to strip of the preposition English still needs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch arrive at/in (not to), listen to, wait for, look at, and talk about. Dropping the satellite or using the wrong one after movement and perception verbs is the test.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the verb can take a bare object in standard English. If it cannot, restore the missing preposition before you decide true or false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She goes to work by foot every morning.
They travelled to the coast by train.
The match starts in Monday evening.
I usually read in night when the house is quiet.
We met on a cold Friday afternoon.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She goes to work by foot every morning.**

Walking uses on foot, not by foot. By is for vehicles (by bus, by train, by car).
**B) They travelled to the coast by train.**

By train correctly names the means of transport. The coast line is fine.
**C) The match starts in Monday evening.**

Days and dated evenings take on: on Monday / on Monday evening. In Monday is wrong.
**D) I usually read in night when the house is quiet.**

At night is the fixed time phrase. Bare in night is not standard.
**E) We met on a cold Friday afternoon.**

On plus a day or date phrase is standard: on a cold Friday afternoon works in everyday and exam English alike.

The adjective cold sits inside the noun phrase and does not change the preposition lock.
tasks.solution_overview:
Time and transport prepositions are closed sets: English picks by, on, in, or at by rule, not by feel.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Remember by + vehicle, on foot (the walking exception), on + day/dated time, and at night. In Monday and in night are classic calendar false friends.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Classify each phrase as transport means or time slot, then apply the closed-set rule instead of translating from another language.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.
Don't blame me about the burnt toast.
Thanks for helping me move the sofa.
The hostel provided us with clean towels.
Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.**

Congratulate someone on an achievement. For after congratulate is weaker and typically marked wrong in exams.
**B) Don't blame me about the burnt toast.**

Blame someone for something. About does not replace for after blame.
**C) Thanks for helping me move the sofa.**

Thanks for plus a gerund or noun is the correct gratitude frame, and helping fits it cleanly.

Thank someone for doing X follows the same for lock in full-sentence form.
**D) The hostel provided us with clean towels.**

Provide someone with something is the classic ditransitive lock, and clean towels fit it.

Provide something to someone is another acceptable shape; with is right here.
**E) Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.**

Charge someone with an offence. Of belongs to accuse, not to charge.
tasks.solution_overview:
Speech-act and legal-ish verbs look alike when someone blames, thanks, or charges — but each head keeps its own preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate congratulate on, blame for, thank for, provide with, and charge with. Mixing for/of/about across those heads is the designed trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Identify the speech act first, then recall its private preposition. Near-synonyms do not share satellites.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.
She is fond from old jazz records.
They take pride of their community garden.
I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.
He gets bored of the same playlist every day.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.**

Keen on plus a noun or gerund expresses enthusiasm, same neighbourhood as interested in.

The canal-run line is correctly locked.
**B) She is fond from old jazz records.**

Fond of names people or things you like. Fond from is never the pattern.

Trap: fond from → fond of old jazz records.
**C) They take pride of their community garden.**

Take pride in an achievement. Pride of mixes the noun pride with the adjective proud of.

Trap: take pride of → take pride in their community garden.
**D) I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.**

Tired of plus a gerund or noun is fixed for weariness with a situation.

Exhausted from effort is a different idea with a different preposition.
**E) He gets bored of the same playlist every day.**

Careful English prefers bored with (or by). Bored of is informal and often marked non-standard in exams.

Trap: bored of → bored with the same playlist. (Fed up with is the of-cousin.)
tasks.solution_overview:
Attitude words — keen, fond, pride, tired, bored — each lock to one preposition, and near-synonyms refuse to share.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hold keen on, fond of, take pride in, tired of, and bored with. From/of swaps and informal bored of are the failure modes.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Memorise the pair as a single chunk. If a synonym would take a different preposition, do not import that preposition onto this head.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.
We stayed home because of the flooding.
She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.
In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.
As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.
tactical_explanations:
**A) According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.**

According to plus a source is the reporting phrase. According with is not used for this meaning.

The weather-app line is correctly formed.
**B) We stayed home because of the flooding.**

Because of plus a noun phrase correctly gives a reason for staying home.

Because + clause would need a finite clause, not of.
**C) She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.**

Instead of coffee is the comparison lock. Bare instead cannot take a following noun this way.

Trap: instead coffee → instead of coffee. (Adverb instead stands alone.)
**D) In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.**

In addition to stretching pairs with as well as — both keep to, not of.
**E) As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.**

As a result of plus a noun phrase is the fixed causal chunk, and the delay line uses it well.

As a result alone needs a comma and a following clause.
tasks.solution_overview:
Multi-word prepositions are all-or-nothing chunks: miss or swap the final preposition and the whole phrase collapses.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set locks according to, because of, instead of, in addition to, and as a result of. Stripped of/to after instead and addition are the main traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat each opener as a fixed string. If the last word of the chunk is missing or wrong, mark false without rewriting the rest of the clause.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.
The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.
Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.
Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.
He specialised in marine biology at university.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.**

Insist that plus a clause is a valid frame alongside insist on + -ing. Leaving before dawn is correctly embedded under that.

Both frames are fine; they are just different shapes.
**B) The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.**

Discourage someone from swimming, not to swim. The from + -ing pattern matches prevent and keep.
**C) Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.**

Recover from an illness is the standard medical collocation. Recover of is wrong.

The warm-soup line stands.
**D) Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.**

For prevention, stop someone from finishing (or stop someone finishing). Stop her to finish means pause in order to finish — the wrong reading here.
**E) He specialised in marine biology at university.**

Specialise in a field is fixed. Marine biology at university fits the lock.
tasks.solution_overview:
Some verbs invite an infinitive that is actually illegal — they want from + -ing, or a that-clause instead.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep insist that (alongside insist on), recover from, and specialise in. Catch discourage and preventive stop, which take from + -ing rather than to-infinitives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When a verb seems to take to + V, pause: is it really a prevent/encourage family member that wants from + -ing? Check that family first.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm used to waking up before sunrise.
She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.
They are accustomed with long bus rides.
He prefers walking to cycling in the city.
We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I'm used to waking up before sunrise.**

Be/get used to plus a gerund means accustomed to a habit. Waking before sunrise fits that familiarity frame.
**B) She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.**

Past habit needs used to + base verb: used to wake, not used to waking.

Trap: used to waking → used to wake when she worked nights. Do not confuse with be used to + -ing.
**C) They are accustomed with long bus rides.**

Accustomed to mirrors used to for familiarity. Accustomed with is wrong.

Trap: accustomed with → accustomed to long bus rides.
**D) He prefers walking to cycling in the city.**

Prefer X to Y correctly stacks two options: walking to cycling.

That to comparison is the standard exam shape; than would belong to rather, not prefer.
**E) We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.**

Prefer … than is not the English comparison. Use prefer walking to cycling, or would rather walk than cycle.
highlights: used to waking up before sunrise when
tasks.solution_overview:
Used to and be used to look like the same phrase; prefer … to/than collides the same way. This task forces you to keep the frames apart.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate past-habit used to + base verb from be used to + -ing, keep accustomed to, and compare with prefer A to B — never prefer … than.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask first whether used to means past habit or present familiarity. Then check prefer comparisons for to versus than.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.
In spite the heat, they finished the hike.
Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.
She refrained to comment during the argument.
Please refrain from posting spoilers online.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.**

In spite of plus a noun phrase equals despite. The of is part of the chunk, and the hike line keeps it.
**B) In spite the heat, they finished the hike.**

In spite must be followed by of before a noun. In spite the heat is incomplete.
**C) Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.**

Notwithstanding takes a noun phrase with no extra of, like despite. The choir line is correct.
**D) She refrained to comment during the argument.**

Refrain from commenting, not refrain to comment. Abstain follows the same from + -ing shape.
**E) Please refrain from posting spoilers online.**

Refrain from plus a gerund is the fixed restraint pattern, and posting spoilers fits it.

Keep from after refrain; a to-infinitive would break the same head you fixed in the previous false line.
tasks.solution_overview:
Contrast markers and restraint verbs look interchangeable until you notice which ones keep of and which ones refuse it.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Despite and notwithstanding take a noun with no of; in spite of needs of. Refrain takes from + -ing, not a to-infinitive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For contrast phrases, check whether of is required or forbidden. For refrain, demand from + -ing every time.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.
Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.
She has no intention to cancel the trip.
There is no point of arguing about the score.
What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?
tactical_explanations:
**A) The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.**

Depend on correctly ties the outcome to temperature. Outcome of X and depend on Y can both be right in one sentence.
**B) Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.**

Access to a place is the fixed pattern for entry rights. Access of is not used for places.
**C) She has no intention to cancel the trip.**

Have no intention of cancelling is the preferred exam lock. Intention to is often marked wrong even when heard elsewhere.
**D) There is no point of arguing about the score.**

No point in arguing is the frame here. Point of arguing mismatches this no-point structure (though what's the point of is a related pattern).
**E) What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?.**

What's the point in staying matches an acceptable rhetorical frame with in + gerund.

Point in and point of both appear; match the whole fixed question shape.
tasks.solution_overview:
Abstract nouns — outcome, access, intention, point — each pick a locked preposition that does not follow from "future" intuition alone.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep depend on and access to. Prefer intention of + -ing and match point in/of to the whole fixed frame; bare intention to is the soft trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Do not assume to after every noun that looks ahead. Check the collocation dictionary pattern for that noun before judging.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.
He was angry about the cancelled ferry.
They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.
I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.
We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.**

Angry with a person plus for a reason is a solid double pattern: with her brother for borrowing the headphones.

With names the person; for names the offence — both locks can sit in one sentence.

**Tip:** ** Angry with people; about situations.
**B) He was angry about the cancelled ferry.**

Angry about a cancelled ferry correctly targets a situation or event, not a person.

If the complement were a sibling or colleague, you would switch to angry with instead.

**Tip:** ** About for things; with for people.
**C) They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.**

Pleased with or by — not pleased of. Proud of is the of-cousin; do not import it onto pleased.
**D) I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.**

Delighted with a result is natural and grammatical. Delighted by also works; delighted to hear that… is another frame.
**E) We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.**

Surprised by or at the news — not surprised from.
tasks.solution_overview:
Emotion adjectives split people from situations, and they reject of/from transfers that proud sometimes invites.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Use angry with for people and angry about for situations; keep pleased/delighted with and surprised by/at. Pleased of and surprised from are the traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the complement is a person or a situation, then lock the preposition. Reject of/from unless the adjective truly owns them (proud of, not pleased of).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.
This jacket smells like woodsmoke.
She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.
Can you remind me of locking the back door?
Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.**

Taste of a flavour is the fixed sensory pattern for substances in the soup.

Smell of works the same way for a substance.
**B) This jacket smells like woodsmoke.**

Smell like for resemblance is acceptable and grammatical here.

Smell of woodsmoke would also work as a substance reading.
**C) She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.**

Remind someone of a person or thing triggers memory or resemblance. The teacher line uses of correctly.

**Tip:** ** Remind of a memory; remind to do a duty.
**D) Can you remind me of locking the back door?.**

For a future action, remind me to lock — not remind me of locking. Of would suggest memory or resemblance, not a prompt.
**E) Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.**

Remind someone to plus an infinitive correctly issues a prompt about a future action.

That to-frame is the instruction reading; of would be for memory or resemblance, not for "bring the blanket."

**Tip:** ** Reminder for actions → to + V.
tasks.solution_overview:
Sensory of/like patterns are usually safe; remind is the hard verb because it splits into two different frames.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Taste of and smell like are fine for flavour and resemblance. Remind of covers memory or resemblance; remind to covers a future prompt — do not mix them.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For remind, ask whether the complement is a memory trigger or an instruction to act. That single question chooses of versus to.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.
Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.
The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.
Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.
Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.**

Owing to plus a noun phrase is a formal because-of equivalent. High winds fit the causal slot.
**B) Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.**

Owing needs to before the noun phrase. Bare Owing the… is incomplete.

Trap: insert to → Owing to the high winds.
**C) The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.**

Due to plus a noun is widely accepted as a causal preposition in modern exam English, matching because of.

Flooding on the trail fills that noun slot, so the postponed-hike line stands.
**D) Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.**

Due the flooding drops the required to.
**E) Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.**

Thanks to plus a noun credits a (usually positive) cause. Clear sky and meteor shower fit that shade.

**Tip:** ** Thanks to (positive); owing/due to (neutral/negative).
tasks.solution_overview:
Causal multi-word prepositions all keep a final to: strip it and the phrase is broken even if the nouns are clear.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Owing to, due to, and thanks to are complete only with to. Owing the… and Due the… are automatic fails; the full forms with to are true.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for owing/due/thanks and confirm the next word is to. Missing to alone decides false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She accused him for leaving the gate open.
They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.
He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.
The club banned him from using the tennis courts.
Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She accused him for leaving the gate open.**

Accuse someone of doing, not for. For belongs to blame.

Trap: accused him for → accused him of leaving the gate open.
**B) They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.**

Suspected of plus a gerund is the fixed collocation for alleged wrongdoing.

The same of satellite appears after accuse; do not swap in for here.
**C) He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.**

Convicted of an offence is the standard legal/exam pattern. For appears in loose usage but of is the safer lock here.
**D) The club banned him from using the tennis courts.**

Ban someone from plus a gerund or noun is correct. Prohibit follows from; forbid someone to is a different shape.
**E) Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.**

Compensate for a loss. In this sense compensate cannot take the loss as a bare object.

Trap: compensate the loss → compensate for the loss of the old oak.
tasks.solution_overview:
Fault, suspicion, conviction, bans, and compensation are preposition-heavy: one wrong satellite and the legal flavour collapses.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hold accuse/suspect/convict of, ban from, and compensate for. Accuse for, convict for, and bare compensate the loss are the designed errors.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Pair each verb with its private preposition before you care about the gerund. Dropping or swapping that satellite fails the item.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.
Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.
She prides herself in finishing every crossword.
She takes pride in finishing every crossword.
He is proud for his daughter's science prize.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.**

Contingent on plus a noun or gerund matches depend on for conditions. Dry weather fits.
**B) Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.**

Contingent of is a depend-of style transfer. The condition lock is on.
**C) She prides herself in finishing every crossword.**

Pride oneself on doing, not in, after the reflexive verb. In belongs to take pride in.

Trap: prides herself in → prides herself on finishing every crossword.
**D) She takes pride in finishing every crossword.**

Take pride in plus a gerund is fixed and correct here.

Be proud of is the adjective cousin with of.
**E) He is proud for his daughter's science prize.**

Proud of an achievement, not proud for.

Trap: proud for → proud of his daughter's science prize.
tasks.solution_overview:
Pride frames look identical until you notice the verb under them: pride oneself, take pride, and be proud each want a different preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Contingent follows depend → on (never of). Then separate pride oneself on, take pride in, and be proud of — importing in/for across those frames fails.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the exact verb phrase first. Only then pick on, in, or of. Contingent always tracks depend on.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.
The café had run out from cups before noon.
I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.
She objects to being photographed without consent.
He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.
tactical_explanations:
**A) By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.**

Run out of plus a noun is the depletion pattern. Cups before arrival fits of.
**B) The café had run out from cups before noon.**

Run out from cups is wrong; materials take of after run out.
**C) I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.**

Looking forward to the hike, not for. To is part of the multi-word verb and takes a noun or -ing.
**D) She objects to being photographed without consent.**

Object to plus a gerund is correct: objects to being photographed. Against is a false friend from other languages.
**E) He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.**

Succeeded in repairing, not on. On belongs to insist, not succeed.

Trap: succeeded on → succeeded in repairing the leaky tap.
tasks.solution_overview:
Close with the high-frequency exam cluster: run out, look forward, object, and succeed — each fails or passes on one satellite preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Lock run out of, look forward to, object to, and succeed in. From/for/on swaps are the only difference between true and false here.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ignore how natural the sentence feels in translation. Match the exact multi-word verb to its textbook preposition, then decide.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wonder where he is.
I wonder where is he.
Could you tell me what time the train leaves?
Could you tell me what time does the train leave?
She asked whether the bakery was still open.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I wonder where he is.**

After wonder, the embedded clause must keep statement order: where + subject + verb. Here that gives where he is, which matches the pattern exactly. The outer I wonder already asks; the inner clause does not need to.
**B) I wonder where is he.**

where is he inverts the verb and subject, which belongs only in a direct question. After I wonder you need where he is. Cover I wonder and you immediately hear a stand-alone quiz question — that is the scar.
**C) Could you tell me what time the train leaves?**

The polite frame Could you tell me… embeds what time the train leaves with subject before verb. No does appears inside the clause, which is exactly what an indirect question wants. The outer Could you… supplies the interrogative force for the whole sentence.
**D) Could you tell me what time does the train leave?**

does the train leave is direct-question word order jammed into an indirect question. Repair it to what time the train leaves. Any do/does/did that jumps before the subject after tell me is almost always wrong.
**E) She asked whether the bakery was still open.**

whether correctly opens a yes/no embed and keeps statement order: the bakery was still open. There is no were-fronting after whether. Yes/no embeds follow the same calm subject–verb rule as wh-embeds.
tasks.solution_overview:
You are judging whether each sentence embeds its question the English way — as a calm statement clause after wonder, tell me, or ask — rather than as a stand-alone question.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Indirect questions keep statement word order after the wh-word or after whether/if. The outer softener (I wonder, Could you tell me) already carries the questioning force. What fails is stray do-support or a swapped auxiliary–subject pair smuggled into the embed.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the outer frame and read only the clause after where / what time / whether. If that clause still looks like a quiz show question (where is he?, does the train…?), mark it false. If it reads like ordinary news (where he is, the train leaves, the bakery was), mark it true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Do you know if the library has opened yet?
Do you know if has the library opened yet?
Please explain why the soup burned.
Please explain why did the soup burn.
They could not decide which route was safer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Do you know if the library has opened yet?**

if embeds a yes/no clause with normal order: the library has opened yet. has stays after the library, not before it. The outer Do you know… is already the direct question; the inner clause stays flat.
**B) Do you know if has the library opened yet?**

if has the library… wrongly inverts the auxiliary into the embedded clause. Keep if the library has…. Treat any has/is/will sitting right after if as a red flag.
**C) Please explain why the soup burned.**

why the soup burned is statement order after explain; no auxiliary is needed. The past verb burned already carries tense, so there is nowhere for did to go. Explain why… invites a reason clause, not a second question.
**D) Please explain why did the soup burn.**

why did the soup burn mirrors a direct question. The embedding verb already carries the interrogative force, so drop did: why the soup burned. If you can strip the outer Please explain and still have a complete quiz question, the embed is inverted.
**E) They could not decide which route was safer.**

which route was safer keeps subject–verb order inside the embedded choice. route is the subject of was; nothing is fronted. which + noun + verb is the calm pattern you want.
tasks.solution_overview:
These items sit after know, explain, and decide — verbs that swallow a full subordinate question without letting it keep direct-question gymnastics.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on if/whether and on wh-clauses (why, which). Correct items keep the subject before the finite verb. Wrong ones smuggle has…? or did…? inversion into the subordinate clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find the embed opener (if, why, which) and check the next two words. If an auxiliary has already jumped ahead of the subject, the item is false. If you hear a quiet subject–verb pair, the item is true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The question is how the team will respond.
The question is how will the team respond?
I am not sure what caused the blackout.
I am not sure what did cause the blackout.
She asked whether were the tickets still valid.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The question is how the team will respond.**

After The question is, how the team will respond uses statement order: subject team before will. The noun-phrase frame does not license inversion. Read it aloud without rising question intonation inside the how-clause — it should sound like news.
**B) The question is how will the team respond?**

how will the team respond? is a direct question glued onto The question is. Repair to how the team will respond — subject, then modal. The trailing question mark is another giveaway that someone forgot the clause was embedded.
**C) I am not sure what caused the blackout.**

what is the subject of caused, so no do-support is required or allowed. Subject wh-clauses already have their actor in the wh-word. what caused the blackout is the whole story.
**D) I am not sure what did cause the blackout.**

what did cause forces unnecessary do-support into an embedded subject question. Use what caused, not what did cause. Save did for object questions that need tense support in direct speech — not for subject who/what embeds.
**E) She asked whether were the tickets still valid.**

whether were the tickets… inverts were and the subject after whether. Repair to whether the tickets were still valid. whether never takes the yes/no flip that stand-alone Were the tickets…? uses.
tasks.solution_overview:
Noun-phrase frames (The question is…, I am not sure…) still demand embedded statement order — and subject questions refuse fake did.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Two classic traps: modal inversion after how (will the team…) and unnecessary do-support in a subject question (what did cause…). A third trap is were-fronting after whether.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the wh-word is the subject of the next verb. If it is, you never need did. Otherwise check that any modal or be-form sits after its subject, not before. Correct embeds read like calm statements parked inside a larger sentence.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They could not decide which option was it safer.
I'd like to know when the guests arrive.
I'd like to know when do the guests arrive.
Can you remind me where the spare keys are kept?
Can you remind me where are the spare keys kept?
tactical_explanations:
**A) They could not decide which option was it safer.**

Extra pronoun it after was breaks the clause; which option was safer is already complete. Never park a dummy it after the verb in an embedded which-clause. The option is the subject — you do not need a second subject.
**B) I'd like to know when the guests arrive.**

when the guests arrive keeps subject–verb order after I'd like to know. Softeners do not change the embedded word-order rule. arrive sits after guests, exactly where a statement puts it.
**C) I'd like to know when do the guests arrive.**

when do the guests arrive inserts do-support as if the clause were a direct question. Delete do: when the guests arrive. The outer I'd like to know already asks; the inner clause should not.
**D) Can you remind me where the spare keys are kept?**

where the spare keys are kept is passive statement order inside a polite question. are stays after the subject keys. Passives still obey the same subject-before-finite-verb rule.
**E) Can you remind me where are the spare keys kept?**

where are the spare keys… flips are before the subject inside the embed. Repair to where the spare keys are kept. where + subject + are/is is the pattern; where + are + subject is the scar.
highlights: where the spare keys are kept
tasks.solution_overview:
Polite frames such as I'd like to know and Can you remind me feel soft, but they still forbid inversion inside the embedded clause — and they reject an extra dummy it.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Dummy it after which… was is a common repair that actually breaks the clause. Separately, do-support and be-fronting after when/where are direct-question leftovers.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First check whether the which-clause already has a subject (which option…); if it does, add nothing. Then strip the softener and see whether the remaining clause still sounds like a quiz question. If it does, mark false; if it sounds like a statement, mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nobody could say who had locked the gate.
Nobody could say who had the gate been locked by.
We need to establish whether the courier can arrive by noon.
We need to establish whether can the courier arrive by noon.
Tell me how much the tickets will cost.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Nobody could say who had locked the gate.**

who is the subject of had locked, so statement order is natural and correct. Nobody could say… merely frames a subject question. Subject who/what never invert with the verb.
**B) Nobody could say who had the gate been locked by.**

who had the gate been… forces awkward inversion and a stranded by that belongs in a rewritten object question. Prefer who had locked… or the formal by whom the gate had been locked. If the embed starts shoving auxiliaries past the subject just to save a passive, rewrite instead.
**C) We need to establish whether the courier can arrive by noon.**

whether the courier can arrive… keeps modal can after the subject. That is the textbook whether + subject + modal + verb pattern. The outer We need to establish… does not license a yes/no flip inside.
**D) We need to establish whether can the courier arrive by noon.**

whether can the courier… is direct yes/no inversion after whether. Never put the modal before the subject in an embedded clause. Slide can back after courier.
**E) Tell me how much the tickets will cost.**

how much the tickets will cost is statement order after Tell me. will stays after tickets, not before how much. Degree how much/how many phrases behave like other wh-embeds.
highlights: how much the tickets will cost
tasks.solution_overview:
Subject who stays simple; modal whether-clauses and how much-clauses keep the modal after the subject. Awkward passive inversions are a separate red flag.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

who as subject needs no flip and no stranded-by rewrite that drags the auxiliary forward. whether + subject + can… is fine; whether can the… is not. how much… will… similarly refuses will-fronting.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Locate who / whether / how much and check what immediately follows. If a modal or auxiliary has jumped ahead of its subject, reject the item. Prefer the clean subject who + past participle pattern when both active and awkward passive are offered.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tell me how much will the tickets cost.
The note does not say how long the delay lasted.
The note does not say how long did the delay last.
Parents asked what the school intended to do next.
Parents asked what did the school intend to do next.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tell me how much will the tickets cost.**

how much will the tickets cost inverts will and the subject after Tell me. Repair to how much the tickets will cost. The same how much phrase was correct in the previous task with statement order — that contrast is intentional.
**B) The note does not say how long the delay lasted.**

how long the delay lasted keeps statement order after say. lasted is a plain past verb after its subject; no auxiliary is waiting to front. Duration how long-clauses follow the same calm pattern as why-clauses.
**C) The note does not say how long did the delay last.**

how long did the delay last smuggles do-support into the embed. Delete did: how long the delay lasted. If the clause would be a perfect stand-alone question, it is too inverted for this frame.
**D) Parents asked what the school intended to do next.**

what the school intended… is an object-wh clause with subject before verb. school sits before intended; what is the object of intended. After asked, keep what + subject + verb.
**E) Parents asked what did the school intend to do next.**

what did the school intend… is a direct question sitting inside asked. Drop did and keep intended after school. Object what often tempts learners into full question order — resist it in embeds.
highlights: how much will the tickets cost
how long did the delay last
tasks.solution_overview:
how much, how long, and object what-clauses all crash when will or did jumps before the subject. Correct embeds keep the finite verb after the subject noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Tell me / say / asked open the frame; the damage lives inside the subordinate clause. will-fronting after how much and did-support after how long or what are the usual scars.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read from the wh-word to the verb and ask whether anything has skipped ahead of the subject. If will or did appears before the noun that should be the subject, mark false. If the subject sits in its ordinary slot, mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I can't remember where I put my passport.
I can't remember where did I put my passport.
Have you found out whether the museum opens on Mondays?
Have you found out whether does the museum open on Mondays?
She wondered why everyone was whispering.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I can't remember where I put my passport.**

where I put my passport is statement order after remember. I is the subject; put is the past verb — nothing is inverted. Memory verbs still take embedded statement order.
**B) I can't remember where did I put my passport.**

where did I put… is direct-question do-support inside an embedded clause. Repair to where I put…. can't remember does not license a second, inverted question.
**C) Have you found out whether the museum opens on Mondays?**

whether the museum opens… keeps opens after the subject. No does appears, and none is needed. Perfect for a yes/no fact-check after find out.
**D) Have you found out whether does the museum open on Mondays?**

whether does the museum open… invents do-support after whether. Use whether the museum opens…. does belongs in Does the museum open…? as a stand-alone question, not here.
**E) She wondered why everyone was whispering.**

why everyone was whispering keeps was after the subject. wonder why… wants a reason clause, not a flipped be-question. The progressive was whispering stays intact after everyone.
tasks.solution_overview:
Memory, discovery, and wonder verbs — remember, find out, wonder — all embed statement order. Stand-alone question shapes after where or whether do not belong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

did-fronting after where and does-fronting after whether are the scrapes. Correct why / where / whether clauses place the subject before was, opens, or the past verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the matrix verb and judge only the subordinate string. If it still sounds like a quiz (where did I…?, whether does the…?), reject it. If it sounds like a report (where I put…, whether the museum opens…), accept it.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She wondered why was everyone whispering.
Let me know which bus you are taking.
Let me know which bus are you taking.
We still don't know who broke the window.
We still don't know who did break the window.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She wondered why was everyone whispering.**

why was everyone… inverts was before the subject after wondered. Repair to why everyone was whispering. The previous task showed the correct version; this is the scarred twin.
**B) Let me know which bus you are taking.**

which bus you are taking keeps you before are. which + noun + subject + verb is the embedded choice pattern. Let me know simply softens the request; it does not invert the clause.
**C) Let me know which bus are you taking.**

which bus are you taking flips are before you inside the embed. Repair to which bus you are taking. If you can hear Are you taking…? after stripping the frame, the item is false.
**D) We still don't know who broke the window.**

who broke the window is a clean subject question with no do-support. who is the agent; broke is the past verb. Subject who + past verb — no did.
**E) We still don't know who did break the window.**

who did break adds unnecessary emphatic or wrong do to a subject question. Use who broke, not who did break. Emphatic did can appear in speech for contrast, but it is not the neutral embed pattern tested here.
tasks.solution_overview:
This set pairs be-inversion after why with are-fronting after which, then finishes on subject who without fake did.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

why was everyone… and which bus are you… both mark direct-question order. Subject who broke… stays simple: never who did break in this embed.

**Part 2: How to decide.**
